Camera-conditioned models specify viewpoint motion geometrically through camera trajectories [22, 46, 48]. Beyond navigation, online text instructions allow users to request changes in character behavior or scene events during a rollout [68, 52]. Several models support both navigation and text-directed interventions in the same rollout [17, 5]. Zing-0.5 [4] uses separate conditioning streams for keyboard actions and text instructions so that either input can change as generation proceeds. Over longer interactions, spatial memory helps preserve consistency across viewpoints [66, 46, 51]. To improve consistency with game mechanics, StatePlay [37] jointly predicts game state and video. GameDirector [36] separates rule enforcement from rendering, but updates game state using generated observations and guides the video model through prompts. Controllable Rendering instead determines action outcomes by executing commands under the environment’s rules, without inferring state from generated frames. In Zing-1.0, WorldKit executes each command before rendering and the renderer never receives the raw command, so displacement, collisions, and scores are determined by engine state rather than estimated by the video model.

    Agent-based world construction.

    Under Controllable Rendering, the control side must exist before play, and agent-based construction is what makes it cheap to produce. Existing work ranges from producing editable 3D scenes to delivering testable games. WorldClaw [18] plans terrain and object placement from text and refines the resulting scene with editable assets. AutoUE [69] and Code2Games [62] address the additional task of coupling scenes to executable interactions in Unreal Engine: AutoUE generates gameplay code and runs automated playtests, while Code2Games uses compilation and playtesting feedback to revise generated worlds. In the browser-game setting, Game-Creation-Agents [53] verifies implemented mechanics through actual interaction with the generated game. For an engine-driven system, the relevant output of construction is not only a scene but an executable environment whose rules determine how its state changes. It need not include final appearance. In these systems, final appearance still depends on conventional engine assets and rendering, while high-quality character animation, movement, and camera behavior require suitable assets and carefully integrated runtime components. Zing-1.0 asks the agent to build only a proxy world, supplies character, camera, and control as prebuilt assets, and leaves final appearance to the renderer.

    Controllable Rendering systems.

    The systems closest to ours follow Controllable Rendering under other names, including code world models, programmable world models, and code worlds [7, 29, 15, 8]. Each describes the division through its own components: a game engine and a render server [74], simulators and a shared neural renderer [8], or an engine, a coding agent, and a video model [76]. They differ in which responsibilities they specify and in the interface between control and rendering. Executable worlds constrain the layout and motion of generated observations through state-derived inputs, from proxy videos and rendered buffers [7, 29, 35, 41] to object layouts with explicit state attributes [64]. Several interactive systems pair these structural controls with a first-frame image to specify appearance [28, 74], while Wizard [63] also uses skeletal proxies to bind separate character references to their subjects. Streaming renderers use sliding-window bidirectional attention [42] or block-causal generation [8, 76, 14]. To reduce streaming latency, Zing-1.0 uses short autoregressive blocks to limit proxy buffering and caches past keys and values to avoid recomputation. Its renderer conditions on separate scene and subject reference images.

    Differences from prior systems.

    Zing-1.0 differs from these systems in three respects. First, appearance is specified per entity and persists throughout play. Magpie, Code World Model, and Matrix-Game 4.0 anchor appearance to a first frame [74, 7, 76], and AgentGarten uses a single appearance reference [8]. Zing-1.0 assigns separate reference images to the scene and to each subject, so the same executable world can be re-rendered by replacing its references. Second, the renderer is also a general streaming video editor. To our knowledge, prior systems in this line do not report general video-editing benchmarks, whereas we evaluate the Zing-1.0 renderer on OpenVE [21], LongV2VBench [65], and StreamEval [49]. Third, the world that is validated is the world that is executed. A coding agent compiles, previews, and playtests a world before sealing it, the same engine runs the sealed package offline and online, and each proxy frame carries the simulation step that produced it.

    3  Playable World System

    3.1  Principle and System Architecture

    Controllable Rendering separates world-state evolution from observation synthesis. An explicit, executable control process maintains the world state and updates it by executing player commands under the world’s rules, whereas a generative video model synthesizes observations from the resulting state. Two conditions define this separation.

  • •

    C1 (state from execution). Every change of world state results from executing a command under the world’s rules.

  • •

    C2 (rendering from state). The video model is conditioned on the result of execution, not on the command itself.

    • Under C1, rendering errors may affect the player’s decisions but do not directly alter world state, a property also implemented in earlier engine-based systems [74, 8]. Under C2, the outcome and magnitude of an action are determined by execution before rendering, while text and appearance references condition visual synthesis without directly updating world state.

    A Playable World System implements this separation through four responsibilities with explicit interfaces. Table2 specifies their required behavior and realization in Zing-1.0. Between execution and synthesis, a state-to-observation interface derives rendering conditions from updated world state, conveying scene structure, entity states, and interaction outcomes relevant to the player’s view [56, 8]. Although appearance may vary, generated observations must preserve the visible consequences of execution that are relevant to interaction. These responsibilities define functional boundaries without prescribing a particular state representation or requiring separate implementations.

    Figure2 illustrates how Zing-1.0 connects offline world construction to online execution and rendering. During construction, a coding agent uses WorldKit to define, test, and package an executable proxy world. During online play, WorldKit executes player commands under the world’s rules and produces proxy RGB frames from the updated state. The streaming renderer combines these frames with text and appearance references to synthesize the player’s view. The interaction runtime forwards player inputs to execution, coordinates capture, generation, delivery, and playback, and returns the generated video to the browser as feedback for subsequent actions.

    3.2  WorldKit Engine

    WorldKit supports agent-based World Construction and performs World Execution in Zing-1.0. Its design follows three principles.

    Interfaces designed for coding agents.

    WorldKit exposes authoring capabilities through structured interfaces that coding agents can query and inspect. Worlds are TypeScript programs built on Three.js [54] and Rapier [11] for scene graphs and rigid-body physics, allowing agents to use familiar programming patterns. Structured, versioned asset records support asset selection, while authoring tools return compilation diagnostics, preview images, and playtest traces in machine-readable form for behavioral verification and iterative revision.

    Execution in the engine, appearance in the renderer.

    WorldKit maintains entity state, world rules, collision handling, and camera behavior while leaving final appearance to the renderer. Proxy authoring uses simple geometry and restrained, distinguishable colors that remain consistent for each subject during play. Shadows, reflections, detailed materials, and atmosphere are synthesized by the renderer described in Section3.3. This separation reduces the need for photorealistic asset production during world construction without changing the engine-defined rules and interaction outcomes.

    Prebuilt Character, Camera, and Control.

    Coding agents can lay out scenes and implement world rules, but high-quality character animation, movement, and camera behavior require suitable assets and carefully integrated runtime components. These include rigged and skinned models, motion clips that transition smoothly between locomotion states, controllers tuned to each mode of movement, and cameras that follow a subject without being occluded. WorldKit provides these Character, Camera, and Control (3C) capabilities as reusable assets and runtime components, allowing agents to focus on world-specific content and interaction logic.

    Figure3 shows the resulting components. Atlas, our asset library for WorldKit, stores versioned 3C assets. Creator exposes authoring, testing, and packaging tools to coding agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [2] and a JSON command-line interface. The WorldKit Engine executes scene updates, physics, 3C, and world rules during both authoring and online play. The WorldKit CLI loads a sealed world package for an online session.

    3.2.1  Offline Proxy World Authoring

    3C assets.

    Character assets are versioned records that bind a model to its skeleton, motion clips, attachment sockets, and declared capabilities. Clips are referenced through semantic aliases, such as an idle loop or a standing jump, and through a declared skeleton type, so that motion packs can be shared by every subject with a compatible skeleton. For example, version 0.1.8 of the humanoid asset, used for the engine checks in Section5.1, has a 101-joint skeleton and draws its motions from three version-locked motion packs. Control is organized into seven motion families: humanoids, ground vehicles, watercraft, aircraft, flying creatures, underwater subjects, and spacecraft. A controller converts player input into motion intent, and physics and world rules determine the result. Camera provides first-person, third-person, and over-the-shoulder modes, together with named views and scripted shots defined by each world. A follow camera mounted on a spring arm shortens the arm when geometry blocks the line of sight and extends it again once the view is clear.

    Atlas distinguishes automated asset checks from per-version runtime acceptance. Upload checks verify byte integrity, content hashes, and file formats, and detect skeletons and motion clips where possible. Runtime acceptance requires a reviewer to check skeleton compatibility, wheel and seat placement, and controller behavior in the runtime before releasing an asset version for production.

    Authoring workflow.

    Creator supports a structured authoring workflow in which each stage returns feedback that the agent can inspect. The agent first queries the authoring schema and minimal examples, then searches Atlas, inspects candidate assets, and seals an asset plan that pins exact versions and their dependencies. Based on this plan, it defines the scene, entities, cameras, and rules, compiles the program, and validates the world. Verification combines previews from the opening view, from above, and around key objects with playtests that replay scripted player inputs. Playtest traces record positions, actions, animation clips, camera state, and input events at each sampled simulation step, allowing the agent to compare execution with the intended behavior. After validation, submission produces a sealed package containing the executable world, frozen runtime, asset lock, source code, previews, and playtest record.

    3.2.2  Online World Execution

    During online play, WorldKit advances the world at a fixed simulation step of 1/60 s. At each step, the engine processes player input, executes world rules, converts input into motion intent through the active controllers, solves physics with Rapier, updates animation and camera, and publishes the new state. Presentation runs independently of this schedule and samples the latest available state. Captured proxy frames carry the simulation step, world revision, source-frame identifier, and capture time, enabling the Interaction Runtime to associate generated observations with their source world updates.

    The WorldKit CLI loads a sealed package, receives player input, and emits raw RGB proxy frames in one of two output modes, 480p or 720p. Game commands, such as entering a vehicle or picking up an object, are routed to WorldKit through the input channel, whereas text instructions and appearance references are supplied only to the renderer as conditioning inputs. Generated frames are never read back into the engine, so position, collision, and scoring are always determined by WorldKit state.

    3.3  Rendering Side: Streaming Renderer

    The streaming renderer is the rendering side of Zing-1.0 and performs Observation Synthesis. Controllable Rendering sets its task: follow the structure and motion of the proxy, take appearance from references and text, and do both causally as the proxy stream arrives. We describe the model, the data, its training, and the decoder that meet these requirements.

    3.3.1  Model Architecture

    We obtain the Zing-1.0 streaming renderer by post-training MiniMax-H3 (H3) [44], starting from its H3-Base-Ref2VA checkpoint. The renderer comprises a block-causal diffusion transformer (DiT) and a streaming decoder. The DiT generates short video-latent blocks from the proxy stream, appearance references, text, and generated history. Within a fixed-condition segment, text and reference conditions are shared across blocks, while each new proxy block supplies updated scene structure and motion. The decoder emits RGB frames from each completed latent without waiting to decode the entire block. Figure4 traces this path from input encoding to RGB output.

    Rendering formulation.

    Let c be the instruction, r the appearance references, sₖ the encoded proxy for block k, and xₖ the corresponding target video latents. Within a fixed-condition segment, we model

    p_θ(x_1:K|c,r,s_1:K)=∏ₖ₌₁^Kp_θ(xₖ|c,r,s_≤k,x_

    		(1)

    Text specifies the rendering goal and links references to elements in the proxy. References provide scene and subject appearance independently of the proxy pose. The proxy specifies layout, camera motion, and visible object motion. No player command appears in this factorization: the renderer observes an action only through its executed result sₖ, which is condition C2 of Section3.1.

    Conditioning representations.

    The renderer combines static conditioning from the instruction and appearance references with dynamic conditioning from live proxy video. As in the original H3, Qwen jointly encodes the instruction c and appearance references r into semantic context, while the visual VAE preserves the appearance details of r in reference latents. Together, these representations form the static prefix C for each fixed-condition segment, and both encoders remain frozen in Zing-1.0. Qwen derives its visual context only from reference frames, without access to future proxy or target frames. For dynamic conditioning, Zing-1.0 adds a live proxy input, using the same visual VAE to encode each incoming proxy block as sₖ in Equation (1). To align sₖ with the corresponding target block xₖ, the two streams share block boundaries and temporal coordinates in H3’s multimodal rotary position embedding (MM-RoPE), while separate spatial grids support different proxy and target resolutions.

    The original H3 DiT uses one video branch of adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) for Qwen visual features and the visual latents of the references and target. With the addition of the live proxy, the renderer processes three types of visual tokens in the same sequence: (i) reference and target latents that encode the intended appearance and the video being generated, respectively; (ii) Qwen visual features that help interpret the references in the context of the instruction; and (iii) proxy latents that specify the layout and motion of the current block. As shown in Figure4, each layer retains H3’s video AdaLN for reference and target latents and uses its weights to initialize separate branches for Qwen visual features and proxy latents. Qwen text retains its original branch. The token role and timestep determine the scale, shift, and gate for each sublayer, while the attention and feed-forward weights are shared across token roles.

    Block-causal streaming.

    To implement Equation (1), the DiT arranges its inputs in the sequence shown in Figure4. After the static prefix C, each proxy block Sₖ precedes its aligned target block Xₖ. Attention is full within a block and causal across blocks. Training and inference share this rule but differ in how they obtain the target history.

    Training. Clean targets Xⱼ are available from the training video, so we can use parallel teacher forcing to predict multiple blocks without generating their history sequentially. As shown in Figure5(a), each noisy target query X̃ₖ attends only to itself, the static prefix C, and the visible blocks among the proxies S_≤k and clean targets X_

    Inference. No clean targets are supplied during inference, so the DiT must generate X_Figure5(b). After the final denoising step, the DiT runs another forward pass on the clean block Xₖ and caches the resulting K/V for generating subsequent blocks.

    In-play prompt updates.

    The cached K/V for generated history depend on the conditioning prefix C. When an in-play event prompt updates the conditioning at a block boundary, the renderer retains recent generated latents as a visual prefix P and recomputes their K/V under the updated conditioning prefix C^′. Subsequent blocks are generated using the refreshed cache and the incoming proxy stream. To train the model to continue from a visual prefix, autoregressive (AR) adaptation keeps an observed target prefix fixed and computes the loss only on the remaining target latents.

    3.3.2  Training Data

    To synthesize coherent video that follows the proxy’s structure and motion while matching the specified appearance, we train the renderer with four complementary forms of supervision. General generation data supports the model’s visual and motion capabilities, paired editing data teaches it to transform a source while retaining content outside the requested edit, and reference-conditioned examples teach it to use images as appearance controls. Training examples for proxy-based rendering combine these forms of supervision under the input conditions used during play. Figure6 illustrates selected examples of the data design.

    General generation.

    To preserve the general generation capabilities of the base MiniMax-H3 model during adaptation to proxy-conditioned rendering, we include image and video generation data covering a range of appearances, compositions, and motion. The image mixture includes quality-filtered images, game artwork, synthetic examples for text rendering and facial detail, and images synthesized using compositions from selected open-source examples. Video sources include open-source footage, film and television, game cinematics, and sports clips that cover large and rapid motion. The mixture includes text-conditioned audiovisual and image-conditioned video generation. Selected single-shot clips retain audio, and multi-shot clips are segmented using audio and subtitles to reduce cuts in speech and other continuous audio.

    Paired editing.

    Paired editing examples consist of a source image or video, an edit instruction, and the corresponding target. The target provides supervision both for applying the requested change and for preserving source content outside the edit. We filter open-source image and video editing examples for visual quality and edit correctness, and reannotate video editing examples in the MiniMax-H3 format.

    Reference conditioning.

    Reference-conditioned generation and editing data provide supervision for reproducing scene or subject appearance from one or more reference images. In editing, text identifies the element to modify, the reference specifies its appearance, and the source constrains what remains unchanged. Some image and video pairs provide three views of the same subject (Figure6(c)), supplying appearance cues across viewpoints without fixing the output pose or position.

    Proxy-based rendering.

    Proxy–target pairs combine the preceding forms of supervision to align training with the rendering task during play. The goal is coherent video that follows proxy structure and motion while matching the specified appearance. We construct proxy–target pairs from game imagery, film and television, gameplay recordings, and targeted animal and vehicle footage. For images, we abstract appearance while retaining composition and use the original image as the target. For video, the proxy and target are aligned in time (Figure6(d)) to supervise the preservation of camera and subject motion and the timing of occlusions and visibility changes. Some pairs use proxy video produced by WorldKit, matching the type of input used during play. Proxy inputs range from coarse masses through structural blockouts to detailed clay representations (Figure7).

    3.3.3  Training and Distillation

    To support low-latency streaming during play, we train a block-causal generator that produces each video block in a few denoising steps. Starting from the same H3 checkpoint, training proceeds through AR adaptation, ODE endpoint initialization, and distribution matching distillation (DMD). Figure8 summarizes these DiT training stages and the separate adaptation of the decoder to process one latent frame at a time.

    Autoregressive adaptation.

    This stage adapts the DiT to generate one target block at a time during inference. Training and inference use the same block layout, alternating between full blocks of three and two latent frames (3,2,3,2,…) to align each block pair with one five-latent temporal cycle of the original H3. The flow-matching objective [38] follows H3’s convention that the velocity points from noise toward data. Given clean latents x₀, Gaussian noise ε, and noise fraction σ, the noisy latents, velocity target, and basic regression objective are

    x_σ=(1-σ)x₀+σε, u^⋆=x₀-ε, L_FM=𝔼 [\lVertû_θ-u^⋆\rVert₂²].

    		(2)

    Here û_θ is the velocity prediction used for regression. The model timestep is t=1-σ, with t=1 denoting clean media. Different target blocks are trained at independently sampled noise levels. The flow regression loss is computed only on noisy target queries, as shown in Figure5(a).

  • Guidance-aware adaptation. The released H3 checkpoint [44] is CFG-distilled, so we use inverse classifier-free guidance (CFG) [24] regression, related to the H3 guidance loss in Musubi Tuner [45], to retain the learned guidance during autoregressive adaptation. As shown in Figure9(a), the conditional branch uses all inputs, while the unconditional branch replaces only the Qwen context with a blank-prompt embedding. For the conditional prediction p_θ and unconditional prediction n_θ, inverse CFG gives the corrected velocity

    û_θ=(p_θ+(s-1)sg(n_θ))/(s),

    		(3)

    where s is the guidance scale and sg denotes stop-gradient. We regress û_θ against the flow-matching target u^⋆ in Equation (2).

  • Resampling forcing. Teacher forcing uses ground-truth history, whereas at inference the model conditions on its own past predictions. Resampling Forcing (RF) [19] adds noise to selected ground-truth history blocks, then uses the current model without gradient tracking to denoise each block in one step, with earlier blocks resampled in the same rollout as history (Figure8(a)). This exposes the model to its own prediction errors without requiring a full denoising schedule for each history block.

    • ODE endpoint initialization.

    After autoregressive adaptation, the model still relies on many-step sampling to generate each block. Reducing this to a few steps requires larger updates, over which the velocity can change along the denoising trajectory. Flow matching supervises the instantaneous velocity at each sampled noise level rather than the total change over an interval, so extrapolating a single prediction over a large interval can produce an inaccurate endpoint.

    Following the mid-training principle of CMT [25], we train the student to predict the clean endpoint of a frozen causal AR teacher’s multi-step denoising trajectory directly from an intermediate state, with both models conditioned on the same ground-truth history. In addition, we apply an auxiliary reconstruction loss with the original clean video latents as targets to avoid relying solely on teacher-generated endpoints.

    Distribution matching distillation.

    After ODE endpoint initialization, the student is trained with distribution matching distillation (DMD) [70, 71] to improve the quality of few-step generation by matching the output distribution of a frozen multi-step teacher. A frozen real scorer and a separately trained fake scorer estimate the scores of the teacher and student distributions, respectively. Following Self Forcing [27], we generate samples via autoregressive self-rollout of the current student and use them to train the fake scorer with flow matching.

  • Decoupled DMD. In practice, DMD often applies CFG to the teacher score but not to the student score, combining distribution matching and guidance in a single update. Decoupled DMD [40] decomposes this update into distribution matching (DM) and CFG augmentation (CA); we evaluate the two terms at independently sampled noise levels. For each term, the teacher’s conditional score is recovered from the real scorer’s guided and blank-context predictions using the inverse CFG transformation in Equation (3). DM aligns the student and teacher distributions by comparing their conditional scores, whereas CA strengthens adherence to the conditioning inputs by comparing the teacher’s conditional and blank-context scores.

  • Data-Forcing Distillation. To preserve sample diversity and mitigate oversaturation during few-step distillation, we apply Data-Forcing Distillation [6] to a subset of samples by evaluating the real scorer on noised ground-truth latents instead of noised student outputs.

  • Self Gradient Forcing. When historical K/V is detached during self-rollout training, gradients from later blocks cannot reach the computation that encodes earlier blocks into the cache. Self Gradient Forcing [80] restores this gradient path with a two-pass procedure (Figure9(b)). First, an autoregressive rollout without gradient tracking records each block’s noisy input, timestep, and clean prediction at the selected denoising step. Second, a packed causal replay recomputes the predictions and history K/V, treating the generated history latents as fixed inputs. DMD gradients computed on the original rollout predictions are then backpropagated through the replay.

    • 3.3.4  Streaming Decoder

    Jointly decoding a DiT block preserves temporal context but postpones the first RGB output until the block has been decoded. Decoding each latent independently allows earlier output but discards the history needed for coherent transitions. To reduce first-frame latency without discarding temporal context, we adapt the pretrained lightweight H3 VAE decoder from LynnReal-Omni [43] for causal decoding. The adapted decoder emits RGB frames one latent at a time using the current latent and cached history.

    Phase embedding.

    The number of RGB frames emitted per decoding step depends on the latent’s position in H3’s temporal cycle. Each cycle maps five latents to 17 RGB frames in the pattern 1,4,4,4,4, as shown in Figure10(b). The phase aⱼ=j\bmod5 uses the zero-based latent index j across the full stream, rather than an index reset for each DiT block. A learned phase embedding conditions the decoder on aⱼ to account for this periodic pattern in RGB frame counts.

    Causal decoding with bounded history.

    As in the original H3 VAE decoder, decoding uses overlapping spatial tiles whose outputs are blended to form full frames. Within each tile, the decoder attends to all positions in the current latent and to the cached K/V qⱼ₋₁ from a fixed window of preceding latents. Each step of our causal decoder D_φ processes a single latent zⱼ, emits RGB frames Yⱼ according to the output phase aⱼ, and updates the cache to qⱼ (Figure10(a)):

    (Yⱼ,qⱼ)=D_φ(zⱼ,qⱼ₋₁,aⱼ).

    		(4)

    Decoder training.

    As shown in Figure8(b), the decoder is trained separately from the DiT to reconstruct the original RGB frames from latents produced by the frozen H3 encoder. To process latent steps in parallel during training, we use a causal attention mask that reproduces the history window used at inference and prevents attention across samples and spatial tiles. For a clip of T frames, the training objective combines a Charbonnier loss [3] for RGB reconstruction with temporal difference matching:

    L_dec=1/N[∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ∥√(ŷₜ-yₜ)²+ε²∥₁+λₜₑₘₚ∑ₜ₌₂ᵀ∥(ŷₜ-ŷₜ₋₁)-(yₜ-yₜ₋₁)∥₁].

    		(5)

    Here ŷₜ and yₜ are the predicted and target RGB frames, respectively, and N is the total number of RGB values in the clip. The parameter ε>0 is the Charbonnier smoothing constant, and λₜₑₘₚ is the coefficient of the temporal difference loss.

    4  Interaction Infrastructure

    The Interaction Runtime integrates the streaming renderer in Section3.3 with world execution and output delivery to provide timely visual feedback as the world advances and rendering conditions change. Within this runtime, Zing-1.0 builds its model inference infrastructure on SGLang [79] and optimizes generation and condition updates for low-latency streaming.

    4.1  Streaming Runtime

    World execution, video generation, and delivery need not advance in lockstep. The streaming runtime coordinates these stages by bounding queued work and tracking the proxy frames and rendering conditions used to generate each output batch.

    Source admission and flow control.

    As described in Section3.2.2, WorldKit executes gameplay commands and supplies proxy frames sampled from the evolving world state. Text and reference updates reach the renderer as separate conditions. The rendering service accepts ordered batches of RGB proxy frames under a credit-based protocol that limits the number of outstanding frames and bytes. Receipt acknowledgements confirm acceptance of submitted frames, but only consumption acknowledgements restore the corresponding credits. This limits input buildup when proxy frames arrive faster than the renderer can process them.

    Pipelined generation and session state.

    While the DiT generates the current target block, the Encoder prepares inputs for subsequent blocks and the streaming Decoder converts completed latents into RGB frames. Bounded buffers limit queued work between stages. The evaluated serving group admits one active session at a time. Within a session, window attention and designated sink blocks bound the retained history. A preallocated KV pool holds the conditioning prefix, retained window, and temporary working rows. The pool is updated in place, and fixed-address metadata supports CUDA Graph replay as the window advances. Condition-encoding and Block0 caches reuse initial computations when inputs and model configuration match. Stage overlap improves sustained throughput. The joint execution scheme in Section4.2 further reduces backbone work per block, while the sparse attention and compressed KV techniques in Section4.3 reduce the cost of reading and storing history.

    Output delivery and provenance.

    Session and generation identifiers distinguish streams, and each output batch identifies its aligned proxy frame spans and the condition event used to generate it. The proxy frame tags relate those spans to the sampled world updates. Generating frames under an updated condition requires the state refresh described in Section4.4, so acknowledging the update is distinct from delivering those frames. Decoded RGB frames are published at the serving gateway, and the resulting video stream is delivered to the browser for playback.

    4.2  Cross-Block Joint Execution

    As described in Section3.3.1, an additional DiT forward pass computes the K/V of the clean target block Xₖ₋₁ after denoising. The decoder consumes the clean latents directly, so this pass can be deferred without delaying decoding. Once the next proxy block Sₖ is available, a single DiT forward computes the K/V for Xₖ₋₁, processes Sₖ, and performs the first denoising step on X̃ₖ. The joint forward batches the three branches for backbone projections and feed-forward layers while retaining branch-specific modulation and attention visibility.

    The joint forward preserves the causal dependencies among these branches. The previous clean target does not attend to the current block, and the current proxy does not attend to the noisy target. The noisy target can attend to both, but its K/V are not retained as history. With two denoising steps, a baseline that already combines proxy processing with the first step still needs separate passes for the second step and the clean target. Cross-block joint execution reduces the steady-state schedule from three to two DiT forwards per eligible block without changing the number of denoising steps. Stream boundaries are handled separately, and the runtime falls back to separate passes when joint execution is not applicable.

    4.3  Frame-Aligned Sparse Attention and Compressed KV

    Joint execution in Section4.2 reduces the number of DiT calls without changing the context visible to each denoising step. Even with the bounded window in Section4.1, the retained history occupies GPU memory and is read repeatedly during denoising. We compress the keys and values when they enter the cache and use the same cached representation to attend to different parts of the history at different resolutions.

    Frame-aligned KV compression.

    We partition each latent frame into near-square spatial tiles of at most 64 tokens. Keeping a tile within one frame ensures that its tokens share a temporal RoPE position, and keeping it spatially compact limits the variation a pooled summary must represent. Within each tile, the pooling layout groups tokens into four spatial quadrants on a 2×2 grid. When writing a tile to the cache, we store its key and value means in BF16 and quantize the centered token-level residuals to FP8. Subtracting the mean allows the residual quantizer to represent differences among tokens without allocating range to their shared offset. We also store FP8 means for the tile and for each quadrant, together with quantization scales and routing statistics, so these quantities can be reused across denoising steps.

    For a tile before any window-induced position shift, its unscaled token-level attention logit is approximated by

    ⟨qᵢ,k_m,j⟩≈⟨qᵢ,k̄ₘ⟩+s_qs_k,m⟨qᵢ^FP8,Δk_m,j^FP8⟩,

    		(6)

    where qᵢ is the query at token i, k_m,j is the key at token j in tile m, and k̄ₘ is the stored BF16 key mean. The FP8 query and key residual have scales s_q and s_k,m, respectively. For a given query, the first term is shared by every token in the tile, while the second recovers token-specific differences. Values use the same mean–residual representation with their own scale.

    Query-adaptive three-tier attention.

    We retain all visible tokens in the current block and apply three-tier routing only to eligible historical tiles. For the retained history, Refine reads the token-level representation, Skim uses four quadrant means, and Skip uses the whole-tile mean. The router uses both the relevance of a tile to the current query and the spatial distribution of its key variance. A tile whose variation lies mainly between quadrants can retain that structure through four means, whereas substantial variation within quadrants makes token-level attention more useful.

    For each query tile and attention head, let H contain all history tiles eligible for routing, and let ℂ be the relevance-ranked list of candidates drawn from H. The router combines relevance and cached tile statistics into a base utility and weights it by the variance distribution to obtain the promotion utilities uₘ^refine and uₘˢᵏⁱᵐ for candidate m. In the budget-anchored routing mode, it derives a shared price π^* from the order statistic of the base utilities at the Refine quota and the relative cost c_rf of token-level attention. The price sets the two promotion thresholds τ_rf and τₛₖ. Given these thresholds and quotas B_rf and Bₛₖ, the router selects Refine first and Skim second, assigning all remaining eligible tiles to Skip:

    T_refine=First_B_rf({m∈ℂ:uₘ^refine>τ_rf}),(7)
    Tₛₖᵢₘ=First_Bₛₖ({m∈ℂ∖T_refine:uₘˢᵏⁱᵐ>τₛₖ}),
    Tₛₖᵢₚ=H∖(T_refine∪Tₛₖᵢₘ).

    Here First_B keeps at most B qualifying tiles in candidate order. The default serving budget is 16% Refine, 32% Skim, and 52% Skip, with c_rf=12. The Skip set is taken over H, so tiles outside the candidate list still contribute to attention through their means. This reduces the number of keys and values evaluated without dropping eligible history tiles. The logits for pooled summaries include a log-cardinality correction for the number of represented tokens, with an additional variance correction for Skip. The kernel packs summaries from multiple history tiles into aligned compute tiles and evaluates all three tiers in one online-softmax pass.

    Sliding-window RoPE updates.

    As the window advances, retained tiles can shift to new logical temporal positions. For the residual term in Equation (6), forward rotation of a key residual is equivalent to inverse rotation of the query in the dot product before quantization. Applying the relative shift on the query side lets the runtime reuse the cached FP8 key residuals. It does not need a separate unrotated copy of the token-level keys or repeated dequantization, rotation, and requantization of the residuals.

    4.4  Low-Latency Condition Updates

    An in-play update to the prompt or reference media changes the conditioning for subsequent blocks. The renderer retains recent generated latents but rebuilds their DiT K/V under the updated condition before generation resumes. To reduce the cost of an update, we reuse Qwen prefix computations when possible and combine the DiT cache rebuild with the first denoising step under the new condition.

    Incremental Qwen conditioning.

    Within each session, we cache Qwen attention K/V and output features. For a text update with unchanged reference media, token IDs and multimodal position IDs identify the longest common prefix, so Qwen encodes only the portion after that prefix. The suffix queries attend to the cached prefix K/V, and the resulting features are concatenated with the cached prefix features. This supports appended events and edits to existing descriptions. A change to the reference media invalidates the Qwen prefix cache and requires a full Qwen encoding pass.

    Joint state rebuilding.

    We extend the joint execution in Section4.2 to evaluate the conditioning prefix, recent clean target history, current source, and first target denoising step in one forward pass. The same branch-specific attention, modulation, and commit ordering preserve serial dependencies. If the DiT prefix K/V for the updated condition are already cached, the runtime reuses them instead of recomputing the prefix in the joint forward. The stream then continues under the updated condition.

    5  Results

    We assess reproducible world execution and agent-based world construction in Section5.1, video editing and controllable world rendering in Section5.2, and the inference infrastructure’s streaming throughput, latency, and memory efficiency in Section5.3.

    5.1  Engine Capabilities

    Controllable Rendering places two demands on the control side. It must decide every outcome by executing commands under the world’s rules (C1), so that the outcome and magnitude of an action are fixed before rendering begins. It must also be inexpensive to build, so that a coding agent can produce a new executable world for each form of play. We first examine execution in offline proxy worlds, reading WorldKit state at each 60 Hz simulation step without the renderer. We then follow a coding agent through a complete authoring session, and finally examine gameplay execution in an agent-authored world.

    5.1.1  Rule Execution and Prebuilt 3C

    WorldKit’s prebuilt 3C supplies reusable assets and controllers for the interactions and locomotion in Figure11 (Section3.2.1). Object pickup, carrying, and placement establish and release an attachment between the object and character (Figure11(a)), while mounting and dismounting establish and clear the rider relationship (Figure11(b)). Vehicle driving and fixed-wing flight in Figure11(c) illustrate continuous motion governed by subject-specific controllers and engine physics. In separate humanoid and vehicle tests, fixed inputs lasting 0.5, 1, and 2 s were each repeated five times from identical initial states, producing matching displacements and headings up to floating-point round-off. Environment geometry constrains this motion, as illustrated by the humanoid stopped at a wall under continued forward input in the left image of Figure11(c). A 90-step collision check recorded no collision-capsule penetration and less than 10⁻⁵ m of position variation after contact. Together, these interaction sequences and motion checks illustrate the extensible interactions and geometric motion control compared in Table1. Changes in pose, attachment, and control are determined by the engine from world state, rules, and controllers rather than inferred by the video model.

    The camera is the last part of the observation that the engine fixes before rendering. The three prebuilt camera modes observe the same subject from different viewpoints (Figure12(a)). Switching among them at one simulation step left every entity pose unchanged, so the choice of view changes what is observed but not what happens. The follow camera keeps an explicit arm length in the engine state. When a wall enters its line of sight, the engine shortens the arm so that the subject stays visible, and it extends the arm again once the view is clear (Figure12(b)). The renderer therefore receives a proxy view in which viewpoint and occlusion have already been resolved, as C2 requires.

    5.1.2  Authoring by a Coding Agent

    Using WorldKit’s prebuilt components and Creator tools, a coding agent constructed a small executable collection course from a one-paragraph task description. It selected and pinned assets, assembled the scene, and compiled the world. During construction, Creator returned structured feedback on an invalid asset-search response and an unresolved asset definition. The agent used these diagnostics to retry the search and correct the asset-loading configuration without manual intervention (Figure13(a)). After compilation, it inspected Creator previews of the scene (Figure13(b)) and ran a playtest that replayed player-input events. The recorded trajectory reached all eight target regions (Figure13(c)), showing that the planned locations were reachable through the world’s controls. The final submission passed technical verification and produced a sealed package containing the executable world, previews, and playtest record.

    5.1.3  Executing Playable Worlds

    The harvest race in Figure14 illustrates how an agent-authored world combines reusable controls with persistent spatial state and executable game rules.

    The player and an AI-controlled opponent operate combine harvesters in the same wheat field, competing to harvest the larger area within 30 s. Given a short task description, the coding agent assembled a combine harvester from custom geometry and WorldKit’s wheeled-vehicle drive because Atlas contained no such asset. Both drivers reuse the same humanoid asset and version-locked motion packs. The world overview and player-view proxy in Figure14(d–e) show the resulting world at scene-wide and local scales.

    WorldKit derives each vehicle’s cutting footprint from its pose at every simulation step and identifies the cell centers it covers. A cell contributes to the vehicle’s harvested area only if it was previously uncut, after which its harvested state persists. The update in Figure14(a–c) illustrates how new coverage changes this state without crediting already harvested cells again. Vehicle motion, the shared harvest state, and cumulative areas are therefore updated by the same executable world rules.

    When the 30 s time limit expires, the accumulated areas are fixed. In a complete standard round, WorldKit computed final areas of 291 m2 for the player and 187 m2 for the AI opponent. These totals provide the endpoints of Figure14(f). The example combines continuous vehicle control, persistent spatial state, and competitive scoring within one agent-authored world. More generally, the same construction and execution interfaces enable agents to build diverse worlds with explicitly defined rules and interaction mechanics, providing a reusable foundation for playable environments.

    5.2  Renderer Capabilities

    Fixed-instruction and continuous-editing benchmarks quantitatively assess instruction following, reference adherence, content preservation, visual quality, and temporal stability. Qualitative examples of controllable world rendering illustrate reference-conditioned appearance variation, sustained rendering across scene transitions, and interaction outcomes retained across revisits.

    5.2.1  Fixed-Instruction Video Editing

    Evaluation setup.

    All editing benchmark evaluations use 480p source-aligned rendering with two sink blocks in a nine-block attention window. We evaluate 308 short videos from OpenVE-Bench [21] under the five-category protocol used by JoyAI-Video-Edit [65]. We also evaluate LongV2VBench, introduced by the same work, which comprises 229 editing tasks on approximately one-minute videos. The instruction is fixed throughout each video. We follow the published scoring rubrics with Gemini 2.5 Pro and compute overall scores by macro-averaging the five categories.

    Zing-1.0 achieves overall scores of 3.90 on OpenVE and 3.44 on LongV2VBench, outperforming all listed streaming editors on both benchmarks (Table3). JoyAI-Video-Edit, the strongest streaming baseline in this comparison, scores 3.60 and 3.30, respectively.

    Style and local appearance changes are particularly effective, with scores above 4.0 on both benchmarks (Table4). Background editing also improves over JoyAI-Video-Edit in both settings. These results support control over the visual style, subject appearance, and surroundings of an evolving scene. Object addition and removal remain more challenging on LongV2VBench, leaving room to improve persistent changes to scene content.

    5.2.2  Continuous Editing in Streaming Sessions

    Evaluation setup.

    We evaluate all 60 cases in each of the two editing tracks of StreamEval [49]: Instruction Editing and Reference Editing. Successive requests require the system to add, replace, or selectively cancel edits while preserving those that remain active. The evaluated system combines the renderer with the online multimodal model that rewrites instructions and updates reference conditions.

    We average three runs per case, then cases within each duration tier, and weight the five tiers equally (15, 30, 60, 120, and 300 seconds). Overall is the mean of the five metrics on a 0–100 scale. Edit Success assesses complete fulfillment of the requested change, while Preservation assesses retention of protected source content. Baseline scores are taken from the official leaderboard [50].

    The combined system obtains provisional overall lower bounds of 57.86 and 54.06 on the two tracks, exceeding the published baselines in Table5.

    For instruction-driven editing, the principal gain is a more stable output stream during successive updates. Zing-1.0 reaches a Stability score of 47.80, compared with 13.94 for Vidu S2 Editing, while maintaining comparable Edit Success. This improvement is accompanied by higher visual quality, showing that effective instruction execution can be combined with cleaner, more stable rendering during continuous interaction.

    For reference-driven editing, Zing-1.0 more reliably adopts the requested appearance and completes the transformation. Reference and Edit Success scores reach 70.19 and 51.22, compared with 31.20 and 15.00 for Vidu S2 Editing. Together with the highest Preservation score among the compared systems, these results support reference-conditioned appearance updates that retain protected source content. Visual refinement remains an opportunity, with Vidu scoring higher in Quality and Stability on this track.

    The recorded sequence in Figure15 illustrates selective control over accumulated edits. Later requests revise selected appearance attributes while preserving earlier edits that remain active, allowing users to compose and partially cancel changes within the same ongoing session.

    5.2.3  Controllable World Rendering

    Reference-conditioned appearance and proxy-guided dynamics.

    Figure16 shows renderings of a shared Shanghai proxy sequence conditioned on scene and vehicle references in summer-anime, Chinese-inspired, and felt styles. The opening shot presents the city skyline with distinct materials, lighting, and architectural treatments of the same layout across the three styles. The sequence then cuts to a third-person driving view, where aligned proxy and rendered frames show propulsion, camera rotation, airborne travel, and particle effects. The renderer produces distinct vehicle designs, building appearances, and dynamic effects for each reference style while following the viewpoint and motion supplied by the proxy. These examples illustrate appearance variation and dynamic rendering without introducing action-specific control channels to the renderer.

    World traversal and persistent interaction state.

    Figure17 presents two exploration sequences. Broom flight in panel (a) follows a broom rider from the stadium, beneath a stone bridge, and through the first portal into a shop street. After passing a train and traversing the great hall, corridor, stairwell, and library, the broom rider enters the final portal and returns to the stadium. This sequence illustrates sustained rendering through successive scene transitions. Museum exploration in panel (b) shows a cat pressing a button to lower the hall barrier and switch on the overhead light. The cat traverses the galleries and crypt, then steps on a pressure plate to open the return doors. On return, the barrier remains lowered and the light remains on, accounting for the brighter final view. This round trip illustrates state-controlled interactions and the persistence of their visible effects across revisits.

    5.3  Inference Efficiency and Streaming Performance

    We evaluate four 832×480 serving workloads on one H200 (140 GB) for the DiT and two H100s, one each for encoding and decoding. The proxy input is configured at 24 FPS. In steady state, the DiT alternates between target blocks of three and two latents and uses two denoising steps per block (σ∈{1.0,0.5}). Each comparison holds hardware, parallel layout, inputs, and the denoising schedule fixed. The serving results are from a warmed run. Session timing runs from request arrival to decoded RGB publication at the serving gateway and excludes subsequent transport and browser presentation.

    Streaming throughput and latency.

    Table6 measures how the optimizations affect serving performance. Starting from Dense BF16, Dense FP8 adds W8A8 projections in the attention and feed-forward layers and enables fused quantization, while retaining the BF16 token refiner, dense FlashAttention, and an uncompressed KV pool. The full stack then adds three-tier attention and compressed KV. All configurations share offline AdaLN preparation, 50-layer CUDA Graph replay, and the fused decoder.

    In the representative short-sequence workload (Scenario 1), post-TTFF throughput rises from 18.88 to 23.15 FPS with W8A8 and fused quantization and then to 23.82 FPS with the full stack, a 26% improvement over Dense BF16. Warmed time to first frame (TTFF) falls from 1.39 to 0.70 seconds. The full stack also improves throughput over Dense BF16 across the longer and condition-changing workloads, reaching 20.40 FPS in the longest session compared with 16.09 FPS for Dense BF16.

    Output fidelity relative to Dense BF16.

    We compare generated streams with Dense BF16 using the same seeds and denoising schedule. Table6 reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [77] as measures of agreement with that reference. The full stack improves PSNR over Dense FP8 in three of the four workloads, including gains of 1.19 dB in the short sequence and 1.67 dB in the longest session. The table presents the per-workload fidelity results alongside throughput and memory.

    Attention efficiency and KV footprint.

    Table7 evaluates attention kernels and resident KV storage on H100 GPUs (80 GB) at 832×480 and 1280×736. The query/KV lengths are (780,9,360) and (1,840,22,080). The three-tier configuration assigns 22/44/88 and 48/96/186 historical tiles to Refine/Skim/Skip at the two resolutions, respectively, while keeping the current block at token granularity.

    Frame-aligned three-tier attention achieves approximately 2.8× kernel speedup over Dense BF16 at both resolutions, while compressed KV reduces the resident pool by approximately 63%. Both FP8 configurations share the same compressed pool; evaluating selected history tiles at coarser resolutions provides a further 3.31× and 3.24× kernel speedup over token-level FP8 attention at the two resolutions. Attention output cosine similarity remains above 0.9998 for the tested inputs. In the serving workloads, compressed KV reduces the reported pool from 64.80 to 24.08 GiB across all four scenarios.

    6  Discussion and Limitations

    Controllable Rendering makes world-state updates independent of generated video. Several design challenges remain in building playable world systems around this separation. Addressing them will be important for extending this approach to more diverse worlds and forms of play.

    Long-horizon rendering fidelity.

    The streaming renderer conditions each block on the current proxy and recent generated history. A deviation in an earlier block can make these signals conflict, with the history favoring continuity with the generated layout or trajectory and the proxy specifying a different one. The model can then struggle to determine which signal to follow when generating the next block. Continuing from the erroneous history can compound the deviation and degrade visual quality over long rollouts, while an abrupt correction toward the proxy can disrupt temporal continuity.

    The division of responsibilities between the engine and the renderer.

    Authority over world state does not determine how much of the player’s view the engine should prescribe. For locomotion, the engine could supply a trajectory and leave the gait to the renderer, or specify additional details such as body pose and foot contacts. Similarly, a new object could be introduced into the executable world or appear only in the rendered scene. These choices become consequential when a footstep triggers a mechanism or a player expects to pick up a rendered object. Determining where to draw this boundary for different forms of play remains a central design question.

    Richer conditioning interfaces.

    Once the system determines which execution details the renderer must preserve, it still needs to decide how to convey those details to the renderer. Depth and semantic maps could supplement RGB proxy video, while entity identifiers and event signals could make particular objects and interactions explicit. Image references could be combined in different ways, such as pairing a scene reference with multiple views of a subject or assigning separate references to several entities. Beyond still images, other reference formats such as video clips could convey changes in appearance over time. Combining these inputs requires maintaining their correspondence to the relevant entities and world updates.

    World construction and gameplay experience.

    A central challenge is to broaden the range of executable worlds that coding agents can build while reducing the time needed to author and validate them. Meeting both goals places greater demands on the agent harness and its supporting component libraries. The libraries need to offer a wider range of reusable interactions, such as driving, climbing, and object manipulation, while the harness needs to help agents discover these components, combine them with rules and objectives to create distinct forms of play, and playtest the resulting worlds. Overlays for inventory, progress, and scores could further improve the player experience by presenting engine state alongside the generated view.

    Interaction latency.

    Further reducing the time from proxy input to rendered output is important for playability. Latency can determine whether timing-sensitive interactions and game mechanics are viable in practice. Rendering, however, accounts for only part of the delay between a player input and the first displayed frame that shows its effect. World execution, proxy capture, transport, and display also contribute. Shortening the full path while preserving visual quality and the correspondence between displayed frames and world updates remains an end-to-end systems challenge.

    7  Conclusion

    We presented Zing-1.0, a Playable World System built on Controllable Rendering. Its design follows a clear division of responsibilities: determinism comes from control, and imagination comes from generation. We formalized this division with an explicit criterion and specified four responsibilities and their interfaces. For World Construction, a coding agent authored an executable world with WorldKit. During World Execution, the engine applied the rules, computed all scores from its state, and supplied live proxy video throughout a full round of play. The renderer used that stream for Observation Synthesis, and the Interaction Runtime delivered the synthesized view to the player. In benchmark comparisons, the renderer leads the streaming editors evaluated on OpenVE and LongV2VBench, while the full editing system outperforms the reported baselines on both StreamEval editing tracks. Pipelined serving and DiT inference optimizations enable Zing-1.0 to sustain 23.82 FPS at 832×480 in steady state, using a three-GPU deployment comprising a single H200 for the DiT and one H100 each for the encoding and decoding services.

    Contributions and Acknowledgments

    Zing-1.0 was developed by the SeedLeap.ai team. We thank the MiniMax-H3 team, the authors of the training and distillation methods used in this work, and the SGLang, OpenVE-Bench, LongV2VBench, and StreamEval teams for making their research and implementations available.

    We are especially grateful to Loopit’s engineering, product, and operations teams for their substantial support in preparing and launching Zing-1.0, including improving the user experience, showcasing model capabilities, and selecting demos.

    Contributors

    Contributors are listed in reverse alphabetical order by surname, not in order of contribution.

    Wenbo Zhang, Guoli Zhang, Xuewen Yu, Xueliang Yang, Jiangqiao Yan, Teng Xia, Xinmiao Wu, Zeyang Tian, Haoze Sun, Jinghui Niu, Hongli Ning, Zhiyuan Liu, Xinna Liu, Weimin Liu, Jialin Liu, Tianpeng Li, Kejun Li, Jun Li, Jiawen Li, Yirong He, Haoyuan Guo, Bosheng Gong, Junhao Gao, Xiaoxiao Fu, Xuezhi Chen, Shengdong Chen, Mingyang Chen, Diying Chen, Yinglun Chai, Yiwen Cai.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 世界模型会让物体互相穿模：NoPeBench 一测发现开源模型全都防不住，但它们其实「知道」该怎么防 ｜ Non-penetrating World Models
item.description:
一句话：模型内部已经编码了判断穿模所需的信息，只是没被用上。

要点：

  • 提出的是个新问题：如何**阻止交互式视频世界模型里的物体穿插**
  • 为此作者构建 **NoPeBench**，评测世界模型面对物理障碍时会怎么反应；结论很直接——**没有任何一个开源模型能可靠地避免这类失败**
  • 但关键发现是：这些模型**已经编码了预测这类违规所需的信息**，只是没有把它用起来；作者据此给出利用这些内部信息来防止穿模的做法

为什么值得看：穿模是玩家最不能容忍的错误之一，而这条把它的性质说清了：不是模型「不懂物理」，而是信息在内部存在、没接到输出上。这个诊断决定了修法——不需要重训一个更大的模型，而是把已有表征接到约束上。

中文摘要：这篇研究交互式视频世界模型里的一个具体失败模式：物体互相穿透。为了解现有模型如何处理这类情况，作者构建了 NoPeBench 基准，评测世界模型面对物理障碍时的反应，结果发现没有任何一个开源模型能够可靠地避免穿模。但更有价值的发现是：这些模型其实已经编码了预测此类违规所需的信息，只是没有把它用于输出。基于这一诊断，作者提出利用模型内部的既有信息来施加约束、防止穿插。对把世界模型用于游戏的团队，这条意味着「修穿模」可能不必靠更大力度的重训。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

Non-penetrating World Models

Abstract

We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT’s hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights at the links above.

Project page·Code·Models·Data

00footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

In the world of Harry Potter, Platform 9¾ allows travelers to pass through a solid wall and enter another world [36]. In reality, however, a wall cannot be crossed because it’s solid. Today’s world models [7, 43, 18, 38, 35, 15, 51, 53, 48, 8] may still behave as if every wall were Platform 9¾. As shown in Fig.1, when commanded to move into a wall, five of the six generators we evaluate pass through it, while the remaining one moves against the user’s command. These failures reveal that current world models struggle to enforce the non-penetration constraint.

The underlying principle, however, is not new. In computer graphics, non-penetration requires that solid objects cannot occupy the same space [4]. Simulators and game engines have long enforced this constraint through collision detection and collision response[25]. They detect collisions and adjust the motion to prevent penetration while preserving the intended movement as much as possible.

Unfortunately, this mechanism is missing from today’s video world models. Basically, they are designed to follow user commands, whether camera poses [15, 38, 53, 48, 8] or key inputs [51], without checking whether the motion is physically possible. Since their training videos rarely, if ever, show a command blocked by a wall, such a command is likely out of distribution. As a result, cameras may pass through walls, or obstacles simply disappear. Worse still, existing benchmarks largely use collision-free trajectories, making it difficult to evaluate how well world models handle non-penetration [46, 49, 45, 14].

To prevent such failures, two straightforward solutions seem promising at first glance. The first is to simply prompt the model to stop or slide along obstacles. However, we find that such prompts have little effect on penetration. The second is to use an external depth estimator [21, 30] to detect obstacles and stop unsafe motions. While effective, this requires post-hoc processing with an additional network for every generated frame. Moreover, stopping alone may sacrifice the user’s intended motion. In that sense, both methods have their own limitations.

Surprisingly, we find that the generator itself already contains information needed to prevent penetration. Prior studies have shown that video diffusion models encode 3D structure and physical plausibility [13, 9, 50]. We find that this knowledge extends to predicting penetration. Specifically, the hidden states of a diffusion transformer (DiT) can predict whether a commanded action will cause penetration, even before the next video chunk is generated. In short, the generator already knows where its walls are, but its output fails to act on that knowledge.

Building on this observation, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration in video world models. The rough idea is that rather than relying on external tools, we directly read the generator’s hidden states to detect unsafe actions (Fig.2). Specifically, we train a small prediction head on a frozen DiT to predict collision risks and distances to obstacles. The head is trained using ground-truth distance and collision labels from Unreal Engine simulations. During inference, unsafe motions are replaced with safe alternatives that best preserve the user’s intent, while safe motions remain unchanged.

We achieve this through two detection modes. In collision mode, the head reads the initial denoising features of the current chunk to detect potential penetration. In prediction mode, it uses features from the previous chunk to predict penetration in the upcoming chunk.

A new task, of course, requires a new benchmark. To evaluate this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that deliberately challenges world models with obstacles (Sec.4.1). It consists of three levels of tasks. Task 1 evaluates, on ground-truth histories, whether a method keeps safe commands and corrects those that would penetrate. Task 2 evaluates whether generated videos respect non-penetration using the ground-truth geometry of scenes from UnrealZoo [55]. Task 3 tests generalization to open-domain scenes using vision-language model (VLM) as judges.

Our experiments show that NoPeWorld robustly detects and prevents penetration across diverse video world models. On LingBot-World 2.0 [15], NoPeWorld intercepts nearly all unsafe commands (Tab.3), which cuts violations from 89% to 4% and lifts the Safe-Intent Score, zero for any video with a violation, from near zero to about half (Secs.4.4 and 4). Moreover, the heads transfer without retraining: trained only on first-person walks through static scenes from UnrealZoo, they reduce Task 3 violations on all six generators, on open-domain imagery, from a third-person viewpoint, and around moving obstacles.

Our contributions are fourfold. (i) Problem: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to study the problem of penetration prevention in video world models. (ii) Method: We introduce NoPeWorld, which detects collisions by probing the hidden states of a frozen DiT and replaces unsafe motions with the safe motion that best preserves the user’s intent. (iii) Insights: We show that frozen world generators encode collision information even before future frames are generated (Sec.5.1). Such collision awareness can be exploited across visual domains, camera viewpoints, and moving obstacles without retraining. (iv) Benchmark: We collect a new benchmark called NoPeBench. It evaluates whether video world models can prevent penetration when given commands that would otherwise lead to collisions.

2 Related work

Interactive video world models.

Interactive video generation has progressed from early action-conditioned predictors [7, 43, 2] to diffusion transformers [28, 41] that denoise video chunk by chunk under camera-pose or keystroke control [17, 29, 54, 18, 38, 35, 15, 53, 48, 20, 51, 8]. Because actions condition denoising in an open loop without scene geometry, these models “do not explicitly enforce collision constraints” [30]. Prompting with obstacle descriptions fails to prevent clipping, while guarding decoded frames with an external depth estimator [21, 30] requires VAE decoding and auxiliary 3D inference at every chunk and only halts motion (Secs.4.3 and 5.3). NoPeWorld instead keeps the generator frozen and enforces collision-aware control directly inside the DiT loop (Sec.3).

Collision handling in computer graphics.

Computer graphics and mechanics have enforced solid non-penetration since the 1980s through collision impulses [25, 16], unilateral contact constraints [22, 23, 26, 4, 5, 37], and penalty potentials [42], later extended to continuous swept collision detection against thin-wall tunnelling [33] and intersection-free solvers [19]. All of these methods require explicit 3D geometry and solve contact mechanics on known surfaces. Rather than simulating contact forces, we adapt two kinematic principles, continuous swept clearance and frictionless collide-and-slide projection (Sec.3.1), to a video generator that stores no geometry, replacing unsafe commands with admissible stops or wall slides.

Internal representations of diffusion models.

Intermediate features of image and video diffusion models capture semantic correspondence, depth, and 3D structure beyond surface appearance [6, 40, 9, 50]. Recent studies probe hidden states [1] on intuitive-physics tasks [34] to show that video DiTs encode physical plausibility offline even when generated frames violate it [13], or train a verifier on frozen DiT features to select among multiple sampled trajectories [39]. Consistent with this view, we find that frozen DiT states already predict upcoming obstacle contact before the next chunk is synthesized, whereas the same readout on VAE latents or decoded pixels falls short (Sec.5.1). Rather than offline probing or multi-sample rejection after generation, NoPeWorld queries frozen DiT tokens with a lightweight cross-attention head (Sec.3.2) to score and replace unsafe actions prior to chunk synthesis (Sec.3.3).

World model benchmarks.

Physical video benchmarks [3, 24, 27] evaluate passive clips without user control, whereas interactive world-model benchmarks [14, 52, 47, 46, 49, 45] focus on visual quality, memory, and action following along open paths: WorldMark [46] removes wall-blocked trajectories, WBench [49] scores clipping as one VLM rubric item along mostly unobstructed routes (Sec.4.1), and WorldRoamBench [45] tests 58 clipping and 14 collision cases with VLMs. To evaluate non-penetration directly, NoPeBench (Sec.4.1) commands every test route into an obstacle alongside open-path controls across teacher-forced (Task 1), closed-loop (Task 2), and open-domain (Task 3) settings, pairing verified 3D reconstruction [44] and human-validated VLM judges with a hard-gated Safe-Intent Score inspired by NAVSIM [10] (Sec.4.2).

3 NoPeWorld

3.1 Problem formulation

An interactive video world model synthesizes video chunk by chunk: given past frames x_

Non-penetration in graphics. Computer graphics enforces solid boundaries through two principles. First, “A realistic simulation of rigid bodies demands that no two bodies inter-penetrate” [4]: a unilateral constraint requires the signed obstacle gap g(γ(ρ))≥0 along a swept path γ(ρ) for ρ∈[0,1][22, 26, 5], tested over the full step so fast motion cannot tunnel through thin walls [25, 33]. Second, upon contact with surface normal n=∇g, a frictionless response that “can ‘push’ but not ‘pull’ ” [4, 16] projects a commanded motion u onto the closest admissible velocity, v_S(u)=*arg min_v^′·n≥0∥v^′-u∥²=u-\min(0,u·n) n, halting head-on and sliding along oblique walls.

Non-penetration in World Model. Bringing both principles into a world model recasts chunk synthesis as constrained generation over chunk xₖ and executed action aₖ:

(xₖ^⋆,aₖ^⋆)=\argmax_xₖ, aₖ\logp_θ(xₖ|x_
s.t.\min_ρ∈[0,1]g_S(γ(ρ; aₖ))≥0.(1)

Here \min_ρ∈[0,1]g_S(γ(ρ; aₖ))≥0 enforces continuous non-penetration against scene geometry S, λ>0 weighs intent against likelihood, and ε_S(aₖ,uₖ) is the distance of aₖ’s displacement from the collide-and-slide response v_S(uₖ), relative to |uₖ|, its cross-slide part weighted by w=0.5, allowing contact while penalizing stops or retreats. A generated video has a violation if its trajectory enters solid geometry (penetration), crosses an obstacle between frames (tunnelling), or erases an obstacle on approach (vanishing); obstacles may still move.

Freezing θ fixes the visual prior p_θ and leaves aₖ as the sole optimization variable; assuming that the generator renders the executed motion within the scene it has already shown, which Task 2 tests, the likelihood term of Eq.1 no longer separates admissible actions, and a non-penetrating aₖ yields a non-penetrating video. Sweeping a collision disc (r=0.25 m) over a discrete candidate set ℂ of 34 motions (the raw input c₀=uₖ, a stop, shortened steps, and turns up to 90^∘) with margin m=0.05 m reduces Eq.1 to

aₖ^⋆=*arg min_cᵢ∈ℂ ε_S(cᵢ,uₖ)² s.t. g_S(cᵢ)≥m,

(2)

with g_S(cᵢ)\triangleq\min_ρ∈[0,1]g_S(γ(ρ; cᵢ)), the margin tightening ≥ 0 to ≥ m (uₖ is safe if admissible and unsafe otherwise) and xₖ^⋆∼p_θ(·|x_Eq.2, the constraint and the intent, from the DiT’s hidden states, before any frame of the chunk is drawn.

3.2 Constraint-aware training

Prior to synthesizing chunk k, intermediate hidden states H of a frozen video DiT f_θ already encode 3D scene structure and impending contact, whereas identical probes on VAE latents or decoded pixels fall well short (Secs.5.1 and 6). Building on this property, NoPeWorld (Non-Penetrating World) trains a compact prediction head (weights φ, under 2M parameters) on mid-to-deep DiT blocks while keeping every weight of θ frozen (Tab.1; Fig.2, Training, left). A token projector ψ_H compresses all tapped tokens to width 128 without spatial pooling; candidate cᵢ∈ℂ (and raw command uₖ when H precedes uₖ) is encoded by the generator’s own frozen control encoder E and projected onto the same token grid via ψ_c. A learned query q then attends over the action-conditioned state tokens H̃ᵢ via two cross-attention blocks:

(ℓᵢ,ĝᵢ,Âᵢ)=CrossAttn_φ(q, H̃ᵢ),(3)
H̃ᵢ=ψ_H(H)+ψ_c(E(cᵢ),E(uₖ)),

predicting a safety logit ℓᵢ, swept clearance ĝᵢ, and intent score Âᵢ per candidate (details in Sec.S2.2).

To supervise the head on the unobserved terms of Eq.2, we replay 729 Unreal Engine [12] videos across 44 training scenes from UnrealZoo [55] (disjoint from all benchmark scenes) through the frozen DiT via teacher forcing (Fig.2, Training, left). On the simulator’s true occupancy map (Fig.2, Training, right), sweeping the collision disc gives the clipped clearance gᵢ=clip(g_S(cᵢ),-0.25,1) m, while comparing cᵢ against the simulator’s collide-and-slide displacement v_S(uₖ) gives the intent error εᵢ=ε_S(cᵢ,uₖ) of Eq.2. Because the hard step I[g_S(cᵢ)≥m] is discontinuous, we form smooth safety and intent targets (s=0.5):

Pᵢ=Φ((gᵢ-m)/(0.03 m)), Aᵢ=e^-εᵢ²/(2s²), Rᵢ=PᵢAᵢ,

(4)

with standard normal CDF Φ. Here Pᵢ softens the constraint of Eq.2, g_S(cᵢ)≥m, Aᵢ maps its intent penalty εᵢ² monotonically into (0,1], and Rᵢ ranks candidates that are both safe and intent-aligned. We train φ via multi-task supervision:

L(φ)=∑ᵢωᵢ[BCE(σ(ℓᵢ),Pᵢ)+1/2 Huber(ĝᵢ,gᵢ)
+BCE(Âᵢ,Aᵢ)]+KL(π(R) ∥ π(R̂)),(5)

so the head learns the constraint (Pᵢ, with dense Huber regression on gᵢ where Pᵢ saturates) and the objective (Aᵢ) of Eq.2, plus a listwise ranking over ℂ with logistic σ, R̂ᵢ=σ(ℓᵢ)Âᵢ and π(R)ᵢ∝Rᵢ¹⁰. Weights ωᵢ sum to one, and chunk indices are reweighted to equalize unsafe rates so predictions rely on geometry, not time. A motion c has regret\maxᵢRᵢ-R_c.

3.3 Two-mode closed-loop inference

At test time, plugging the head into the rollout solves Eq.2 before any frame of chunk k is decoded (Fig.2, Inference). Given calibrated safety probabilities P̂ᵢ=σ(ℓᵢ/T), candidates above threshold τ form the feasible set Sₖ={i:P̂ᵢ≥τ}, the learned constraint of Eq.2, and uₖ is projected onto the closest admissible motion:

aₖ^⋆=\begincasesuₖ,&if0∈Sₖ, \max_i∈SₖÂᵢ≤Â₀+δ, [4.0pt] \argmax_i∈SₖÂᵢ,&otherwise,\endcases

(6)

defaulting to a stop when Sₖ=∅, with (T,τ,δ) fixed on validation scenes (Sec.4.3). In words, a safe input runs as is (kept, aₖ^⋆=uₖ), and an unsafe one is replaced by the safe motion closest to the intent (changed, aₖ^⋆≠uₖ). NoPeWorld runs this loop in two modes that differ in where H is tapped:

Hₖ₋₁ᶜᵒᵐ=f_θ(ẑₖ₋₁, 0|aₖ₋₁^⋆,Mₖ₋₂)(prediction),(7)
Hₖˢᵗᵉᵖ=f_θ(zₖ⁽⁰⁾, t₀|uₖ,Mₖ₋₁)(collision).

Prediction mode (Pred).

After chunk k-1 is denoised into clean latent ẑₖ₋₁, the generator runs a noise-free commit pass to write attention memory Mₖ₋₁. Pred reads this cached state Hₖ₋₁ᶜᵒᵐ with the incoming uₖ, between chunks k-1 and k. Choosing aₖ^⋆ before chunk k is denoised, Pred reruns no step and adds no DiT pass.

Collision mode (Coll).

Coll instead enters chunk k and taps the first denoising pass Hₖˢᵗᵉᵖ (step 0, initial noise zₖ⁽⁰⁾ at level t₀), where uₖ already interacts with memory Mₖ₋₁, so the head needs no separate E(uₖ). If uₖ is kept, denoising proceeds directly from step 1 with no rerun. If uₖ is changed to aₖ^⋆, Coll reruns only step 0 once with aₖ^⋆ (f_θ(zₖ⁽⁰⁾,t₀|aₖ^⋆,Mₖ₋₁)) and completes the remaining steps.
