We achieve this through two detection modes. In collision mode, the head reads the initial denoising features of the current chunk to detect potential penetration. In prediction mode, it uses features from the previous chunk to predict penetration in the upcoming chunk.

A new task, of course, requires a new benchmark. To evaluate this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that deliberately challenges world models with obstacles (Sec.4.1). It consists of three levels of tasks. Task 1 evaluates, on ground-truth histories, whether a method keeps safe commands and corrects those that would penetrate. Task 2 evaluates whether generated videos respect non-penetration using the ground-truth geometry of scenes from UnrealZoo [55]. Task 3 tests generalization to open-domain scenes using vision-language model (VLM) as judges.

Our experiments show that NoPeWorld robustly detects and prevents penetration across diverse video world models. On LingBot-World 2.0 [15], NoPeWorld intercepts nearly all unsafe commands (Tab.3), which cuts violations from 89% to 4% and lifts the Safe-Intent Score, zero for any video with a violation, from near zero to about half (Secs.4.4 and 4). Moreover, the heads transfer without retraining: trained only on first-person walks through static scenes from UnrealZoo, they reduce Task 3 violations on all six generators, on open-domain imagery, from a third-person viewpoint, and around moving obstacles.

Our contributions are fourfold. (i) Problem: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to study the problem of penetration prevention in video world models. (ii) Method: We introduce NoPeWorld, which detects collisions by probing the hidden states of a frozen DiT and replaces unsafe motions with the safe motion that best preserves the user’s intent. (iii) Insights: We show that frozen world generators encode collision information even before future frames are generated (Sec.5.1). Such collision awareness can be exploited across visual domains, camera viewpoints, and moving obstacles without retraining. (iv) Benchmark: We collect a new benchmark called NoPeBench. It evaluates whether video world models can prevent penetration when given commands that would otherwise lead to collisions.

2 Related work

Interactive video world models.

Interactive video generation has progressed from early action-conditioned predictors [7, 43, 2] to diffusion transformers [28, 41] that denoise video chunk by chunk under camera-pose or keystroke control [17, 29, 54, 18, 38, 35, 15, 53, 48, 20, 51, 8]. Because actions condition denoising in an open loop without scene geometry, these models “do not explicitly enforce collision constraints” [30]. Prompting with obstacle descriptions fails to prevent clipping, while guarding decoded frames with an external depth estimator [21, 30] requires VAE decoding and auxiliary 3D inference at every chunk and only halts motion (Secs.4.3 and 5.3). NoPeWorld instead keeps the generator frozen and enforces collision-aware control directly inside the DiT loop (Sec.3).

Collision handling in computer graphics.

Computer graphics and mechanics have enforced solid non-penetration since the 1980s through collision impulses [25, 16], unilateral contact constraints [22, 23, 26, 4, 5, 37], and penalty potentials [42], later extended to continuous swept collision detection against thin-wall tunnelling [33] and intersection-free solvers [19]. All of these methods require explicit 3D geometry and solve contact mechanics on known surfaces. Rather than simulating contact forces, we adapt two kinematic principles, continuous swept clearance and frictionless collide-and-slide projection (Sec.3.1), to a video generator that stores no geometry, replacing unsafe commands with admissible stops or wall slides.

Internal representations of diffusion models.

Intermediate features of image and video diffusion models capture semantic correspondence, depth, and 3D structure beyond surface appearance [6, 40, 9, 50]. Recent studies probe hidden states [1] on intuitive-physics tasks [34] to show that video DiTs encode physical plausibility offline even when generated frames violate it [13], or train a verifier on frozen DiT features to select among multiple sampled trajectories [39]. Consistent with this view, we find that frozen DiT states already predict upcoming obstacle contact before the next chunk is synthesized, whereas the same readout on VAE latents or decoded pixels falls short (Sec.5.1). Rather than offline probing or multi-sample rejection after generation, NoPeWorld queries frozen DiT tokens with a lightweight cross-attention head (Sec.3.2) to score and replace unsafe actions prior to chunk synthesis (Sec.3.3).

World model benchmarks.

Physical video benchmarks [3, 24, 27] evaluate passive clips without user control, whereas interactive world-model benchmarks [14, 52, 47, 46, 49, 45] focus on visual quality, memory, and action following along open paths: WorldMark [46] removes wall-blocked trajectories, WBench [49] scores clipping as one VLM rubric item along mostly unobstructed routes (Sec.4.1), and WorldRoamBench [45] tests 58 clipping and 14 collision cases with VLMs. To evaluate non-penetration directly, NoPeBench (Sec.4.1) commands every test route into an obstacle alongside open-path controls across teacher-forced (Task 1), closed-loop (Task 2), and open-domain (Task 3) settings, pairing verified 3D reconstruction [44] and human-validated VLM judges with a hard-gated Safe-Intent Score inspired by NAVSIM [10] (Sec.4.2).

3 NoPeWorld

3.1 Problem formulation

An interactive video world model synthesizes video chunk by chunk: given past frames x_

Non-penetration in graphics. Computer graphics enforces solid boundaries through two principles. First, “A realistic simulation of rigid bodies demands that no two bodies inter-penetrate” [4]: a unilateral constraint requires the signed obstacle gap g(γ(ρ))≥0 along a swept path γ(ρ) for ρ∈[0,1][22, 26, 5], tested over the full step so fast motion cannot tunnel through thin walls [25, 33]. Second, upon contact with surface normal n=∇g, a frictionless response that “can ‘push’ but not ‘pull’ ” [4, 16] projects a commanded motion u onto the closest admissible velocity, v_S(u)=*arg min_v^′·n≥0∥v^′-u∥²=u-\min(0,u·n) n, halting head-on and sliding along oblique walls.

Non-penetration in World Model. Bringing both principles into a world model recasts chunk synthesis as constrained generation over chunk xₖ and executed action aₖ:

(xₖ^⋆,aₖ^⋆)=\argmax_xₖ, aₖ\logp_θ(xₖ|x_
s.t.\min_ρ∈[0,1]g_S(γ(ρ; aₖ))≥0.(1)

Here \min_ρ∈[0,1]g_S(γ(ρ; aₖ))≥0 enforces continuous non-penetration against scene geometry S, λ>0 weighs intent against likelihood, and ε_S(aₖ,uₖ) is the distance of aₖ’s displacement from the collide-and-slide response v_S(uₖ), relative to |uₖ|, its cross-slide part weighted by w=0.5, allowing contact while penalizing stops or retreats. A generated video has a violation if its trajectory enters solid geometry (penetration), crosses an obstacle between frames (tunnelling), or erases an obstacle on approach (vanishing); obstacles may still move.

Freezing θ fixes the visual prior p_θ and leaves aₖ as the sole optimization variable; assuming that the generator renders the executed motion within the scene it has already shown, which Task 2 tests, the likelihood term of Eq.1 no longer separates admissible actions, and a non-penetrating aₖ yields a non-penetrating video. Sweeping a collision disc (r=0.25 m) over a discrete candidate set ℂ of 34 motions (the raw input c₀=uₖ, a stop, shortened steps, and turns up to 90^∘) with margin m=0.05 m reduces Eq.1 to

aₖ^⋆=*arg min_cᵢ∈ℂ ε_S(cᵢ,uₖ)² s.t. g_S(cᵢ)≥m,

(2)

with g_S(cᵢ)\triangleq\min_ρ∈[0,1]g_S(γ(ρ; cᵢ)), the margin tightening ≥ 0 to ≥ m (uₖ is safe if admissible and unsafe otherwise) and xₖ^⋆∼p_θ(·|x_Eq.2, the constraint and the intent, from the DiT’s hidden states, before any frame of the chunk is drawn.

3.2 Constraint-aware training

Prior to synthesizing chunk k, intermediate hidden states H of a frozen video DiT f_θ already encode 3D scene structure and impending contact, whereas identical probes on VAE latents or decoded pixels fall well short (Secs.5.1 and 6). Building on this property, NoPeWorld (Non-Penetrating World) trains a compact prediction head (weights φ, under 2M parameters) on mid-to-deep DiT blocks while keeping every weight of θ frozen (Tab.1; Fig.2, Training, left). A token projector ψ_H compresses all tapped tokens to width 128 without spatial pooling; candidate cᵢ∈ℂ (and raw command uₖ when H precedes uₖ) is encoded by the generator’s own frozen control encoder E and projected onto the same token grid via ψ_c. A learned query q then attends over the action-conditioned state tokens H̃ᵢ via two cross-attention blocks:

(ℓᵢ,ĝᵢ,Âᵢ)=CrossAttn_φ(q, H̃ᵢ),(3)
H̃ᵢ=ψ_H(H)+ψ_c(E(cᵢ),E(uₖ)),

predicting a safety logit ℓᵢ, swept clearance ĝᵢ, and intent score Âᵢ per candidate (details in Sec.S2.2).

To supervise the head on the unobserved terms of Eq.2, we replay 729 Unreal Engine [12] videos across 44 training scenes from UnrealZoo [55] (disjoint from all benchmark scenes) through the frozen DiT via teacher forcing (Fig.2, Training, left). On the simulator’s true occupancy map (Fig.2, Training, right), sweeping the collision disc gives the clipped clearance gᵢ=clip(g_S(cᵢ),-0.25,1) m, while comparing cᵢ against the simulator’s collide-and-slide displacement v_S(uₖ) gives the intent error εᵢ=ε_S(cᵢ,uₖ) of Eq.2. Because the hard step I[g_S(cᵢ)≥m] is discontinuous, we form smooth safety and intent targets (s=0.5):

Pᵢ=Φ((gᵢ-m)/(0.03 m)), Aᵢ=e^-εᵢ²/(2s²), Rᵢ=PᵢAᵢ,

(4)

with standard normal CDF Φ. Here Pᵢ softens the constraint of Eq.2, g_S(cᵢ)≥m, Aᵢ maps its intent penalty εᵢ² monotonically into (0,1], and Rᵢ ranks candidates that are both safe and intent-aligned. We train φ via multi-task supervision:

L(φ)=∑ᵢωᵢ[BCE(σ(ℓᵢ),Pᵢ)+1/2 Huber(ĝᵢ,gᵢ)
+BCE(Âᵢ,Aᵢ)]+KL(π(R) ∥ π(R̂)),(5)

so the head learns the constraint (Pᵢ, with dense Huber regression on gᵢ where Pᵢ saturates) and the objective (Aᵢ) of Eq.2, plus a listwise ranking over ℂ with logistic σ, R̂ᵢ=σ(ℓᵢ)Âᵢ and π(R)ᵢ∝Rᵢ¹⁰. Weights ωᵢ sum to one, and chunk indices are reweighted to equalize unsafe rates so predictions rely on geometry, not time. A motion c has regret\maxᵢRᵢ-R_c.

3.3 Two-mode closed-loop inference

At test time, plugging the head into the rollout solves Eq.2 before any frame of chunk k is decoded (Fig.2, Inference). Given calibrated safety probabilities P̂ᵢ=σ(ℓᵢ/T), candidates above threshold τ form the feasible set Sₖ={i:P̂ᵢ≥τ}, the learned constraint of Eq.2, and uₖ is projected onto the closest admissible motion:

aₖ^⋆=\begincasesuₖ,&if0∈Sₖ, \max_i∈SₖÂᵢ≤Â₀+δ, [4.0pt] \argmax_i∈SₖÂᵢ,&otherwise,\endcases

(6)

defaulting to a stop when Sₖ=∅, with (T,τ,δ) fixed on validation scenes (Sec.4.3). In words, a safe input runs as is (kept, aₖ^⋆=uₖ), and an unsafe one is replaced by the safe motion closest to the intent (changed, aₖ^⋆≠uₖ). NoPeWorld runs this loop in two modes that differ in where H is tapped:

Hₖ₋₁ᶜᵒᵐ=f_θ(ẑₖ₋₁, 0|aₖ₋₁^⋆,Mₖ₋₂)(prediction),(7)
Hₖˢᵗᵉᵖ=f_θ(zₖ⁽⁰⁾, t₀|uₖ,Mₖ₋₁)(collision).

Prediction mode (Pred).

After chunk k-1 is denoised into clean latent ẑₖ₋₁, the generator runs a noise-free commit pass to write attention memory Mₖ₋₁. Pred reads this cached state Hₖ₋₁ᶜᵒᵐ with the incoming uₖ, between chunks k-1 and k. Choosing aₖ^⋆ before chunk k is denoised, Pred reruns no step and adds no DiT pass.

Collision mode (Coll).

Coll instead enters chunk k and taps the first denoising pass Hₖˢᵗᵉᵖ (step 0, initial noise zₖ⁽⁰⁾ at level t₀), where uₖ already interacts with memory Mₖ₋₁, so the head needs no separate E(uₖ). If uₖ is kept, denoising proceeds directly from step 1 with no rerun. If uₖ is changed to aₖ^⋆, Coll reruns only step 0 once with aₖ^⋆ (f_θ(zₖ⁽⁰⁾,t₀|aₖ^⋆,Mₖ₋₁)) and completes the remaining steps.

item.title: 把力当成「运动轨迹」喂给世界模型是错的：PhysForce 说内部表征根本没定位到「力改变了哪里」 ｜ PhysForce: Physics-aware Force Control for Interactive Video World Model
item.description:
一句话：现有做法把力表示成运动轨迹，会引入不恰当的运动先验，让模型过度依赖已编码的位移模式。

要点：

  • 目标：交互式视频世界模型要预测环境如何在用户干预下演化，包括**施加力所带来的、物理一致的状态变化**
  • 两个根本缺陷：现有方法常把力表示成**运动轨迹**，这会引入不恰当的运动先验、让模型过度依赖已编码的位移模式；更根本的是，模型的内部表征**无法可靠地定位「力所引发的状态变化」**，因此难以把施加的力与它的物理响应关联起来
  • PhysForce 用两阶段框架（监督微调 + 强化学习）配合三个互补组件来解决，同时应对「力标注数据有限」的问题

为什么值得看：「力」是交互式世界模型最不该用位移来代替的量。这条指出了内层表征的问题（定位不到受影响的区域），而不是只在外层换个输入格式——这才是有可能解决「推不动/推错」的路径。

中文摘要：交互式视频世界模型需要预测视觉环境如何随用户干预演化，其中包括施加力之后产生的、物理一致的状态变化。作者指出两个根本缺陷：其一，现有方法常把力表示成运动轨迹，这会引入不恰当的运动先验，使模型过度依赖已编码的位移模式；其二，更根本的是模型的内部表征无法可靠地定位「力所引发的状态变化」，因此难以把施加的力与其物理响应关联起来。此外，力标注数据有限也使得模型在未见场景中难以给出物理一致且时间稳定的预测。PhysForce 因此提出两阶段框架，把监督微调与强化学习结合起来，并设计三个互补组件来分别处理上述问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

PhysForce: Physics-aware Force Control for Interactive Video World Model

Abstract

Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model’s internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.

22footnotetext: Corresponding Author33footnotetext: Work done during an internship at GigaAI

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models aim to simulate how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions [(Bruce et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026c; Huang et al., 2025)]. For force-conditioned interaction, the model must predict future states from an initial state and a force defined by its application point, direction, and magnitude, while ensuring that the resulting dynamics are physically plausible and consistent with the applied force.

Existing methods [(Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a)] introduce force conditioning to model physical interventions, yet face three limitations. First, trajectory-based force representations may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing models to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns rather than infer force induced results, as shown in Fig. 2(a). Second, internal representations such as attention maps and PCA features do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, as shown in Fig. 2(b). This limits their ability to provide explicit supervision for physical response regions. Third, limited annotated force data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios, as shown in Fig. 2(c).

To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we introduce Latent Force Intervention Encoder (LFIE) to eliminate future-motion leakage from moving Gaussian blobs. In Fig. 2(a), the leaked trajectory drives the ball along a straight path, overriding its physically plausible motion down the stairs. LFIE directly maps force location, direction, and magnitude into a learnable latent condition without exposing temporal trajectories or future displacement, requiring the model to infer the resulting state changes.

Second, inspired by how children acquire intuitive physics through interaction and observation [(Piaget and Cook, 1952; Gopnik et al., 2004)], we introduce the Physics Attribution Network (PAN) to connect force interventions with observed state changes. Self-attention and cross-attention capture feature relationships but fail to reliably trace physical responses, while PCA remains entangled with appearance. PAN instead aligns force-conditioned latent responses with temporal differences to localize where and how strongly state changes occur, as shown in Fig. 2(b). This supervision makes the relation between intervention and response explicit, encouraging the model to learn how forces drive scene evolution rather than reproduce generic motion patterns.

During reinforcement learning (RL), we introduce Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning (PARL) to improve physical consistency and generalization to unseen scenes, as shown in Fig. 2(c). PARL derives an attribution-guided physics reward from the learned dynamics prior of a self-supervised V-JEPA encoder and predictor [(Mur-Labadia et al., 2026; Assran et al., 2025)], reinforcing physically coherent state evolution within PAN-localized response regions. Since the reward can be hacked by generating static videos or visual artifacts, we introduce a Dynamic Gate that evaluates motion, temporal stability, and visual quality to filter such degenerate rollouts.

Extensive evaluations on in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks show that PhysForce improves force controllability, physical consistency, and generalization while preserving visual quality and temporal coherence. These results establish PhysForce as an effective framework for physics-aware interaction and state prediction in video world models.

Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce the Latent Force Intervention Encoder, which encodes force location, direction, and magnitude in the video latent space without trajectory leakage, allowing the model to predict state changes caused by the applied force.

  • •

    We propose the Physics Attribution Network, which learns a force conditioned response map that localizes state changes associated with the intervention.

  • •

    We develop Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning to improve physical consistency and generalization using attribution guided self-supervised rewards from videos, with a Dynamic Gate mitigating reward hacking.

  • •

    PhysForce achieves state-of-the-art force controllability, physical consistency, and generalization while preserving video quality and temporal coherence.

    • 2 Related Works

    Video Diffusion Transformer. Diffusion models [(Wang et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Mi et al., 2026; Mi et al., 2025)] have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality videos [(Blattmann et al., 2023; Singer et al., 2023; Khachatryan et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024a)]. Leveraging the scalability of the Diffusion Transformer architecture [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], recent models [(Yang et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026e)] have substantially improved both visual fidelity and motion quality. Building upon these advances, controllable video generation [(Ma et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2025c; Ma et al., 2026c; Ma et al., 2025d; Xu et al., 2026d; Xu et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026e; Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., ; Li et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025a)] enables generated videos to adhere to specific control conditions, thereby laying a solid foundation for action-conditioned video world models.

    Physics-aware Video Generation. Despite the impressive progress of existing video generation models in producing cinematic and visually appealing videos, their ability to faithfully follow real-world physical consistency remains limited. Physics-aware video generation aims to enhance the capability of foundation video generation models to perceive, represent, and generate videos that conform to physical laws. Existing methods can be broadly categorized into several lines. Some approaches [(Zhang et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a)] introduce implicit physical modeling by converting physical correctness into computable losses or rewards. Other works [(Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026h; Yuan et al., 2026a)] align physical representations with model features through external networks or physics priors. Another line of research [(Wang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b; Foo et al., 2026)] reconstructs particle fields and combines them with physics solvers, using predicted future particle trajectories to guide video generation. In addition,  [(Yuan et al., 2025)] explicitly models dynamics and supervises model learning with Newtonian laws of motion.

    Interactive World Model. An interactive world model aims to predict future state transitions based on user-specified initial conditions. Recent works [(Sun et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026g; Wang et al., 2026f; Ma et al., 2026b; Team et al., 2026)] further incorporate control signals, such as camera parameters and trajectories, enabling video models to interactively explore and predict real-world dynamics. However, these control signals typically contain little explicit physical information. In contrast, another line of work [(Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b; Narayanan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026d; Zhong et al., )] introduces physical quantities, such as forces, as initial triggering conditions, with the goal of improving models’ understanding of physical interactions and eliciting physically consistent responses to such conditions.

    3 Method

    In this section, we present PhysForce, a two-stage framework for physics-aware force control in interactive video world models. The SFT stage learns latent force conditioning and intervention-response attribution, while the reinforcement learning stage improves physical consistency in unseen scenarios. The overall pipeline is shown in Fig. 3. Sec. 3.2.1 presents the Latent Force Intervention Encoder (LFIE), which maps outcome-agnostic force conditions into the video latent space. Sec. 3.2.2 introduces the Physics Attribution Network (PAN), which associates force interventions with localized latent-state changes. Finally, Sec. 3.3 describes Physics-aware Reinforcement Learning (PARL), which combines attribution-guided self-supervised rewards with a Dynamic Gate to improve unseen-state prediction and mitigate reward hacking.

    3.1 Preliminary

    Online Diffusion Reinforcement Learning. Reinforcement learning approaches [(Liu et al., 2026a; Guan et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b)] leverage policy-gradient methods to optimize sequential decision-making processes. DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2025b)] performs reinforcement learning directly on the forward process by contrasting generated samples based on rewards.

    Given a generated sample x₀, its condition c, and a normalized reward r(X₀,c)∈[0,1], DiffusionNFT constructs implicit positive and negative velocity predictors:

    v_θ⁺(zₜ,c,t)=(1-β)v_old(zₜ,c,t)+βv_θ(zₜ,c,t),(1)
    v_θ⁻(zₜ,c,t)=(1+β)v_old(zₜ,c,t)-βv_θ(zₜ,c,t),

    where v_old denotes the data-collection policy and β controls the reinforcement strength. The model is then optimized using the reward-weighted flow matching objective

    L_NFT=𝔼_X₀,c,t[r(X₀,c)∥v_θ⁺-vₜ∥₂²+(1-r(X₀,c))∥v_θ⁻-vₜ∥₂²].

    		(2)

    where the arguments (zₜ,c,t) of v_θ⁺ and v_θ⁻ are omitted for brevity. This objective promotes high-reward samples while leveraging low-reward samples as negative feedback.

    3.2 Stage1: Force-conditioned supervised fine-tuning

    3.2.1 Latent Force Intervention Encoder

    Trajectory-based force representations specify a sequence of positions and therefore expose the expected motion. To avoid this trajectory leakage, we introduce the LFIE, which represents only the applied force without prescribing its outcome. Given an application point p, a normalized magnitude s, and direction (\cosθ,\sinθ) in the image coordinate, we construct a four-channel force field:

    F(p)=[M(p),W(p)\cosθ,W(p)\sinθ,W(p)s],

    		(3)

    where M is a truncated Gaussian centered at p₀, and W denotes its binary support. The support has a fixed spatial extent, ensuring that force magnitude is represented by s rather than by the size of the force region. For global forces such as wind, we set M(p)=W(p)=1. The same force field is repeated along the temporal dimension while its center remains fixed. Consequently, the condition contains no future position, displacement, or object trajectory.

    LFIE projects the force condition into the video latent space through two parallel branches. The first branch constructs spatially localized directional components:

    Fₓ(p)=M(p)·s·\cosθ, F_y(p)=M(p)·s·\sinθ,

    		(4)

    A fixed mapping φ converts these components into the native control format of the pretrained model. The frozen video VAE then produces the Directional Force Embedding:

    z_DFE=𝔼_VAE(φ(Fₓ,F_y)),

    		(5)

    This branch contains no trainable parameters and preserves compatibility with the pretrained control pathway. In parallel, a trainable adapter A_ψ maps the complete factorized force field directly onto the video latent grid. The two branches are combined by elementwise addition:

    z_f=z_DFE+A_ψ(F).

    		(6)

    The output projection of A_ψ is initialized to zero, so LFIE initially follows the frozen directional embedding and progressively learns complementary representations of force location, direction, and magnitude. Finally, the resulting force embedding is concatenated with the visual conditioning latent along the channel dimension. Since neither branch receives the future motion, the model must infer the resulting state evolution from the interaction between the applied force and the current scene.

    3.2.2 Physics Attribution Network

    Standard video-generation objectives supervise the generated video globally without explicitly associating force interventions with their induced state changes. Inspired by Piaget’s sensorimotor theory, which relates physical knowledge to actions and their observed consequences [(Piaget and Cook, 1952)], we introduce the PAN to strengthen intervention-response learning.

    At timestep t, let ẑₜ and zₜ^∗ denote the predicted and target latent sequences under the same noise realization, and the force embedding z_f from Sec. 3.2.1. Their temporal responses are defined as:

    Δẑ_t,i=ẑ_t,i+1-ẑ_t,i, Δz_t,i^∗=z_t,i+1^∗-z_t,i^∗.

    		(7)

    Here, i indexes temporal positions in the latent sequence. Since the simulated videos are captured by static cameras and their state changes are driven by the applied force, these temporal differences provide dense cues for localizing state changes caused by the applied force. PAN encodes the predicted response and detached force embedding through separate branches. The force feature modulates the response through a zero-initialized residual gate to produce the attribution feature âᵢ. PAN aligns it with the observed temporal response:

    âᵢ=PAN(Δẑ_i,t,sg(z_f)), Lₐₜₜᵣ=1/T-1∑ᵢ₌₁ᵀ⁻¹∥âᵢ-Δz^*_i,t∥₁,

    		(8)

    Here, sg(·) denotes gradient detachment. This alignment captures where and how strongly states change without region annotations. The SFT objective is:

    L_SFT=L_FM+λₐₜₜᵣLₐₜₜᵣ.

    		(9)

    where L_FM denotes the loss of flow matching. By conditioning temporal response alignment on z_f, PAN encourages the generator to associate force interventions with their induced state changes rather than rely only on correlations in the training distribution. We further include 3,000 force free videos from WISA-80K [(Wang et al., 2026c)] and drop the force embedding for 10% of simulated samples to improve OOD robustness and support Stage 2. Further details are provided in Appendix A.2.

    3.3 Physics-aware Reinforcement Learning

    Supervised force interaction data cover only limited physical dynamics. We introduce PARL to improve physical consistency and generalization using auxiliary OOD videos. PARL combines an attribution-guided world model reward with a Dynamic Gate that filters degenerate rollouts.

    Given an OOD initial state I_ood and a force-free embedding z_∅, the old policy generates K clean rollout latents z₀^1:K. These latents are decoded into videos X^1:K for reward evaluation and forward noised into zₜ^1:K for DiffusionNFT optimization.

    Attribution-aligned physics reward.

    Following [(Yuan et al., 2026a)], we divide each decoded video Xᵏ into C context frames and T future frames. For each window ℓ, the frozen V-JEPA predictor P_φ estimates the future features from the context, while its encoder E_ψ extracts the corresponding target features from the complete window:

    Ĥ_ℓ^k,fut=P_φ (E_ψ(X_ℓ-C+1:ℓᵏ),Δₜ), H_ℓ^k,fut=[E_ψ(X_ℓ-C+1:ℓ+Tᵏ)]_Δₜ,

    		(10)

    where Δₜ specifies the future-token positions. The predicted and target features are arranged in their original spatiotemporal token layouts for subsequent attribution weighting.

    Following Sec. 3.2.2, PAN produces a signed latent response âᵏ∈ℝ^B×Cₐ×Tₐ×Hₐ×Wₐ from each clean rollout. We convert it into a nonnegative attribution map by taking the channelwise L₂ norm:

    âᵏ=PAN(Δz₀ᵏ,sg(z_∅)), Aᵏ=(∑_c=1^Cₐ|âᵏ|²)^1/2,

    		(11)

    Thus, Aᵏ≥0 measures the response magnitude at each latent location. We resize and temporally pool the PAN attribution map Aᵏ to match the spatial patches and temporal tubelets of the V-JEPA features. The resulting nonnegative weight map Wᵏ assigns an attribution weight to each predicted future token. Thus, each V-JEPA token is assigned a nonnegative attribution weight.

    The aligned map is broadcast over the feature dimension and applied to the V-JEPA prediction error:

    Lₐₜₜᵣᵏ=(∥Wᵏ⊙(Ĥ_ℓ^k,fut-H_ℓ^k,fut)∥₁)/(D∥Wᵏ∥₁+ε), R_phyᵏ=-Lₐₜₜᵣᵏ,

    		(12)

    This formulation evaluates local predictability at the V-JEPA token level, assigning higher rewards to predictable state changes in PAN-identified regions.

    Dynamic Gate.

    The physics reward may assign high scores to degenerate rollouts, including static videos and motion caused by visual artifacts. We therefore introduce a reward-independent Dynamic Gate implemented by a VBench Judger. For each rollout Xᵏ, it evaluates the dynamic ratio dᵏ, temporal stability qₜₑₘₚᵏ, and visual quality qᵥᵢₛᵏ:

    mᵏ=I[τ_d⁻≤dᵏ≤τ_d⁺∧qₜₑₘₚᵏ≥τₜₑₘₚ∧qᵥᵢₛᵏ≥τᵥᵢₛ], ℕ={k|mᵏ=1}.

    		(13)

    The thresholds are calibrated on held-out SFT rollouts and remain fixed during reinforcement learning. The additional tolerance ε_A excludes empty or near-zero attribution maps. Only rollouts in ℕ participate in reward normalization and optimization. The gate therefore prevents static collapse, excessive motion, visual artifacts, and invalid attribution maps from exploiting the physics reward.

    Forward-process reinforcement learning.

    Following DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2025b)], we convert the physics rewards within the eligible set into relative optimality probabilities:

    R̄_c=(1)/(|ℕ|)∑_j∈ℕR_phyʲ, r(X₀ᵏ,c)=1/2+(R_phyᵏ-R̄_c)/(2\max_j∈ℕ|R_phyʲ-R̄_c|+ε), k∈ℕ.

    		(14)

    Here, rewards above and below the group mean are mapped above and below 1/2, respectively. Conditions with fewer than two eligible rollouts are skipped, and rejected rollouts are excluded from both normalization and optimization. Noise is added to each eligible latent z₀ᵏ to obtain zₜᵏ, which is optimized using Eq. 1 and Eq. 2. The data-collection predictor v_old is updated from v_θ through exponential moving average.

    4 Experiment

    4.1 Experimental Settings

    Implementation Details. PhysForce builds on the DiT-based Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control model [(Peebles and Xie, 2023; Wan et al., 2025)] and is trained on eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Stage 1 jointly optimizes LFIE, PAN, and a rank-64 DiT LoRA for 4,600 steps at up to 832×480 resolution. Stage 2 applies DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2025b)] for 55 updates using a rank-32 policy LoRA initialized from the frozen Stage 1 model. Each update uses two conditions and six 30-step rollouts per condition. Further details are provided in Appendix D.

    Dataset.Training data. Stage 1 uses approximately 12K point-force videos from GoalForce [(Gillman et al., 2026b)], 15,359 wind-force videos from ForcePrompting [(Gillman et al., 2026a)], and 3K force-free videos from WISA-80K [(Wang et al., 2026c)]. Stage 2 uses 100 static-camera WISA-80K videos without force annotations. Evaluation benchmarks. For OOD evaluation, we use the official ForcePrompting test set [(Gillman et al., 2026a)], containing 305 point-force and 52 wind-force cases disjoint from training. For ID evaluation, GT80 contains 20 held-out cases each for balls, dominoes, plants, and wind. ForcePrompting evaluates force alignment and video quality, while GT80 additionally evaluates ground-truth physics alignment. Details are provided in Appendix F.

    Metrics. Following prior work [(Wang et al., 2026b; Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b)], we evaluate ID and OOD performance using 14 metrics across three dimensions. (1) Force Alignment.Directional Cosine Similarity (DCS) measures the directional agreement between the applied force and generated motion. DA@30∘ and DA@45∘ report the percentages of samples with directional errors below 30^∘ and 45^∘, respectively. Motion Response Rate (MRR) measures the frequency of valid motion responses, while ROI Motion Magnitude (RMM) quantifies motion strength within the affected region. (2) Video Quality.CLIP-T and PickScore[(Kirstain et al., 2023)] evaluate text alignment and learned human preference, respectively. We further adopt Motion Smoothness, Aesthetic Quality, and Imaging Quality from VBench [(Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025a)] to assess temporal consistency, visual appeal, and image fidelity. (3) Physics Alignment. For cases with paired ground-truth videos, we follow the Physics-IQ evaluation protocol [(Motamed et al., 2026)]. Spatial IoU, Spatiotemporal IoU (ST-IoU), and Weighted IoU measure agreement between the generated and ground-truth motion regions, while MSE measures their pixel-level discrepancy.

一句话：现有做法把力表示成运动轨迹，会引入不恰当的运动先验，让模型过度依赖已编码的位移模式。

要点：

  • 目标：交互式视频世界模型要预测环境如何在用户干预下演化，包括**施加力所带来的、物理一致的状态变化**
  • 两个根本缺陷：现有方法常把力表示成**运动轨迹**，这会引入不恰当的运动先验、让模型过度依赖已编码的位移模式；更根本的是，模型的内部表征**无法可靠地定位「力所引发的状态变化」**，因此难以把施加的力与它的物理响应关联起来
  • PhysForce 用两阶段框架（监督微调 + 强化学习）配合三个互补组件来解决，同时应对「力标注数据有限」的问题

为什么值得看：「力」是交互式世界模型最不该用位移来代替的量。这条指出了内层表征的问题（定位不到受影响的区域），而不是只在外层换个输入格式——这才是有可能解决「推不动/推错」的路径。

中文摘要：交互式视频世界模型需要预测视觉环境如何随用户干预演化，其中包括施加力之后产生的、物理一致的状态变化。作者指出两个根本缺陷：其一，现有方法常把力表示成运动轨迹，这会引入不恰当的运动先验，使模型过度依赖已编码的位移模式；其二，更根本的是模型的内部表征无法可靠地定位「力所引发的状态变化」，因此难以把施加的力与其物理响应关联起来。此外，力标注数据有限也使得模型在未见场景中难以给出物理一致且时间稳定的预测。PhysForce 因此提出两阶段框架，把监督微调与强化学习结合起来，并设计三个互补组件来分别处理上述问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

PhysForce: Physics-aware Force Control for Interactive Video World Model

Abstract

Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model’s internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.

22footnotetext: Corresponding Author33footnotetext: Work done during an internship at GigaAI

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models aim to simulate how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions [(Bruce et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026c; Huang et al., 2025)]. For force-conditioned interaction, the model must predict future states from an initial state and a force defined by its application point, direction, and magnitude, while ensuring that the resulting dynamics are physically plausible and consistent with the applied force.

Existing methods [(Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a)] introduce force conditioning to model physical interventions, yet face three limitations. First, trajectory-based force representations may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing models to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns rather than infer force induced results, as shown in Fig. 2(a). Second, internal representations such as attention maps and PCA features do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, as shown in Fig. 2(b). This limits their ability to provide explicit supervision for physical response regions. Third, limited annotated force data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios, as shown in Fig. 2(c).

To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we introduce Latent Force Intervention Encoder (LFIE) to eliminate future-motion leakage from moving Gaussian blobs. In Fig. 2(a), the leaked trajectory drives the ball along a straight path, overriding its physically plausible motion down the stairs. LFIE directly maps force location, direction, and magnitude into a learnable latent condition without exposing temporal trajectories or future displacement, requiring the model to infer the resulting state changes.

Second, inspired by how children acquire intuitive physics through interaction and observation [(Piaget and Cook, 1952; Gopnik et al., 2004)], we introduce the Physics Attribution Network (PAN) to connect force interventions with observed state changes. Self-attention and cross-attention capture feature relationships but fail to reliably trace physical responses, while PCA remains entangled with appearance. PAN instead aligns force-conditioned latent responses with temporal differences to localize where and how strongly state changes occur, as shown in Fig. 2(b). This supervision makes the relation between intervention and response explicit, encouraging the model to learn how forces drive scene evolution rather than reproduce generic motion patterns.

During reinforcement learning (RL), we introduce Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning (PARL) to improve physical consistency and generalization to unseen scenes, as shown in Fig. 2(c). PARL derives an attribution-guided physics reward from the learned dynamics prior of a self-supervised V-JEPA encoder and predictor [(Mur-Labadia et al., 2026; Assran et al., 2025)], reinforcing physically coherent state evolution within PAN-localized response regions. Since the reward can be hacked by generating static videos or visual artifacts, we introduce a Dynamic Gate that evaluates motion, temporal stability, and visual quality to filter such degenerate rollouts.

Extensive evaluations on in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks show that PhysForce improves force controllability, physical consistency, and generalization while preserving visual quality and temporal coherence. These results establish PhysForce as an effective framework for physics-aware interaction and state prediction in video world models.

Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce the Latent Force Intervention Encoder, which encodes force location, direction, and magnitude in the video latent space without trajectory leakage, allowing the model to predict state changes caused by the applied force.

  • •

    We propose the Physics Attribution Network, which learns a force conditioned response map that localizes state changes associated with the intervention.

  • •

    We develop Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning to improve physical consistency and generalization using attribution guided self-supervised rewards from videos, with a Dynamic Gate mitigating reward hacking.

  • •

    PhysForce achieves state-of-the-art force controllability, physical consistency, and generalization while preserving video quality and temporal coherence.

    • 2 Related Works

    Video Diffusion Transformer. Diffusion models [(Wang et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Mi et al., 2026; Mi et al., 2025)] have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality videos [(Blattmann et al., 2023; Singer et al., 2023; Khachatryan et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024a)]. Leveraging the scalability of the Diffusion Transformer architecture [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], recent models [(Yang et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026e)] have substantially improved both visual fidelity and motion quality. Building upon these advances, controllable video generation [(Ma et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2025c; Ma et al., 2026c; Ma et al., 2025d; Xu et al., 2026d; Xu et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026e; Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., ; Li et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025a)] enables generated videos to adhere to specific control conditions, thereby laying a solid foundation for action-conditioned video world models.

    Physics-aware Video Generation. Despite the impressive progress of existing video generation models in producing cinematic and visually appealing videos, their ability to faithfully follow real-world physical consistency remains limited. Physics-aware video generation aims to enhance the capability of foundation video generation models to perceive, represent, and generate videos that conform to physical laws. Existing methods can be broadly categorized into several lines. Some approaches [(Zhang et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a)] introduce implicit physical modeling by converting physical correctness into computable losses or rewards. Other works [(Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026h; Yuan et al., 2026a)] align physical representations with model features through external networks or physics priors. Another line of research [(Wang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b; Foo et al., 2026)] reconstructs particle fields and combines them with physics solvers, using predicted future particle trajectories to guide video generation. In addition,  [(Yuan et al., 2025)] explicitly models dynamics and supervises model learning with Newtonian laws of motion.

    Interactive World Model. An interactive world model aims to predict future state transitions based on user-specified initial conditions. Recent works [(Sun et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026g; Wang et al., 2026f; Ma et al., 2026b; Team et al., 2026)] further incorporate control signals, such as camera parameters and trajectories, enabling video models to interactively explore and predict real-world dynamics. However, these control signals typically contain little explicit physical information. In contrast, another line of work [(Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b; Narayanan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026d; Zhong et al., )] introduces physical quantities, such as forces, as initial triggering conditions, with the goal of improving models’ understanding of physical interactions and eliciting physically consistent responses to such conditions.

    3 Method

    In this section, we present PhysForce, a two-stage framework for physics-aware force control in interactive video world models. The SFT stage learns latent force conditioning and intervention-response attribution, while the reinforcement learning stage improves physical consistency in unseen scenarios. The overall pipeline is shown in Fig. 3. Sec. 3.2.1 presents the Latent Force Intervention Encoder (LFIE), which maps outcome-agnostic force conditions into the video latent space. Sec. 3.2.2 introduces the Physics Attribution Network (PAN), which associates force interventions with localized latent-state changes. Finally, Sec. 3.3 describes Physics-aware Reinforcement Learning (PARL), which combines attribution-guided self-supervised rewards with a Dynamic Gate to improve unseen-state prediction and mitigate reward hacking.

    3.1 Preliminary

    Online Diffusion Reinforcement Learning. Reinforcement learning approaches [(Liu et al., 2026a; Guan et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b)] leverage policy-gradient methods to optimize sequential decision-making processes. DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2025b)] performs reinforcement learning directly on the forward process by contrasting generated samples based on rewards.

    Given a generated sample x₀, its condition c, and a normalized reward r(X₀,c)∈[0,1], DiffusionNFT constructs implicit positive and negative velocity predictors:

    v_θ⁺(zₜ,c,t)=(1-β)v_old(zₜ,c,t)+βv_θ(zₜ,c,t),(1)
    v_θ⁻(zₜ,c,t)=(1+β)v_old(zₜ,c,t)-βv_θ(zₜ,c,t),

    where v_old denotes the data-collection policy and β controls the reinforcement strength. The model is then optimized using the reward-weighted flow matching objective

    L_NFT=𝔼_X₀,c,t[r(X₀,c)∥v_θ⁺-vₜ∥₂²+(1-r(X₀,c))∥v_θ⁻-vₜ∥₂²].

    		(2)

    where the arguments (zₜ,c,t) of v_θ⁺ and v_θ⁻ are omitted for brevity. This objective promotes high-reward samples while leveraging low-reward samples as negative feedback.

    3.2 Stage1: Force-conditioned supervised fine-tuning

    3.2.1 Latent Force Intervention Encoder

To avoid this trajectory leakage, we introduce the LFIE, which represents only the applied force without prescribing its outcome.     F(p)=[M(p),W(p)\cosθ,W(p)\sinθ,W(p)s],

    		(3)

    where M is a truncated Gaussian centered at p₀, and W denotes its binary support. The support has a fixed spatial extent, ensuring that force magnitude is represented by s rather than by the size of the force region. For global forces such as wind, we set M(p)=W(p)=1. The same force field is repeated along the temporal dimension while its center remains fixed. Consequently, the condition contains no future position, displacement, or object trajectory.

    LFIE projects the force condition into the video latent space through two parallel branches. The first branch constructs spatially localized directional components:

    Fₓ(p)=M(p)·s·\cosθ, F_y(p)=M(p)·s·\sinθ,

    		(4)

    A fixed mapping φ converts these components into the native control format of the pretrained model. The frozen video VAE then produces the Directional Force Embedding:

    z_f=z_DFE+A_ψ(F).

    		(6)

    The output projection of A_ψ is initialized to zero, so LFIE initially follows the frozen directional embedding and progressively learns complementary representations of force location, direction, and magnitude. Finally, the resulting force embedding is concatenated with the visual conditioning latent along the channel dimension. Since neither branch receives the future motion, the model must infer the resulting state evolution from the interaction between the applied force and the current scene.

    		(8)

    Here, sg(·) denotes gradient detachment. This alignment captures where and how strongly states change without region annotations. The SFT objective is:

    L_SFT=L_FM+λₐₜₜᵣLₐₜₜᵣ.

    		(9)

    where L_FM denotes the loss of flow matching. We further include 3,000 force free videos from WISA-80K [(Wang et al., 2026c)] and drop the force embedding for 10% of simulated samples to improve OOD robustness and support Stage 2. Further details are provided in Appendix A.2.

    3.3 Physics-aware Reinforcement Learning

    Supervised force interaction data cover only limited physical dynamics. We introduce PARL to improve physical consistency and generalization using auxiliary OOD videos. PARL combines an attribution-guided world model reward with a Dynamic Gate that filters degenerate rollouts.

    Given an OOD initial state I_ood and a force-free embedding z_∅, the old policy generates K clean rollout latents z₀^1:K. These latents are decoded into videos X^1:K for reward evaluation and forward noised into zₜ^1:K for DiffusionNFT optimization.

    		(10)

    mᵏ=I[τ_d⁻≤dᵏ≤τ_d⁺∧qₜₑₘₚᵏ≥τₜₑₘₚ∧qᵥᵢₛᵏ≥τᵥᵢₛ], ℕ={k|mᵏ=1}.

    		(13)

    The thresholds are calibrated on held-out SFT rollouts and remain fixed during reinforcement learning. The additional tolerance ε_A excludes empty or near-zero attribution maps. Only rollouts in ℕ participate in reward normalization and optimization. The gate therefore prevents static collapse, excessive motion, visual artifacts, and invalid attribution maps from exploiting the physics reward.

    Forward-process reinforcement learning.

    Following DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2025b)], we convert the physics rewards within the eligible set into relative optimality probabilities:

    R̄_c=(1)/(|ℕ|)∑_j∈ℕR_phyʲ, r(X₀ᵏ,c)=1/2+(R_phyᵏ-R̄_c)/(2\max_j∈ℕ|R_phyʲ-R̄_c|+ε), k∈ℕ.

    		(14)

    Here, rewards above and below the group mean are mapped above and below 1/2, respectively. Conditions with fewer than two eligible rollouts are skipped, and rejected rollouts are excluded from both normalization and optimization. Noise is added to each eligible latent z₀ᵏ to obtain zₜᵏ, which is optimized using Eq. 1 and Eq. 2. The data-collection predictor v_old is updated from v_θ through exponential moving average.

    4 Experiment

    4.1 Experimental Settings

    Implementation Details. PhysForce builds on the DiT-based Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control model [(Peebles and Xie, 2023; Wan et al., 2025)] and is trained on eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Stage 1 jointly optimizes LFIE, PAN, and a rank-64 DiT LoRA for 4,600 steps at up to 832×480 resolution. Stage 2 applies DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2025b)] for 55 updates using a rank-32 policy LoRA initialized from the frozen Stage 1 model. Each update uses two conditions and six 30-step rollouts per condition. Further details are provided in Appendix D.

    Dataset.Training data. Stage 1 uses approximately 12K point-force videos from GoalForce [(Gillman et al., 2026b)], 15,359 wind-force videos from ForcePrompting [(Gillman et al., 2026a)], and 3K force-free videos from WISA-80K [(Wang et al., 2026c)]. Stage 2 uses 100 static-camera WISA-80K videos without force annotations. Evaluation benchmarks. For OOD evaluation, we use the official ForcePrompting test set [(Gillman et al., 2026a)], containing 305 point-force and 52 wind-force cases disjoint from training. For ID evaluation, GT80 contains 20 held-out cases each for balls, dominoes, plants, and wind. ForcePrompting evaluates force alignment and video quality, while GT80 additionally evaluates ground-truth physics alignment. Details are provided in Appendix F.

    Metrics. Following prior work [(Wang et al., 2026b; Gillman et al., 2026a; Gillman et al., 2026b)], we evaluate ID and OOD performance using 14 metrics across three dimensions. (1) Force Alignment.Directional Cosine Similarity (DCS) measures the directional agreement between the applied force and generated motion. DA@30∘ and DA@45∘ report the percentages of samples with directional errors below 30^∘ and 45^∘, respectively. Motion Response Rate (MRR) measures the frequency of valid motion responses, while ROI Motion Magnitude (RMM) quantifies motion strength within the affected region. (2) Video Quality.CLIP-T and PickScore[(Kirstain et al., 2023)] evaluate text alignment and learned human preference, respectively. We further adopt Motion Smoothness, Aesthetic Quality, and Imaging Quality from VBench [(Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025a)] to assess temporal consistency, visual appeal, and image fidelity. (3) Physics Alignment. For cases with paired ground-truth videos, we follow the Physics-IQ evaluation protocol [(Motamed et al., 2026)]. Spatial IoU, Spatiotemporal IoU (ST-IoU), and Weighted IoU measure agreement between the generated and ground-truth motion regions, while MSE measures their pixel-level discrepancy.

item.title: 潜空间世界模型一次决策要几十秒：SOAR 发现规划只看「排序」，于是把 rollout 大胆压掉 ｜ SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
item.description:
一句话：采样式规划器只用预测代价给候选排序——只要排序不变，rollout 压缩多少都行。

要点：

  • 成本来源：潜空间世界模型做规划时，要通过 transformer 预测器** rollout 数百条候选动作序列**，于是一次决策可能花掉几十秒
  • 已有加速沿用了视觉-语言模型里的做法——**剪掉空间 token**；但作者指出采样式规划器只用预测代价**排序**候选，因此 rollout 可以自由压缩，**只要排序不变**
  • SOAR 据此提出免训练的 rollout 压缩方法，目标是保持排序一致而非保持数值精确

为什么值得看：「只要保序、不必保真」是一个非常好的目标降级：把精度要求换成排序不变性，能换来数量级的加速。这类「想清楚下游到底要什么」的思路，比通用加速器更适用于引擎里的规划循环。

中文摘要：潜空间世界模型在规划时需要让 transformer 预测器 rollout 数百条候选动作序列，因此单次决策可能耗时数十秒。已有加速方法沿用视觉语言模型的做法，剪掉空间 token；但这篇指出一个关键区别：基于采样的规划器只使用预测代价来给候选排序，因此 rollout 完全可以自由压缩，只要**候选之间的排序保持不变**即可。SOAR 据此提出一种免训练的 rollout 压缩方法，把优化目标从「数值精确」改成「排序一致」。对需要把世界模型规划器塞进运行时循环的团队，这种按下游需求重新定义精度的做法，比通用加速器更对症。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout
Compression for Latent World Model Planning

Abstract

Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3× speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.

1 Introduction

Latent world models [20, 2, 14] plan by imagination. At every decision, the cross-entropy method (CEM) [12] samples hundreds of action sequences, rolls each one out autoregressively through a transformer predictor over a dense grid of patch features, and keeps the candidates with the lowest predicted cost. With the original budget, one planning call of the released JEPA-WM [14] takes 20–50 seconds on an H100 and recurs at each replanning step.

The natural remedy, and the one recent work has adopted, is token reduction. Sparse Imagination [5], DDP-WM [18], Scope-WM [11] and CostGrad [16] all decide which spatial tokens the predictor should process in full. This framing is inherited from vision-language models [3, 4, 15, 1], where an image is encoded once and the kept tokens must preserve its content. A planner differs in what it consumes. A vision-language model consumes the tokens themselves, whereas CEM consumes only an ordering: it keeps the K lowest-cost candidates and discards the costs. A cheaper rollout is therefore exactly as good as the dense one whenever it selects the same elites, however much its predicted features differ. This changes the question. Token selection asks which tokens best preserve a frame; a planner asks which computation, if removed, reorders the candidates. Because the predictor consumes its own outputs, the answer need not be spatial: an error at the first step is inherited by every later prediction and by the cost; one at the last step is not.

We therefore take the candidate ranking as the criterion and ask along which axis a latent world-model rollout can be reduced without reordering the candidates. We prune along four axes at comparable compute—space, the context frame, the rollout step and predictor depth—using frozen released checkpoints, the original planner budget, and more than 80,000 closed-loop episodes on seven navigation and manipulation tasks. Three findings emerge, and together they determine the design of our method.

  • •

    Which tokens matters little. At a 50% budget, rules from vision-language models are near or below random selection, and planning-aware selectors stop 5 to 8 points below the dense model, within a few points of a fixed checkerboard, as shown in Sec.4.1.

  • •

    When matters: the first step anchors the ranking. Step 0 is the only step that reads the real observation. Computing it in full and compressing only later steps recovers 5.4 points lost to spatial pruning, while spending comparable compute on the last step instead drops success to 0.66 of dense, as shown in Sec.4.2.

  • •

    Context must be kept but not recomputed. After step 0, half of the predictor’s work recomputes the previous frame only to provide keys and values. Dropping that frame is free on navigation and pushing but costs 12 to 43 points on robot-arm reaching; reusing its cached keys and values removes the trade-off and matches dense success at a 1.76× speedup without knowing the task, as demonstrated in Secs.4.3 and 6.

    • The findings also reveal that tasks differ in what they need: halving the spatial positions costs Push-T 27% of its dense successes but leaves MetaWorld Reach unchanged, whereas dropping the context frame does the opposite, as illustrated in Fig.3b. Once the context is cached, the only remaining question is how far the newest frame can be compressed, which varies across tasks and individual decisions.

    We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression online, choosing at every decision how much computation the candidate ranking needs. At each decision, SOAR rolls out 16 candidates of the first CEM population under three nested token budgets and selects the smallest budget whose Spearman rank correlation with the full budget reaches a threshold, so each decision is compressed as far as its ranking allows. This adaptive choice is affordable because the findings fix everything else: SOAR computes the first step in full and reads the context frame from a cache, which leaves a single scalar per decision, the token budget of the newest frame. The probe adds 1–2% to the planning time and requires neither task labels nor training. Without being told the task, SOAR compresses most on MetaWorld and RoboCasa, least on Maze, and differently across decisions on Push-T and Wall, as shown in . It reaches dense-level success at a 2.3× speedup, whereas every cheaper fixed budget loses successes on tasks that need spatial detail, as detailed in Sec.6.

    Contributions.

    Online criterion. We recast rollout compression for sampling-based planning as preserving the elite ranking rather than the predicted features, as established by Proposition1, and show that this criterion is cheap enough to check at every decision: 16 probe candidates, 1–2% of the planning time. Diagnosis. In a closed-loop study along four axes at comparable compute on frozen released checkpoints, we find that spatial selection saturates regardless of the selector, that the first step anchors the ranking, that the context frame must be kept but not recomputed, and that tasks fail along different axes, so no fixed budget is safe for all of them. Method. SOAR keeps what the diagnosis shows must stay exact and lets the ranking decide the rest, reaching dense-level success at a 2.3× speedup and 98% of it at 2.5× with no training and no task label, while avoiding the task-specific failures of cheaper fixed budgets.

    2 Related Work

    Token reduction for vision transformers and VLMs.

    Token merging [3] combines similar tokens inside ViTs, FastV [4] drops visual tokens after the early layers of a vision-language model based on attention scores, DART [15] removes duplicated tokens, and DivPrune [1] keeps a diverse subset. These methods accelerate a single forward pass, whereas a planner calls the predictor repeatedly inside a search and uses only the ranking of the resulting costs; rules that switch token sets inside the network, which work well in VLMs, are harmful in planning, as shown in Sec.4.2.

    Efficient world-model planning.

    Latent world models such as DINO-WM [20], V-JEPA 2-AC [2] and JEPA-WMs [14] plan by optimizing actions with the cross-entropy method [12] over predicted patch features. Several methods reduce the number of spatial tokens the predictor processes. Sparse Imagination [5] trains a predictor on random token subsets and draws a new random mask at each planning step; CostGrad [16] selects tokens without training from gradients of the planning cost and keeps the subset fixed across candidates and CEM iterations of a decision; DDP-WM [18] and Scope-WM [11] train predictors that localize the dynamic tokens of each predicted frame and update the remaining ones with a cheaper module. These methods differ in how tokens are selected, but all reduce computation in space. We instead ask along which axis of the rollout redundancy lies, and show that the answer depends more on when computation is spent than on which tokens are kept.

    Adaptive computation in planning.

    A few works adapt how much computation is spent. Sparse Imagination includes a variant that raises or lowers its drop ratio between CEM iterations according to the variance of latent rollouts [5]; CF-Prune [9] prunes future-frame tokens in diffusion-based world action models and keeps dense computation during phases it detects as precision-critical; SufficientPlan [10] certifies a reduced search budget for each model–task pair from paired closed-loop evaluations and caches static context across search iterations. SOAR differs in its signal and its granularity: it selects the token budget at each decision from the agreement of candidate rankings, the quantity a sampling-based planner actually consumes, rather than from prediction uncertainty or offline closed-loop evaluation, with a frozen, dense-trained predictor.

    Caching in autoregressive video and world models.

    Reusing the keys and values of past frames is standard in autoregressive generation. M* [8] applies KV caching to V-JEPA 2-AC planning rollouts, while TempCache [13], WorldKV [17] and X-Cache [19] compress, retrieve or skip cached computation in video world models. Caching is an existing building block; we show that it resolves a pruning trade-off because some tasks need the context frame and others do not, as detailed in Sec.4.3.

    Temporal context in world models.

    VLWM [6] notes strong redundancy between adjacent frames and replaces step-by-step rollouts with variable-length jumps, and ActSWM [7] reports that richer visual context can make predictors insensitive to actions. Our results refine both for planning: whether the previous frame matters depends on the task dynamics, and when it does, coverage of the frame matters more than its motion.

    3 Preliminaries and Evaluation Protocol

    World model and planner.

    We use the released JEPA-WM checkpoints [14]. A frozen pretrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder maps each image to a 16×16 grid of patch features; RoboCasa instead uses DINOv3 ViT-L/16. An action-conditioned AdaLN transformer predicts the next feature grid; it has 6 layers and width 384 for Maze, Wall, Push-T and MetaWorld, and 12 layers and width 1024 for RoboCasa. Planning uses CEM with N=300 candidates and K=10 elites for 30 iterations on Maze, Wall and Push-T or 15 on MetaWorld and RoboCasa. The horizon H is 6 or 3 steps, and the L2 cost compares the final predicted features, including proprioception when available, with the goal.

    What a planner needs from a rollout.

    Let c(a) be the cost of candidate a under the dense rollout and c̃(a) its cost under a cheaper rollout. Each CEM iteration only refits its sampling distribution to the elite set 𝔼=top_K{-c(aᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^N. A reduced rollout therefore leaves the planner unchanged whenever it selects the same elites, even if c̃ differs greatly from c in value. This is a weaker requirement than faithful feature prediction, and it is the lens we use throughout: a reduction is harmful when it reorders candidates, not when it changes the predicted features.

    Anatomy of a rollout.

    The predictor attends over a sliding window of two frames. At step 0 it reads the observation; from step 1 on it reads the previous frame and the newest frame, recomputes both, and keeps only the newest frame’s output, as illustrated in Fig.2. For a horizon H, a candidate rollout therefore processes 256+512(H-1) tokens per layer, and half of the work after step 0 is spent on a context frame whose outputs are discarded. We count compute as tokens times layers relative to the dense rollout and report the measured speedup alongside it. Unless stated otherwise, pruned positions are removed from the state, and the cost is evaluated on the retained positions of the final frame, with the goal features restricted to the same positions. Keeping stale positions barely changes success: 0.89 versus 0.90.

    Tasks and closed-loop evaluation.

    We evaluate on Maze, Wall, Push-T, MetaWorld Reach (MW-R) and Reach-Wall (MW-RW), and RoboCasa Reach (Rc-R) and Place (Rc-Pl). Each evaluation runs 96 episodes on the first five tasks and 32 on RoboCasa, with the original episode lengths and replanning frequency. All methods share initial states and goals, which gives paired comparisons. We report the task-averaged success rate relative to the dense model evaluated in the same batch, and 95% intervals from a paired bootstrap stratified by task using 10,000 resamples. Latency is the wall-clock time of one complete planning call, including encoding, every auxiliary computation and the full CEM search, measured on a single H100 in FP32 and divided by the dense latency on the same task; we report its inverse as the speedup. SOAR reduces the number of tokens processed and is orthogonal to lower-precision arithmetic and kernel compilation, which reduce the cost per token. Every method is compared with a dense model run on the same episodes in the same batch. Tables1, 2 and 3 report success relative to this dense model, and Tab.4 reports absolute successes. In total, the study comprises more than 80,000 closed-loop episodes.

    4 Where Is a Planning Rollout Redundant?

    We study where a rollout of the frozen predictor can be reduced without hurting closed-loop planning: by examining spatial token selection in Sec.4.1, the timing of reduction in Sec.4.2, and the role of the context frame in Sec.4.3.

    4.1 Spatial token selection saturates

    We first apply the standard recipe: keep 128 of the 256 spatial positions per frame for the whole rollout and choose them with a selection rule. We adapt token merging (ToMe) [3], attention-based FastV [4], duplication-based DART [15] and diversity-based DivPrune [1], and evaluate CostGrad [16] and Guard-rank, a probe-guided variant that picks recipes by rank agreement with the dense model.

    A narrow ceiling.

    Table1 shows the result. Selection rules from vision-language models fail in planning: ToMe and DART achieve only 0.51 and 0.34 of dense success, below random selection at 0.60; FastV and DivPrune barely exceed random selection. Planning-aware selectors do better but stop in a narrow band. The best, Guard-rank, reaches 0.89 of dense success, and CostGrad 0.84. A further family fits this picture. Probe-action responses improve on a fixed checkerboard by at most 1.2 points on paired episodes; shuffling the responses costs about 9 points.

    Interpretation.

    Among planning-aware selectors the spread is small compared with their gap to the dense model, and on matched episodes a content-agnostic checkerboard is as good as response-based selection. Saliency in the VLM sense, meaning tokens that attract attention or carry distinct content, is not what a dynamics predictor needs; uniform coverage of the grid is a better prior, a pattern that also holds for the context frame, as Sec.4.3 shows. As Sec.4.2 shows, the limiting factor is not which tokens are kept but the fact that the same reduced token set is used at every step of every rollout, including the step that reads the real observation. Implication for SOAR: which tokens are kept matters little, so SOAR keeps a fixed nested checkerboard and decides only how many tokens to compute.

    4.2 When matters more than which

    We now hold the selection rule fixed, using a nested checkerboard, and vary where tokens are removed at comparable compute, as reported in Tabs.2 and 3. Space keeps 64, 128 or 192 positions in every frame of the rollout. Context frame keeps the newest frame complete and keeps 0, 64 or 128 positions of the previous frame; with 0 the predictor sees a single frame. Rollout step computes the first one or two steps in full and continues with 128 positions, or does the reverse and completes only the final step. Depth uses all positions for the first m layers and a checkerboard thereafter.

    The first step anchors the ranking.

    Computing only step 0 in full and continuing with 128 positions raises success from 0.90 to 1.03 of dense at a 1.82× speedup, matching the dense model, as shown in Fig.3a. The gain holds in every evaluation, with an average margin of 5.4 points over the 128-position rollout, and the configuration retains 0.94 of dense success in Tab.3. Placing comparable compute on the last step instead achieves only 0.66 of dense success. The asymmetry follows from the structure of the rollout. Step 0 is the only step that reads the real observation, and every later prediction, and hence the cost of every candidate, is conditioned on its output. An error there is inherited by the entire rollout, whereas an error at a later step affects only what follows it. Completing the last step is worse than pruning it, because the dense predictor sees an imputed state unlike anything seen in training.

    Reduce the input, not the computation in flight.

    Processing all positions in the first layers and pruning afterwards is worse than pruning from the input: 0.58 and 0.56 versus 0.89 of dense, with Push-T falling to 5% and 0% of its dense successes. We attribute this to a distribution shift: tokens that have attended to the full grid suddenly lose half of their neighbours, a configuration the dense-trained predictor never encounters. FastV and DART, which keep the first two layers complete and prune afterwards, show the same pattern: they are slower than plain spatial pruning and no more accurate, as Tab.1 shows; DART also fails completely on Push-T. Together with the last-step result, this gives a simple rule for frozen predictors: a uniformly subsampled input is tolerated, but changing the token set inside a forward pass, or running the full model on an imputed state, is not. The exact first step respects this rule: reduction happens only between steps and feeds the next step a cleanly subsampled input.

    Tasks fail along different axes.

    Push-T and MW-R form the double dissociation shown in Fig.3b. Halving the positions keeps 73% of Push-T’s dense successes but 108% on MW-R; dropping the context frame keeps 95% on Push-T but only 18% on MW-R. Pushing a block requires the spatial detail of the contact, whereas reaching with an arm requires information carried by the previous frame, as examined in Sec.4.3. No single uniform budget serves both. Implication for SOAR: the first step must stay exact, reductions must act on the input of a step, and the tolerable budget varies by task, so it must be chosen per decision.

    4.3 The context frame must be kept, not recomputed

    After step 0, half of every step recomputes the previous frame, whose outputs are discarded. Dropping it is therefore the largest single saving available: the predictor then processes only the newest frame. We measure its effect on every task; detailed results are in the supplementary material.

    The value of context is a property of the task.

    On Maze, Wall, Push-T and Rc-Pl, the single-frame predictor matches the dense model, with mean differences between -2.6 and +2.6 points, so the planner does not use the information in the previous frame. On MetaWorld the same change is catastrophic: MW-R loses 31 to 43 points and MW-RW 12 to 30. Rc-R lies in between, with a mean loss of 6.8 points. The split between the first four tasks and MetaWorld is consistent across our evaluations. This is consistent with a single feature grid fixing the configuration of the scene but not its motion. In navigation and pushing, the agent’s next state is largely determined by the current configuration and the action; in arm reaching, the predictor needs two frames to infer the arm’s current velocity.

    How much context, not which context.

    When the context is needed, its value grows smoothly with the number of retained positions: success rises from 0.83 of dense without context to 0.95 with 64 checkerboard positions and 1.00 with the full frame. Selecting positions by the magnitude of their predicted motion reaches only 0.92 of dense success versus 0.95 for a fixed checkerboard at 64 positions. A random subset of about 162 positions also performs comparably to a motion-selected subset of the same size, reaching 0.99 versus 1.01 of dense success. Motion-selected positions cluster around moving objects and cover only 35–62% of the 2×2 cells, whereas a checkerboard covers all of them. The predictor reads the previous frame as a whole, and coverage matters more than concentration on motion. This mirrors the saturation of spatial selection in Sec.4.1.

    A trade-off that pruning cannot resolve.

    If the task type is known, using the single-frame predictor on quasi-static tasks and the first-step-complete rollout on arm tasks reaches 1.00 of dense success at a 1.89× speedup. This oracle shows the cost of the trade-off but requires a label that a planner does not have. Pruning forces a choice between keeping the context, which pays for recomputation on every task, and dropping it, which fails on arm tasks. Because the context frame was computed when it was newest, reading its cached keys and values keeps its information at the cost of a single-frame predictor. Implication for SOAR: keep the context frame, but read it from a cache.

    5 SOAR: Rank-Consistent Compression

    SOAR plans with a frozen latent world model at reduced cost by changing only how CEM evaluates candidate rollouts, as shown in Fig.4. We first establish the criterion in Sec.5.1, reduce the design space to one scalar in Sec.5.2, and select the budget online in Sec.5.3.

    5.1 Rank consistency as the compression criterion

    Let c(a) be the cost of candidate a under the dense rollout and c̃(a) its cost under a compressed rollout. CEM samples N actions from ℕ(μ,σ²), selects the K lowest-cost indices as 𝔼, and refits (μ,σ) to their actions.

    Proposition 1.

    If c̃=g∘c for a strictly increasing function g, then, given the same random samples, CEM selects the same elite sets, follows the same sequence of sampling distributions and returns the same action under c̃ as under c.

    Proof.

    A strictly increasing g preserves the order of the N costs, so the K lowest-cost candidates, and hence 𝔼, are unchanged. The refit uses only the elite actions, not their costs, so (μ,σ) after the iteration is unchanged; induction over iterations gives the claim. ∎

    The proposition has two consequences. First, the error of a compressed rollout in feature or cost space is the wrong criterion: it penalizes compressions that change every cost but none of the decisions. Second, what matters is membership in the top-K set, which for K=10 of N=300 candidates requires near-perfect agreement at the top of the ranking. The argument holds for any planner that uses costs only through their order, but not for cost-weighted schemes such as MPPI.

    5.2 Reducing the design space

    Measuring rank consistency online is affordable because the analysis of Sec.4 fixes all choices but one.

    Exact first step.

    Step 0 is the only step that reads the real observation, and every later prediction is conditioned on it. Keeping all 256 positions recovers 5.4 points on average over compressing every step; see Sec.4.2.

    Cached context.

    From step 1 on, the predictor attends to the previous frame through the per-layer keys and values stored when that frame was the newest one, in the spirit of KV caching for autoregressive models [8], so each frame is computed exactly once. This keeps the context that arm tasks need, as Sec.4.3 shows, at the cost of a single-frame predictor; from step 2 on, the cached keys and values carry one more frame of history than a recomputed context frame, as detailed in the supplement.

    One knob remains.

    The only remaining decision is how many positions of the newest frame to compute at steps 1,…,H-1. SOAR uses one of three nested checkerboard sets, B={256,192,128}, because uniform coverage matters more than content-based selection, as shown in Secs.4.1 and 4.3. It applies the reduction to each step’s input so the predictor never switches token sets within a forward pass, consistent with Sec.4.2. For a horizon of 6, the three budgets cut compute by 1.8×, 2.3× and 3.1×, close to the measured speedups of 1.8×, 2.2× and 3.0× reported in Tab.4.

    5.3 Online budget selection
