    Supplementary Material

    A Evaluation and Implementation Details

    This supplement provides the evaluation settings, full spatial-baseline results, temporal ablations, details of the cached rollout and ranking probe, additional SOAR analyses, trained-model controls, and alternative acceleration experiments. References to numbered sections and tables in the main paper are explicitly marked as such; all tables here use an S prefix.

    A.1 Models, tasks, and planning budget

    We use released JEPA-WM checkpoints [14]. The visual encoder is frozen and runs on the complete image in all experiments. Each frame has 16×16=256 patch positions. The predictor is an action-conditioned AdaLN transformer with six layers and width 384 for Maze, Wall, Push-T and MetaWorld, and twelve layers and width 1024 for RoboCasa. The corresponding encoders are DINOv2 ViT-S/14 and DINOv3 ViT-L/16.

    CEM samples 300 candidates, selects ten elites, and retains the released search budget. Maze, Wall and Push-T use 30 search iterations, a horizon of six, and execute six actions per decision. MetaWorld uses 15 iterations, a horizon of six, and executes three actions per decision. RoboCasa uses 15 iterations, a horizon of three, and executes one action per decision. An episode has one planning call on the first three tasks, seven on MetaWorld and twelve on RoboCasa. The remaining horizon can shrink near the end of an episode. The objective uses the final predicted frame’s L2 distance to the encoded goal, with a 0.1-weighted proprioceptive term where applicable.

    Every complete evaluation contains 96 episodes per task on the first five tasks and 32 per RoboCasa task, or 544 episodes across seven tasks for one evaluation seed. Three such seeds give 1,632 episodes. Development panels and offline probe diagnostics are reported separately from complete closed-loop evaluations.

    A.2 Aggregation and uncertainty

    Let y_m,t,s,i∈{0,1} be the outcome for method m, task t, evaluation seed s and episode i. The task success rate and macro-average are

    S_m,t=(1)/(|Sₜ|)∑ₛ(1)/(n_t,s)∑ᵢy_m,t,s,i, S̄ₘ=(1)/(|T|)∑ₜS_m,t.

    		(S1)

    Success relative to dense is S̄ₘ/S̄_D, using the dense control for the corresponding evaluation. A difference in percentage points is 100(S̄ₘ-S̄_D). Task macro-averages weight all seven tasks equally despite their different episode counts.

    Methods share initial states and goals within a comparison. The main paper’s confidence intervals use 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples stratified by task, preserving the method–control pairing. For tables with seed SDs, captions specify the SD convention and whether the seeds refer to training or evaluation.

    A.3 Timing and memory

    Evaluations use H100 GPUs and FP32 without autocast. The timing scope is one complete GC_Agent.act call: observation encoding, token selection or ranking probes, CEM search and all auxiliary predictor evaluations. Simulator execution, goal pre-encoding and file I/O are excluded. SOAR timing excludes the first five decisions of each job as warm-up. Latency is the mean wall-clock time per planning decision.

    For each task, let L_m,t denote the complete planning latency. The main speed metric uses rₘ=|T|⁻¹∑ₜL_m,t/L_D,t and reports 1/rₘ. This task-normalized metric weights tasks equally; ∑ₜL_D,t/∑ₜL_m,t instead weights by dense latency. Summaries that use other timing weights specify them in their captions. Spatial budgets denote retained position counts, and complete planning latency is measured separately.

    Timing summaries average all recorded runs within each experiment family and use the dense control from that family. TableS3 reports peak PyTorch allocated memory.

    B Spatial Baselines and Recovery Interfaces

    B.1 How the methods are adapted

    Random samples 128 distinct positions without replacement. DivPrune [1] uses greedy diversity selection from cosine distances between DINO features. CostGrad [16] performs a full one-step probe, differentiates its goal error with respect to visual input tokens, and retains the 128 largest gradient norms. Only input gradients are computed; predictor weights are not updated. Its mask stays fixed across candidates, CEM iterations and rollout steps of a real decision and is reconsidered when a new observation arrives.

    ToMe [3] performs bipartite matching at the predictor entrance, merges to 128 groups, uses proportional attention, and reconstructs through a delta update. FastV [4] runs the first two layers on the full grid, then uses actual attention scores to choose 128 positions on each forward pass. DART [15] also computes two full layers before selecting visual pivots and removing redundant features. These methods compute full-grid layers before pruning, adding work relative to pruning at the predictor entrance.

    B.2 State reconstruction and goal cost

    The spatial adaptations in Tab.S1 use method-specific reconstruction. For Random and DivPrune, deleted positions retain the preceding frame’s features and the goal cost uses the complete grid. CostGrad uses the retained-position cost. The compact rollout used for the temporal-axis study propagates only retained positions and restricts the encoded goal to those positions.

    TableS4 reports an additional complete evaluation of the reconstruction interface. CostGrad-copy restores deleted positions with previous features and evaluates the full-grid goal cost. Its MW-R and Rc-R means are 36.11% and 16.67%, compared with 36.46% and 15.62% for retained-cost CostGrad.

    Guard-rank selects a token-selection/reconstruction recipe at each real planning decision. It evaluates 17 fixed action probes and compares the action rankings from six recipes with the dense ranking to choose the recipe. Grid-guide retains a fixed checkerboard, evaluates nine full probes, and uses them to choose a reference trajectory for correcting candidate predictions. Guard-rank gains 2.33 macro-average points over CostGrad-copy. In the recovery controls’ five-task normalized timing summary, planning latency is 12.574 seconds/decision for Guard-rank and 10.963 for CostGrad-copy, an increase of 14.7%. Its Push-T success falls by 9.38 points, and success also decreases on both RoboCasa tasks.

    Per-task variation and timing outliers.

    DART records no Push-T successes, while FastV retains much more of the dense Push-T performance despite its lower overall mean. Rc-Pl exhibits substantial variation across seeds, as reflected in the SDs in Tab.S1. The FastV/Maze run at seed 101 takes 78.905 seconds per decision, contributing to the 48.418-second task mean. DivPrune/Rc-Pl at seed 1001 takes 59.971 seconds, contributing to its 37.272-second task mean. The sources of these timing outliers have not been identified.

    C Temporal Ablations and Context Coverage

    The four-axis study fixes the spatial selection rule and changes where computation is reduced. Spatial variants retain 64, 128 or 192 positions at every step. Context variants retain the full newest frame and 0, 64 or 128 positions of its predecessor. Step variants compute the first step, first two steps, or last step in full. Depth variants compute a full prefix of predictor layers and reduce the positions thereafter. These configurations retain the original planner budget.

    C.1 First-step anchoring across evaluations

    TableS5 expands the repeated temporal evaluations. For the original four matched evaluation seeds (5001, 6001, 8001 and 9001), anchoring improves macro success in every case relative to the 128-position rollout. The mean difference from the rounded entries is 5.43 points. The task split uses a single frame for Maze, Wall, Push-T and Rc-Pl, and the first-step-full two-frame rollout for MW-R, MW-RW and Rc-R. This task-informed split was determined using seed 5001; its entry is marked as in-sample.

    C.2 Dropping the previous frame

    TableS6 reports the per-task seed breakdown. Removing the previous frame reduces success on both MetaWorld tasks in every evaluation. Navigation and pushing have smaller average changes, with variation across seeds: Maze at seed 8001 loses 14.6 points.

    C.3 Context amount versus context selection

    With the newest frame complete, checkerboard context selection achieves 46.4% macro success at 64 positions, versus 45.1% for motion selection. At about 162 positions, random and motion-selected subsets achieve 48.6% and 49.4%, respectively (Tab.S7). Motion-selected positions cover 35–62% of the 2×2 grid cells, while the checkerboard covers every cell. These observations support spatial coverage as a useful prior for context selection.

    D Cached Rollouts and Rank Consistency

    D.1 Cached rollout reference

    KV caching is an existing autoregressive inference technique [8]. The first prediction uses the complete observed feature grid. In the uncompressed cached variant, the next step is identical to the original rollout: the cached observation was computed alone at step 0, as it would be when recomputed as the oldest frame of the two-frame window. From step 2 onward, the cached representations were computed while attending to their own predecessor. They therefore contain an additional historical dependency compared with recomputing that frame in isolation as the oldest frame of a fresh window.

    The cached rollout corresponds to a single forward pass of the same predictor over the imagined trajectory with a banded frame-causal attention mask. Each frame attends to itself and its immediate predecessor, and information can propagate through layers. Cached keys and values at each layer match this reference. Rotary position encodings use absolute temporal indices. The current–previous temporal displacement remains one, as in the original window, because the corresponding rotary attention scores depend on index differences.

    The full-budget SOAR variant isolates the first-step-full cached rollout, while the lower budgets additionally compress the newest-frame computation. Budget selection is held fixed within a real planning decision. The final cost compares predicted state and goal features at the same retained spatial indices.

    D.2 Token-computation accounting

    For H predicted steps and L predictor layers, dense visual token–layer work is proportional to

    C_D=L [256+512(H-1)].

    		(S2)

    With a complete first step and a cached predecessor, computing b newest-frame positions at each remaining step gives

    C_b=L [256+b(H-1)].

    		(S3)

    For H=6, the ratios C_b/C_D at b=256,192,128 are 0.545, 0.432 and 0.318. For H=3 they are 0.600, 0.500 and 0.400. These ratios account for visual token–layer work. Complete planning latency additionally includes probes, encoding and CEM updates, as well as kernel overhead and attention over cached keys.

    D.3 Ranking criterion and CEM updates

    The proposition in main-paper Sec. 5.1 relates candidate ordering to CEM updates. At an iteration, let 𝔼_D and 𝔼_b be the ten lowest-cost candidates under the dense and reduced costs. If 𝔼_D=𝔼_b and refitting uses only their actions, the next CEM distribution is unchanged. With the same random draws, this equality inductively preserves the complete search. A strictly increasing transform of all candidate costs is one sufficient way to ensure it. Consistent tie handling is required when costs tie.

    SOAR estimates rank consistency from 16 candidates in the first 300-candidate CEM population. It selects the smallest tested budget whose probe-cost Spearman correlation with the full-budget cached rollout reaches the shared threshold. CEM then uses that budget to evaluate its candidates and refit the search distribution.

    D.4 Probe implementation

    The 16 probe indices are deterministic and evenly spaced in the initial population:

    pᵢ=round(299i/15), i=0,…,15.

    		(S4)

    The 16 action sequences are evaluated at nested checkerboard budgets of 128, 192 and 256 positions. Nonconstant probe-cost vectors use Spearman correlation with average ranks for ties; the constant-input branch assigns a selection score of one, which passes both thresholds. Budgets are tested in order, 128 then 192, with 256 as fallback. The budget stays fixed for the remaining CEM evaluations of that decision. One-step decisions use the complete first step and skip the probe.

    The full-budget cached rollout supplies the reference costs. For each tested budget, probe goal features use the matching final spatial positions. The probe reuses candidates already sampled for the first CEM population.

    The probe adds at most 48 rollouts per decision, two-thirds at reduced budgets. This is 1.07% of the 300×15 or 0.53% of the 300×30 candidate rollouts in the main search.

    Implementation checks.

    The 261 checks use small randomly initialized predictors with the released architectures, including twelve-layer RoboCasa. They verify recomputed context against the original rollout, caches against an independent banded-mask reference, unchanged weights and CEM random-number state, and one-step horizons. Forcing 256 or 128 positions reproduces fixed-budget actions. Decision audits recompute ranks and budgets from logged costs and check indices, forward counts, rollout layouts and final positions.

    E SOAR: Budget Allocation and Success Profiles

    We expand main-paper Table 4 with per-task latency ratios, budget allocations and probe diagnostics.

    E.1 What adaptivity changes

    At τ=0.9, SOAR achieves 49.26% task-macro success versus 48.96% for dense planning, at a 2.31× speedup. Fixed 192 has the same task-macro success at a 2.21× speedup. Relative to fixed 192, SOAR records seven more Push-T successes and six more Wall successes, four fewer on MW-R and five fewer on MW-RW. TableS9 reports the selected budgets by task and decision.

    The selected budgets vary across both tasks and decisions. Maze uses 256 positions at 97% of decisions, while MetaWorld and RoboCasa select 128 positions more frequently. Wall and Push-T use all three budgets. At τ=0.8, the latency ratio is 0.394 (2.54×); 77% of Push-T decisions use 128 positions, and Push-T records eleven fewer successes than dense, compared with four fewer at τ=0.9.

    E.2 Operating-point criteria and paired comparisons

    The experiment used three point-estimate criteria: a latency ratio at most 0.50, macro success at least the full-budget cached variant minus one percentage point, and Push-T success within five points of dense. At τ=0.9, the respective values are 0.433, -0.89 points and -4.17 points. At τ=0.8, the latter two values are -1.93 and -11.46 points, so that setting does not meet those criteria.

    The paired-bootstrap differences for τ=0.9, with 95% confidence intervals, are +0.30 points versus dense ([-4.17,4.91]), -0.89 versus fixed 256 ([-4.91,3.27]), and 0.00 versus fixed 192 ([-4.17,4.17]).

    E.3 Development probe diagnostics

    TableS10 reports ranking diagnostics on a separate development panel. Planning uses 256 positions, and lower-budget predictions measure rank correlation. The panel uses eight episodes on each of the first five tasks and four per RoboCasa task, all at development seed 7027.

    On the development panel, Push-T has a median probe-cost correlation of 0.85 at 128 positions. In the closed-loop evaluation in Tab.S8, fixed 128 records seventeen fewer Push-T successes than dense. The shared thresholds 0.9 and 0.8 were fixed from development probe statistics before evaluation, as described in main-paper Sec. 5.3.

    F Trained Sparse-Model Controls

    The trained-model comparison evaluates adaptations of Sparse Imagination (SI) [5], Scope [11] and DDP [18] on five tasks using the CEM budget in Sec. A.1. Each adaptation has its own continued-training dense control, giving six branches. Training seeds are 0, 42 and 2026, and evaluation seeds are 1, 101 and 1001. The 270 task–branch–training-seed–evaluation-seed combinations comprise 25,920 method episodes.

    Training budgets and checkpoint choice.

    SI receives 10,000 updates on Maze, Wall and MetaWorld and 7,500 on Push-T. Scope includes 3,000 selector updates and 5,000 fresh-dynamics updates. DDP includes 2,000 localization, 5,000 primary-dynamics and 10,000 cumulative LRM updates. For each branch, checkpoint selection follows a fixed validation-loss criterion; closed-loop success is then measured using the selected checkpoint.

    Scope has the highest five-task macro success among the three trained adaptations and gains 7.52 points on MW-RW against its matched dense branch. SI and DDP have lower macro success than their corresponding dense branches. The training-free experiments use frozen released checkpoints.

    Dense-Scope planning latency reaches 65.531 seconds/decision on Wall at training seed 42 and 66.951 on Maze at training seed 2026. Dense-SI and Dense-DDP also have slow MW-RW runs at training seed 42.

    G Alternative Planning and Selection Strategies

    G.1 Dense rechecking within sparse CEM

    The multi-fidelity experiment in Tab.S13 keeps a 128-position checkerboard for the main search. At each CEM iteration, it recomputes selected candidate trajectories at all 256 positions, uses their full costs to select elites, and refits the CEM distribution to the elite action sequences. The fixed-query controls recheck 20 or 80 trajectories per iteration. Risk-adaptive expansion and stratified witnesses expand the full-query set in stages while retaining the same spatial mask.

    Fixed 80 rechecks restores 6.15 macro points over Grid. Risk-adaptive expansion reaches fewer successes at a higher macro latency: 95.78% of search rounds trigger expansion and 94.04% reach the third stage, leaving an average of 77.11 full queries per round. Stratified witnesses reaches the third stage in 90.29% of rounds, with only a 0.15-point mean gain over fixed 80 and slightly greater latency. Full-cost rechecking determines elite selection within CEM. The planner executes the action prefix of the refitted mean sequence without an additional full-rollout recheck.

    Dense/Rc-Pl at seed 2001 takes 125.468 seconds, versus 50.686 and 50.968 for the other two seeds. The source of this timing difference has not been identified.

    G.2 Action-response token selection

    Nine fixed action probes describe each position’s response to actions. The selectors retain 128 positions by response magnitude or complementarity; a shuffled-correspondence control breaks the association between responses and positions. This experiment contains four new methods, 28 jobs and 2,176 method episodes.

    Response complementarity averages 41.22%, versus Grid’s 40.03% and magnitude selection’s 40.33%. Its gains concentrate on Push-T (52 versus 41 successes out of 96) and Rc-Pl (18 versus 13 out of 32), with losses on both MetaWorld tasks. Its total successes are 233/544 versus Grid’s 237/544, illustrating why pooled success counts and macro success can move in opposite directions.

    Complementarity and magnitude selection share an average of 123.38 of their 128 positions. Shuffling the association between positions and responses reduces macro success from 41.22% for complementarity to 31.40%.

    Complete planning latency, averaged equally across the seven tasks, is 18.716 seconds/decision for complementarity, 18.778 for magnitude selection and 18.714 for the shuffled control. Within the complementarity runs, the instrumented probe and selection times are 89.114 and 6.355 milliseconds. The mean across tasks of their combined share of complete planning time is 0.560%. The Grid-plus-probes run reproduces the Grid actions and outcomes and averages 20.181 seconds/decision. Its reused Grid control was timed in the earlier rechecking batch and averages 18.661 seconds/decision; the MW-R timings differ by approximately 2.14× between these batches.

    Probe-action ranking agreement is 85.59% for Grid, 86.77% for magnitude, 87.15% for complementarity and 79.34% for shuffled correspondence. These agreements are computed on the nine probe actions used for token selection.

    H Evaluation Coverage

    The spatial, recovery, trained, rechecking and response experiments comprise 54,208 formal method episodes, counting reused controls once. The four temporal campaigns contribute 25,024 more, for a subtotal of 79,232. Including cached-rollout and adaptive-budget evaluations brings the study above 80,000 method episodes, as reported in the main paper. Counts refer to executed method–episode pairs; paired comparisons share initial states and goals.

    The spatial, temporal and SOAR evaluations cover seven JEPA-WM tasks with the released CEM search budget. Trained sparse-model controls cover the first five tasks. Development panels provide the ranking and implementation diagnostics reported in Secs. D and E.

item.title: 120p 超分到可玩画质：Causal Diffusion 让游戏超分只依赖过去帧，而不是等未来帧 ｜ Causal Diffusion for Extreme Super-Resolution in Interactive Games
item.description:
一句话：在 120p 这种分辨率上，超分已经从「重建已有信息」变成「合成缺失细节」。

要点：

  • 问题被推到极端：现有游戏超分方法通常只做中等倍率，难以从**极低分辨率（如 120p）**恢复细节；在这个尺度上，超分的性质已经从「重建已有信息」变成「**合成缺失的视觉细节**」
  • 为什么不能直接上视频扩散：扩散模型提供了强生成先验，但它们**依赖未来帧**，这在交互式场景里不可用
  • 这篇因此采用**因果**扩散，只依赖过去帧来做极端超分，从而适配游戏运行时

为什么值得看：「未来帧」是视频扩散进游戏的死穴：无论是渲染还是交互，都不能等。把生成先验改成因果，才有可能在运行时用——这条与 11-21 Streaming-AAA、11-20 FlexVSR 是同一条约束下的不同解法。

中文摘要：现有的游戏超分方法通常只处理中等倍率，难以从极低分辨率（例如 120p）恢复细节；而在这种尺度上，超分的性质已经从「重建已有信息」转变为「合成缺失的视觉细节」。视频扩散模型虽有强大的生成先验，但它们依赖未来帧，这使其无法用于交互式场景。这篇因此提出一种因果扩散方案，只依赖过去帧完成极端超分，从而适配游戏运行时的约束。对需要从极低内部渲染分辨率恢复到可玩画质的管线，这是把生成先验真正接进实时渲染的关键一步。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

Causal Diffusion for Extreme Super-Resolution in Interactive Games

Abstract

Existing game super-resolution methods typically operate at moderate upscaling factors, struggling to recover fine visual details from extremely low-resolution inputs (e.g., 120p). At such resolutions, super-resolution shifts from reconstructing existing information toward synthesizing missing visual details. While video diffusion models offer powerful generative priors for this challenging task, their dependence on future frames limits their applicability to interactive games. We present CIDER, a causal diffusion framework for extreme game super-resolution that synthesizes high-frequency details from current and past low-resolution frames, guided by G-buffers (depth and motion vectors) to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency. We collect data from two AAA games (Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong). To reduce inference load, we develop a lightweight latent projection encoder tailored to ultra-low-resolution inputs, fine-tune a decoder (TAE) on our high-resolution outputs, and distill the diffusion model to reach interactive frame rates. Our experiments demonstrate high-fidelity 8× upscaling from 120p to 960p at around 13 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art game upscalers in visual quality and showing potential for 16× magnification.

1 Introduction

High-quality AAA games often require intensive rendering pipelines with ray tracing, which significantly limits their performance on budget GPUs or edge devices. Neural super-resolution has become an integral component of modern game rendering, enabling high-resolution visual experiences from low-resolution run-time shading. Commercial solutions such as DLSS [26], FSR [1], and XeSS [17] have demonstrated impressive reconstruction quality at moderate upscaling factors. However, how far can we push game super-resolution when the input resolution becomes extremely low? Existing methods typically operate at scaling factors of up to 4× per spatial dimension [50], leaving extreme upscaling ratios such as 8× or even 16× largely unexplored. At these scales, recovering high-fidelity details becomes fundamentally more challenging: an input frame at 120p contains only 1/64 of the pixels of its 960p output, with much of the texture, fine geometry, and high-frequency visual information missing (Fig. a, left).

Such extreme conditions shift super-resolution from primarily reconstructing existing information toward synthesizing missing visual details. Conventional game upscalers, often built on convolutional or other regression-based architectures [37, 13, 31], struggle when the input provides insufficient visual evidence. Diffusion models, in contrast, have demonstrated a remarkable ability to generate realistic, high-frequency content through learned generative priors [27, 44, 43]. This capability makes diffusion particularly promising for extreme game super-resolution, where recovering details directly from the low-resolution input is severely underconstrained. However, generative models also introduce the risk of hallucinating scene content, making fidelity to the original game rendering a critical requirement. As illustrated in Fig.3, extreme super-resolution demands not only plausible detail synthesis but also faithful preservation of scene geometry and appearance.

Applying video diffusion models to interactive games presents an additional challenge: future frames are unavailable. Unlike offline video super-resolution, where models can exploit bidirectional temporal information, interactive games must generate each frame as new gameplay unfolds. A practical approach must therefore operate causally while maintaining temporal consistency and preserving the scene’s geometry and appearance under dynamic motion. These requirements rule out the use of conventional offline video enhancement for extreme game super-resolution. Additionally, current real-time super-resolution approaches using diffusion models mostly generate chunks of frames at a time, which is not applicable to gaming as it leads to high latency. Therefore, super-resolution for gaming must focus on low latency for single frame generation instead of an amortized FPS metric.

To break these limitations, we present CIDER, Causal Interactive Diffusion for Extreme Resolution. By adapting the pretrained video diffusion model [10], CIDER synthesizes high-frequency details using only current and previous low-resolution frames, without relying on future observations nor accumulating generative errors. Similar to prior work [48], we further incorporate in-engine G-buffers, including depth and motion vectors, to guide the generative process with explicit geometric and motion information. Together with game-specific fine-tuning, these conditioning signals help preserve scene structure and temporal consistency while reducing generative artifacts (see a, right).

To make diffusion-based super-resolution suitable for interactive applications, we further optimize the inference pipeline. Specifically, we replace the computationally expensive VAE encoder in the diffusion transformer with a lightweight latent projection designed for ultra-low-resolution inputs and fine-tune a decoder (TAE) for high-resolution reconstruction. We further accelerate inference through student model distillation, temporally local causal attention with key-value caching, and optimized fused attention kernels. Together, these modifications allow our framework to process extreme super-resolution tasks at approximately 0.075 seconds per frame on an NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU, demonstrating the feasibility of causal diffusion-based generation under interactive constraints.

We evaluate CIDER on two graphically demanding AAA games, Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong. Our method achieves high-quality 8× super-resolution from 120p to 960p, substantially outperforming existing game upscalers in visual quality under such extreme input conditions. We further investigate the potential for 16× magnification and reconstruction from inputs as low as 60p. In summary, we make the following main contributions:

  • •

    We demonstrate the feasibility of diffusion-based super-resolution from severely undersampled game frames, achieving high-fidelity 8× upscaling from 120p to 960p, with potential for 16× magnification.

  • •

    We develop a causal diffusion framework that leverages historical low-resolution frames, in-engine G-buffers, and game-specific adaptation to synthesize high-frequency details at frame rates around 13 FPS.

  • •

    We introduce a dataset of 336k frames collected from two recent AAA games, all with corresponding G-buffer information in high-resolution.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video Super-Resolution and Causal Diffusion

    Video super-resolution (VSR) aggregates information across frames to recover missing details. Early deterministic methods, including recurrent networks [28] and bidirectional alignment frameworks [33, 6, 7, 22, 8], perform well at moderate scaling factors but produce overly smooth textures under severe undersampling, as pixel-wise losses average out uncertain high-frequency details [4]. Recent generative VSR methods instead leverage GAN and diffusion priors to synthesize realistic details [38, 49, 21, 32]. However, standard video diffusion models [3, 2] use bidirectional temporal attention across frame chunks, requiring future frames unavailable in interactive games where gameplay depends on live player input.

    Recent works enable online generation by adapting diffusion models into causal, autoregressive pipelines using rolling KV caches, causal attention masks, and sequential denoising [42, 15, 9, 19]. In VSR, Stream-DiffVSR [30] and FlashVSR [50] support past-frame guidance and low-step streaming inference. Even so, autoregressive video models can suffer from exposure bias and drift over long sequences [16], and generic video restorers lack explicit scene geometry and motion cues when inputs are heavily undersampled (8× to 16×). Instead, CIDER maintains causal history over projected low-resolution latents rather than feeding back synthesized high-resolution frames, and anchors generation directly to engine-provided G-buffers (depth and motion vectors), keeping details consistent with the underlying scene without needing future frames.

    2.2 Super-Resolution for Game Rendering

    Modern rendering pipelines rely on temporal super-resolution to reduce shading costs while maintaining high output resolution. Commercial upscalers such as NVIDIA DLSS [26], AMD FSR [1], and Intel XeSS [17], along with academic methods like Neural Supersampling [37] and ExtraNet [13], combine temporal accumulation with engine-generated depth and motion vectors to reproject past frames. Later academic works incorporate richer renderer buffers, such as surface normals and material attributes, for joint denoising and supersampling [31], game-specific reconstruction [25], and radiance demodulation [20]. Notably, RDG [48] processes G-buffers separately from aliased color inputs to better guide temporal feature refinement at up to 4× magnification.

    While these causal, geometry-aware methods perform well up to 4× scaling, they rely on temporal sub-pixel accumulation and reprojection. At extreme scaling factors (8×–16×, e.g., 120p gameplay), each input pixel spans 64 to 256 output pixels, leaving sub-pixel samples too sparse and disoccluded regions unrecoverable through reprojection alone. Rather than claiming G-buffer conditioning or causal processing as individually novel, CIDER combines both within generative diffusion, using depth and motion vectors to guide high-frequency synthesis where the color input provides insufficient evidence.

    2.3 Generative Priors for Visual Restoration

    When inputs are heavily degraded or upscaled by large factors, deterministic regression produces blurry outputs, making generative priors necessary to synthesize plausible high-frequency detail. In image restoration, GAN-based methods such as BSRGAN [45] and Real-ESRGAN [34] handle complex degradations, while diffusion-based approaches, including ResShift [44], DiffBIR [23], PASD [39], SeeSR [36], and SUPIR [43], use learned generative priors to balance realistic texture synthesis with fidelity to the input. For video, VideoGigaGAN [38] shows that high-factor magnification is possible, confirming that extreme upscaling itself is not new. However, standard image and offline video restorers operate without real-time causality or explicit scene constraints. Interactive games require online frame generation where synthesized details stay faithful to scene geometry and motion, which we explore at the highly restrictive 120p input resolution.

    2.4 Efficient Diffusion and Latent Representations

    Latent diffusion models [27, 10] reduce denoising costs by operating in a compressed space, yet VAE encoding, decoding, and iterative denoising remain too slow for interactive pipelines. To speed up inference, distribution matching distillation [41] enables few- or one-step generation, an approach adopted by recent video restoration models such as FlashVSR [50], alongside prediction-and-refinement methods like PS-SR [35]. In addition, standard VAE encoders in diffusion upscalers expect high-resolution inputs, requiring low-resolution frames to be upsampled before encoding and incurring unnecessary compute. Because our ultra-low-resolution inputs already match the spatial dimensions of the backbone’s compressed latent grid at 8× scaling, we replace the expensive upsample-and-encode path with a lightweight convolutional projector that maps 120p inputs directly into the latent space, paired with a modified CogVideoX-compatible tiny autoencoder [5] for efficient single-frame decoding. Rather than claiming a net compute advantage over native rendering, our goal is to make high-quality, causal diffusion upscaling from extreme input resolutions computationally feasible.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    We address causal, frame-by-frame super-resolution of ultra-low-resolution gameplay by adapting the pretrained DOVE [10] backbone through three complementary components: a framewise latent pipeline with cached causal attention; transformer and decoder compression combined with inference optimizations; and model distillation followed by pixel-space refinement to recover reconstruction quality. We adopt DOVE for its strong reconstruction performance and straightforward one-step restoration architecture. Unlike noise-conditioned approaches, DOVE directly restores degraded input latents, allowing us to replace its expensive VAE encoder with a lightweight projector while retaining the pretrained transformer. Our primary configuration performs 8× upscaling from 212×120 to 1696×960. The pipeline generates a single HR frame per generation pass, using only the current and past low-resolution inputs. This avoids waiting for additional frames to form a chunk, enabling the low-latency processing needed for interactive gameplay.

    Let xₜ∈ℝ^H×W×3 denote the low-resolution (LR) frame at time t, with optional engine-provided depth dₜ and screen-space motion vₜ. As shown in Fig.2, for each incoming LR frame xₜ, we project it into the latent space, use a causal diffusion transformer to predict the corresponding high-resolution (HR) latent conditioned on cache history, and decode a single HR output frame:

    zₜ=P_ψ(xₜ),
    (ẑₜ,Cₜ)=F_θ([zₜ₋₈,…,zₜ],dₜ,vₜ;C_t-8:t-1),
    ŷₜ=D_φ(ẑₜ).

    where P_ψ,F_θ,D_φ denote the LR projector, causal diffusion transformer, and single-frame decoder, respectively. We store the projected latents of the eight most recent LR frames and concatenate them with the current frame’s LR latent to form the transformer input. Separately, C_a:b denotes the transformer’s KV cache for frames a through b, inclusive. These two caches avoid repeatedly projecting past LR frames and recomputing their attention keys and values. Only the newly arriving LR frame passes through the projector, and only the current predicted HR latent passes through the decoder. Decoded HR output frames are not fed back into the model, avoiding error accumulation and additional encoding costs.

    3.2 Framewise Causal Super-Resolution

    Direct Latent Projection.

    The original conditioning path of DOVE [10] bilinearly upsamples the LR input to the output resolution and encodes it with the pretrained CogVideoX [40] VAE encoder (127 million parameters) to obtain the LR input latent. We replace this expensive path with a learned latent projection that maps the LR frame directly to the latent grid, trained to reproduce the encoder’s output. The projector is a dilated residual network with approximately 1.2 million parameters, roughly 100× fewer than the original encoder. For 8× super-resolution, the LR frame and target latent grid have the same spatial dimensions, and therefore we avoid constructing and encoding an intermediate HR image.

    Causal Temporal Context.

    We represent each frame with its own latent and use a temporal patch size of one, preserving a separate spatial token grid for each frame. We replace the backbone’s bidirectional temporal attention with a frame-causal mask where current frame tokens can only attend to one another and to the preceding K=8 frames. Each transformer block maintains a KV cache for these past frames, evicting the oldest frame’s entries as each new frame arrives. We fine-tune the backbone using the same bounded temporal attention window as streaming inference, allowing training to capture the full history depth used at inference. To further reduce inference cost, we restrict attention for past frames to local spatial neighborhoods while retaining full spatial attention within the current frame. Specifically, a query at spatial position p in frame t attends to historical tokens within a neighborhood of radius r=4 around p:

    H(t,p)={(τ,q):\max(0,t-K)≤τ

    where ℕᵣ(p) denotes the local spatial neighborhood on the token grid. The temporal window bounds KV cache size independently of sequence length, and the spatial restriction reduces the number of historical tokens accessed per query. We apply this spatial restriction only at inference; training uses the temporal mask with unrestricted spatial attention.

    Engine-Buffer Conditioning.

    We incorporate depth and two-channel motion through separate attention branches inside each transformer block. Lightweight convolutional encoders (70,000 parameters each) map the normalized buffers to spatial tokens aligned with the video-token grid. Following the standard joint self-attention operation, video features query these representations through local depth and motion cross-attention branches, whose outputs enter as scaled residual updates. The buffer encoders operate causally, so processing a frame does not require future engine buffers.

    Single-Frame Reconstruction.

    To reduce decoding overhead, we replace DOVE’s original CogVideoX VAE decoder with the CogVideoX-specific variant of the Tiny AutoEncoder (TAE) [5]. Starting from its pretrained 9.8M-parameter decoder, we retain only the final slice of its temporal-growth output and remove historical memory inputs, reducing the decoder to 7.5M parameters and enabling single-frame reconstruction. We then fine-tune the decoder on the transformer’s predicted HR latents to adapt it to the output distribution of our model. Since temporal context is already incorporated by the transformer, the decoder reconstructs each frame independently without requiring multi-frame decoding.

    3.3 Model Compression and Efficient Inference

    Our teacher is based on DOVE’s 42-block CogVideoX-5B transformer. To reduce inference cost, we construct a compact student with 12 transformer blocks, 24 attention heads, and a hidden dimension of 1536, comprising approximately 378 million parameters including the buffer-conditioning branches. We initialize the student by selecting and transferring teacher weights based on their magnitudes, followed by full-weight knowledge distillation. We additionally fold constant adaptive-normalization modulation into the network and represent fixed text conditioning using learned constant keys and values.

    Following decoder adaptation and joint pixel-space refinement (Sec.3.4), we further compress the student through structured block pruning. We rank transformer blocks by the validation degradation caused by removing each block without retraining, prune three low-impact blocks, and fine-tune the remaining network to recover reconstruction quality. The resulting nine-block deployment model contains approximately 291 million parameters while preserving causal KV caching, engine-buffer conditioning, latent projection, and single-frame decoding.

    We additionally implement a fused Triton streaming-attention kernel. For each new frame, the kernel combines attention over cached local neighborhoods and constant text tokens with the current-frame attention result, reducing intermediate memory traffic and kernel-launch overhead. Together, with the compilation of the transformer and decoder, these optimizations reduce per-frame execution cost while retaining the streaming attention computation.

    3.4 Training Objectives

    Projector Pretraining and Causal Model Training.

    We pretrain the LR projector to produce cached posterior-mean latents from the original input-conditioning path using mean-squared error and an L1 loss. Reference latents are obtained by encoding bilinearly upsampled LR frames with the original VAE encoder. We train the backbone using rank-64 LoRA with a scaling parameter of 64, together with the newly introduced conditioning modules. Training progressively incorporates engine buffers, perceptual supervision, per-frame latents, the learned projector, and causal attention.

    Latent-Space Distillation.

    We use the trained full-size causal model as a teacher for latent-space knowledge distillation. The objective combines mean-squared error between student and teacher predictions of the clean HR latent, an L1 loss matching their consecutive-frame latent differences, and normalized mean-squared error between selected student and teacher block features. This stage operates entirely in the latent space, avoiding decoder execution and perceptual loss evaluation.

    Decoder Adaptation and Joint Refinement.

    We first fine-tune the lightweight decoder on cached student predictions paired with HR targets, while keeping the student fixed. This adapts the decoder to the latent distribution encountered at inference. We then jointly optimize the student and decoder against paired HR sequences without teacher supervision. Both stages use a pixel-space objective combining L1 reconstruction loss, LPIPS, and DISTS [12] with weights of 1, 0.5, and 0.5, respectively, together with a temporal L1 loss matching consecutive-frame differences between predicted and reference sequences. Following block pruning (Sec.3.3), we fine-tune the remaining student and decoder using the same objective to recover reconstruction quality. Joint refinement and pruning recovery preserve the eight-frame causal attention window used during streaming inference.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Dataset.

    Our evaluation requires gameplay footage of state-of-the-art games with ray tracing support and G-buffer recordings. To the best of our knowledge, no publicly available dataset fulfills both requirements sufficiently. We therefore record our own dataset from two AAA games, Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong, using XeSS Inspector. 111 Gameplay footage from Cyberpunk 2077 (© CD Projekt S.A.) and Black Myth: Wukong (© Game Science) is used solely for non-commercial academic evaluation. No affiliation with or endorsement by the respective studios is implied. Raw game assets are not redistributed.Cyberpunk 2077 data is collected with a simple bot. Black Myth: Wukong is collected from human gameplay. We capture frames at 2560×1440 with ray tracing enabled at native resolution, without any upscaling or frame generation. Each recording contains 480 frames captured at 30 FPS. From the G-buffer, we record depth and motion vectors. For Cyberpunk 2077, we record five distinct scenes (100 videos per scene) and 100 additional videos (20 videos per scene) at 3840×2160 (for ablation). Black Myth: Wukong has no distinct scenes, so we treat its 100 videos as a single scene group. We tone-map the linear HDR frames and resize them with bilinear filtering to 1696×960 to obtain our HR targets. For the LR inputs, we point sample from the HR frames on a regular grid (212×120 for 8×) to mimic rendering at lower resolution. We apply an 80/10/10 training–validation–test split to the four Cyberpunk scenes used for training and to the Wukong recordings. We additionally reserve the fifth Cyberpunk scene, Santo Domingo, entirely for held-out generalization evaluation (see Sec.4.3). Unless stated otherwise, we report results for upscaling from 212×120 to 1696×960 (8× per axis), averaged over the four-scene Cyberpunk 2077 test set. Further resolutions, scaling factors, and per-scene results are analyzed in Sec.4.3.

    Comparison Methods.

    Beyond simple bicubic interpolation, we compare our method against two groups of baselines. As an industry-grade real-time upscaler, we evaluate NVIDIA DLSS Super Resolution via NVIDIA Streamline SDK v2.12.0. Since DLSS only supports 1×,2×,3× input-to-output ratio in this setting, we obtain 8× enlargement by cascading three 2× DLSS passes: 212×120→424×240→848×480→1696×960. At each stage, the previous DLSS output is re-fed as the next-stage color input, while depth and motion vectors are resized to the current input resolution (bilinear interpolation); motion-vector magnitudes are rescaled consistently with the resolution change. We report the output of the third pass as the 8× DLSS baseline. Note that the original DLSS output contains an overlay watermark. Therefore, we evaluated DLSS on only the cropped areas outside the masks.

    As state-of-the-art research methods, we evaluate FlashVSR [50], Stream-DiffVSR [30], RDG [48], and InfVSR [47]. All baselines receive the same low-resolution inputs as our method and are used with their released weights. We additionally report DOVE [10] as an offline reference to estimate the quality that a neural upscaler can reach without real-time constraints. DOVE is not applicable to games, as it violates both requirements of the setting: it does not run at interactive frame rates, and it processes whole clips and therefore depends on future frames. For baselines that support only 4× upscaling, we first bicubically upsample the LR input by 2× and then apply the model’s native 4× upscaling to obtain an overall 8× output. We found that this configuration obtains the best performance for these models.

    Evaluation Metrics.

    We measure the quality of the reconstructed frames vs. the rendered ground truth. We report perceptual quality with LPIPS [46] and MILO [11], and pixel-level error with PSNR/SSIM. All quality metrics are computed per frame and averaged over all frames of the test set. CGVQM reports video quality of the full clips in comparison with the reference [18]. In addition, we measure the inference time of the super-resolution step in milliseconds per frame and convert it to the corresponding theoretical frame rate. The timings isolate the super-resolution step and do not include ray tracing of the low-resolution input.

    Implementation Details.

    The compact student is initialized and distilled as described in (Sec.3.3-Sec.3.4), using full-weight optimization for 11,000 steps at a learning rate of 10⁻⁴, followed by 1,200 steps of joint pixel-space refinement at 2×10⁻⁵. The temporal reconstruction loss is weighted by 0.5. After refining the 12-block student, we prune three transformer blocks and fine-tune the resulting nine-block model to recover reconstruction quality. Training preserves an eight-frame temporal context with banded causal attention; inference additionally restricts historical attention to a local spatial window of radius four. Training takes approximately 72 hours in total on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. All evaluations and timings are performed on an NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU.

    4.2 Results

    Quantitative Results.

    Table1 compares CIDER against state-of-the-art video super-resolution methods under extreme 8× upscaling from 120p inputs. At this resolution, much of the high-frequency information is absent from individual frames, making faithful reconstruction particularly challenging. CIDER achieves the best PSNR, LPIPS, and MILO scores across both games, as well as the highest SSIM on Cyberpunk 2077. On Cyberpunk 2077, our method achieves 31.64 dB PSNR, exceeding the next-best result by 2.27 dB, while reducing LPIPS by 49% compared with DOVE. Similar improvements are observed on Wukong, where CIDER reduces LPIPS by 43% compared with the next-best method. CIDER also achieves the highest CGVQM on Cyberpunk 2077, although its score on Wukong is slightly below Bicubic, DLSS, and RDG. These results highlight the advantage of our generative approach in recovering scene details that are difficult to reconstruct through conventional temporal accumulation, while maintaining fidelity to the reference rendering.

    Qualitative Results.

    Figure3 presents visual comparisons on challenging scenes from both games. Existing methods struggle with severe undersampling, often producing blurred textures, distorted fine structures, and residual aliasing artifacts. In contrast, CIDER synthesizes missing high-frequency details while better preserving scene geometry and appearance. Additional visual and temporal comparisons are provided in the supplementary material.

    Discussion.

    Beyond visual fidelity, extreme super-resolution for interactive games must operate causally, since future frames depend on player actions and are unavailable at inference time. Unlike offline video diffusion approaches, CIDER processes each incoming frame using only current and historical observations, guided by engine-provided depth and motion vectors. This design enables frame-by-frame generation without waiting for future frames or feeding synthesized HR outputs back into the temporal history. Meanwhile, our efficient latent representation and model compression reduce inference latency to 75 ms per frame (13.3 FPS), compared with 10.9 seconds of initial latency and 1.21 seconds per frame for the original DOVE. CIDER also achieves lower inference latency than the evaluated diffusion-based VSR baselines. Although it remains slower than conventional non-generative game upscalers such as RDG (see Sec.5 for detailed discussion), CIDER operates in a more challenging reconstruction regime, where missing visual information must be synthesized rather than recovered solely from existing samples. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of causal diffusion for extreme game super-resolution, bridging the gap between high-fidelity generative reconstruction and the latency requirements of interactive rendering.

    4.3 Ablations

    Scaling Factor and Input Resolution.

    We evaluate the limits of extreme super-resolution by varying input resolution and scaling factor shown in Fig.4. In Tab.2, increasing the scaling factor from 4× to 8× at 120p reduces PSNR from 34.23 to 31.64 dB. Even at 16× upscaling from 60p to 960p, CIDER achieves 28.09 dB PSNR and 0.1876 LPIPS, demonstrating its ability to reconstruct visual details from severely undersampled inputs. Inference latency remains similar for the same output resolution, suggesting that computation is primarily determined by output size.

    Engine-Buffer Conditioning.

    Tab.3 evaluates depth and motion-vector conditioning. Compared with RGB-only inputs, incorporating both buffers improves PSNR and LPIPS slightly. Motion vectors contribute most of the improvement, while depth provides smaller additional gains. These results suggest that engine-provided information complements generative reconstruction, with a modest latency increase from 65 to 75 ms.

    Context Memory Length.

    Tab.4 shows the tradeoff between temporal context and inference cost. Increasing memory from 0 to 8 frames improves PSNR from 30.66 to 31.64 dB, demonstrating the benefit of past observations for causal reconstruction. Extending memory to 16 frames offers marginal quality gains at higher latency, while 32 frames degrades quality. We therefore adopt eight memory frames to balance reconstruction fidelity and inference efficiency.

    Held-Out Gameplay Scenes

    . We evaluate the generalization of CIDER to unseen gameplay scenes in Tab.5. We train on four visually distinct scenes from Cyberpunk 2077 and evaluate on Santo Domingo, a fifth scene excluded entirely from training. Despite differences in scenery and visual appearance, CIDER achieves 31.95 dB PSNR and 0.1191 LPIPS on the held-out scene. These results suggest that CIDER learns transferable game-specific visual priors rather than simply memorizing the training scenes, enabling effective reconstruction in previously unseen environments. This supports the practicality of training CIDER once per game and applying it across diverse in-game environments without scene-specific retraining.

    5 Limitations and Future Work

    Despite promising results, CIDER has several limitations. First, we leveraged game-specific LoRA adaptation for accelerated performance. This limits the scalability to unseen games with different rendering styles, textures, and scene content (see supplementary for more details). Techniques such as mixture-of-LoRA experts and LoRA merging [29, 24] may shed light on improving cross-game generalization by learning shared generative priors across diverse game environments while preserving individual details through lightweight adapters.

    Second, although our causal diffusion framework enables extreme super-resolution at around 13 FPS, its inference remains slower than conventional non-generative upscalers. This overhead comes from the computational demands of synthesizing missing high-frequency details rather than reconstructing existing information. Nevertheless, generative upscaling offers opportunities for further efficiency improvements through adaptive computation, compared with fixed-pipeline ray-tracing rendering. For example, future work could selectively allocate generative computation to regions where the low-resolution input provides insufficient detail, while relying on lightweight reconstruction elsewhere. Additionally, jointly optimizing pixel-wise, spatio-temporal ray-tracing samples and generative reconstruction under a shared computational budget could balance visual fidelity and computational cost [14].

    6 Conclusion

    In this work, we present a causal diffusion framework for extreme super-resolution in interactive games, enabling high-quality rendering from ultra-low-resolution inputs as small as 60p. By leveraging generative diffusion priors and G-buffer guidance, our approach synthesizes missing high-frequency details beyond what conventional reconstruction methods can recover.

    LLM Usage Statement

    We used LLMs to revise and improve the manuscript writing and develop code for part of the algorithm under supervision.

    （参考文献见原文。）
