    Appendix A Implementation and Reproducibility Details

    This section lists which components are frozen and trained, the supervision used at each training stage, and the evaluation protocols.

    A.1 Model Inventory and Parameter Accounting

    Table7 summarizes the main components of CADENCE. The C-RADIOv4 encoder is shared by the per-frame estimator and the high-resolution hand pathway. The backbone weights remain frozen; in the final adaptation stage, only lightweight LoRA adapter weights are trained. The temporal refiner is trained after the per-frame estimator and hand pathway are fixed.

    Parameter accounting.

    Table8 reports the parameter count for each component. The frozen C-RADIOv4-SO400M encoder contains 472.35M parameters and is not updated during the main training stages. The per-frame SMPL-X estimator contains 51.8M trainable parameters, including the structured decoder, prediction heads, spatial feedback modules, and lightweight adaptation parameters where enabled. The high-resolution hand pathway adds 21.0M trainable parameters. The temporal refiner is lightweight, adding only 1.88M parameters. Thus, the per-frame and hand modules contain 72.8M trainable parameters, and full CADENCE including the temporal refiner contains 74.7M trainable parameters.

    Per-frame estimator.

    The per-frame estimator takes a person crop, resized to 384×288, and predicts an initial SMPL-X parameter vector. We use C-RADIOv4-SO400M as the shared visual encoder and extract multi-scale visual features. Early features preserve local spatial detail, middle features capture limb structure, and late features provide semantic context. Each feature map is projected to the decoder width before cross-attention.

    The decoder uses structured query tokens rather than a single global regression token. Separate tokens represent camera, shape, global orientation, body joints, left hand, right hand, jaw, and expression. Keypoint tokens represent the projected articulated body in image space. After each decoder layer, lightweight heads predict intermediate SMPL-X updates. The current SMPL-X estimate is converted to joints by forward kinematics, projected to the image, and used to update keypoint-token attention and local feature sampling in later decoder layers. This creates an iterative spatial-feedback loop in which the model refines both the parameter estimate and the image locations it uses for evidence.

    A.2 SMPL-X Parameterization

    CADENCE predicts a 341-dimensional SMPL-X parameter vector for each frame:

    pₜ=[θᵇᵒᵈʸₜ,θˡʰₜ,θʳʰₜ,θʲᵃʷₜ,ψₜ,θᵒʳₜ,βₜ,cₜ],

    where body pose contains 21 body joints in 6D rotation form (21×6=126), the left and right hands contain 15 joints each (15×6=90 per hand), the jaw is represented by one 6D rotation, expression has 10 dimensions, global orientation is one 6D rotation, body shape has 10 dimensions, and the weak-perspective camera has 3 dimensions. Rotations use the continuous 6D representation during learning and are projected to valid rotation matrices before SMPL-X forward kinematics.

    A.3 High-Resolution Hand Pathway

    Section3.2 describes the pathway. FreiHand and HanCo contain right hands only; horizontal-flip augmentation exposes the shared branch to both orientations, so no separate left-hand branch or explicit mirroring step is needed. Figure3 shows examples before and after the pathway.

    A.4 Temporal Refiner Details

    The temporal refiner is trained after the per-frame and hand components are fixed. It operates on stored per-frame CADENCE predictions rather than raw images. Each SMPL-X joint rotation is treated as a token over time. Tokens are first updated with temporal self-attention and then with attention restricted to the SMPL-X kinematic tree, allowing information to pass between each joint, its parent, and its children.

    Each joint chooses its bandwidth per frame from a bank of four learned zero-phase kernels, initialised as the identity and Gaussians with σ=1,2,4 frames. The selector’s per-joint prior starts body and global-orientation joints on the σ=2 kernel and the jaw, forearms, and hands on the identity kernel, and its learned weights are zero-initialised, so training starts from a fixed part-rate filter. Every kernel is symmetric and non-negative with unit sum, so the output cannot lag or amplify the input. The filtered rotations are re-orthonormalised before SMPL-X forward kinematics. The refiner has 1.88M parameters, uses pose only, and runs on 32-frame windows with a hop of 16 frames and Hann-weighted overlap.

    A.5 Losses and Training Schedule

    The per-frame estimator is supervised at each decoder layer using rotation, joint, vertex, 2D keypoint, camera, shape, and expression losses:

    L_pf=λᵣₒₜLᵣₒₜ+λ_j3dL_j3d+λ_j2dL_j2d+λᵥLᵥ
    +λ_camL_cam+λ_βL_β+λ_ψL_ψ.

    The hand pathway adds losses on finger rotations, hand joints, and hand vertices:

    L_hand=λₕᵣₒₜLₕᵣₒₜ+λₕⱼLₕⱼ+λₕᵥLₕᵥ.

    The temporal refiner is trained with reconstruction, velocity, acceleration, and do-no-harm objectives:

    Lₜₑₘₚ=L_pf+λ_dynL_dyn+λ_dnhL_dnh.

    The do-no-harm term is a hinge loss that penalizes temporal predictions when they increase reconstruction error relative to the frozen per-frame estimate.

    Training stages.

    CADENCE is trained in stages so that each module has a clear role. Table11 summarizes the training sequence.

    Optimization and augmentation.

    Training uses AdamW with mixed-precision acceleration. The decoder and prediction heads use a higher learning rate than the LoRA parameters during the final adaptation stage. We apply standard image augmentations including random scale, translation, horizontal flip, color jitter, and synthetic occlusion where appropriate. For video clips, we sample fixed-length windows and apply temporal subsampling during training to improve robustness to different motion speeds.

    A.6 Training Datasets

    CADENCE is trained from a mixture of whole-body SMPL-X data, in-the-wild video data, 2D keypoint supervision, and real hand-3D data. Whole-body datasets provide the main SMPL-X supervision. COCO-WholeBody and MPII provide additional 2D keypoint supervision. FreiHand and HanCo provide real hand-3D supervision for the canonical hand training mode. The temporal refiner is trained on clips from available video sources using stored per-frame CADENCE predictions.

    Sampling.

    During per-frame training, batches are sampled from a mixture of whole-body 3D datasets and 2D keypoint datasets. Loss masks ensure that each sample only contributes to losses for which annotations are available. During hand-pathway training, whole-body samples and canonical hand-only samples are mixed so that the hand branch learns both body-context hand refinement and detailed real hand articulation. During temporal training, the image encoder and per-frame decoder are frozen and the temporal refiner is trained from stored predictions, ensuring that controlled studies change only the temporal processing stage.

    A.7 Evaluation Protocols

    EHF is evaluated with Procrustes-aligned full-body mesh error and regional hand/face metrics. AGORA and UBody use whole-body mesh metrics with full-body and regional breakdowns. 3DPW uses the standard 14-joint body protocol, and EMDB uses the 24-joint body protocol. Acceleration error is computed from the difference of predicted and ground-truth central second differences over valid consecutive frames at the declared FPS.

    CADENCE predicts whole-body SMPL-X, but 3DPW and EMDB evaluate only the body quantities specified by their protocols. These benchmarks therefore do not measure hand accuracy, absolute depth, or global placement.

    Appendix B Extended Benchmark Results

    This section extends Tab.3 with additional 3DPW methods and compares SAM 3D Body on the expressive benchmarks.

    B.1 3DPW Extended Results

    3DPW is a body-centric benchmark. Although CADENCE predicts full SMPL-X parameters, evaluation follows the body protocol used by prior work. Table14 groups methods by representation to make the comparison clearer: whole-body SMPL-X methods, body-focused per-frame or fitting methods, and body-only temporal methods. Acceleration errors are listed in Tab.3.

    SAM 3D Body on EHF, AGORA, and UBody.

    Table3 compares SAM 3D Body [44] with CADENCE on 3DPW and EMDB; here we extend the comparison to EHF, AGORA, and UBody. SAM 3D Body predicts a Momentum Human Rig mesh, a different topology from SMPL-X with no public vertex regressor to SMPL-X, so we compare body joints instead: SAM 3D Body’s own shipped correspondence from its 70-keypoint output to the 13-joint LSP layout, paired with the same 13 SMPL-X joints via the standard SMPL-X joint regressor (7 upper-body joints only on UBody, whose close-up framing leaves hips, knees, and ankles out of frame in many clips). On this joint protocol, SAM 3D Body reaches 38.06/59.94/53.77 mm body PA-MPJPE on EHF/AGORA/UBody, next to CADENCE’s own published number on each dataset’s own protocol of 20.58/42.4/29.25 mm (EHF: 14-joint PA-MPJPE; AGORA/UBody: vertex PA-PVE). These are different metrics on different joint sets, shown for context, not as a matched comparison.

    Appendix C Hand Pathway Diagnostics

    All variants in this section use the same per-frame whole-body estimator, shared encoder, and EHF protocol, and change only the hand pathway. Because the pathway writes only finger rotations, body metrics are identical across variants.

    Table15 compares design choices under an identical single-stage training budget, with the final pathway from Tab.6 as reference. The feature source has the largest effect: sampling late-layer crop features gives 12.89 mm hand P-MVE and 8.72 mm hand P-MPJPE, against 14.93 and 10.07 mm with early-layer features only. The parameterization matters less: removing the zero-initialized residual or predicting the full hand pose directly changes either error by less than 0.5 mm.

    C.1 Per-Finger Diagnostics on Sign Language

    Table16 reports per-finger wrist-aligned PA-MPJPE on an internal UBody sign-language test split with 18,130 samples, chosen because signing contains frequent and varied hand articulation. Errors are largest at the fingertips, especially of the thumb and index finger, where opposition, self-occlusion, and fast motion make articulation hardest. CADENCE has lower error than SMPLer-X-H [5] and Multi-HMR-L [3] on every finger, with hand PA-MPVPE of 6.58 mm against 7.63 and 7.93 mm, and the fraction of joints within 5 mm (F@5 mm) is 7 to 9 points higher.

    Appendix D Temporal Refiner Diagnostics

    This section complements Sec.4.2. All variants start from the same stored per-frame CADENCE predictions, evaluation clips, and metric implementation, and change only the temporal stage.

    D.1 Single-Rate, Multi-Rate, and Component Ablations

    Table17 uses matched 32-frame clip subsets of 3DPW and SignAvatars/How2Sign, with identical stored inputs within each subset. The first block compares fixed filters with one shared bandwidth (single-rate) and with per-joint bandwidths (multi-rate). The second block removes one component at a time from an earlier version of the refiner, which added a residual rotation correction gated by a learned HOLD/STROKE phase on hand and jaw joints; the released refiner (Sec.3.4) does not use these components. Clip pools and conditioning signals differ from Sec.4.2, so absolute values are not comparable with Tabs.1 and 2.

    The single-rate and multi-rate filters have identical body accuracy, acceleration error, and jitter, but the multi-rate filter keeps more of the hand motion: Peak-R rises from 0.63 to 0.76 and Peak-A from 0.55 to 0.63. At equal smoothness, the per-joint bandwidth is therefore what preserves hand-speed peaks.

    In the earlier refiner, the component rows change body accuracy and acceleration error by at most 0.06 mm and 0.03 mm/s2. Removing the phase gate, the do-no-harm term, or the residual’s conditioning leaves all metrics within 0.01, which is why the released refiner drops the residual and the gate and keeps the filter selection. Removing kinematic-tree attention raises Peak-A from 0.61 to 0.74 at higher jitter (0.69 against 0.64).

    D.2 Low-Frame-Rate and Missing-Frame Robustness

    Temporal filters can be sensitive to frame rate and missing observations. We therefore evaluate CADENCE temporal refinement under simple test-time degradations: temporal downsampling and random frame dropping. In each case, the same per-frame model is used and only the temporal input sequence is degraded. For downsampling, we evaluate on the retained frames. For missing frames, dropped frames are masked during temporal refinement and metrics are computed on frames with available ground truth.

    The results show graceful degradation rather than collapse. Random frame dropping is handled robustly: PA-MPJPE rises from 40.2 to 40.8 mm when a quarter of frames are removed. Temporal downsampling is more demanding because the inter-frame interval grows, which both widens the motion gap the refiner must bridge and increases the measured finite-difference acceleration. Even so, accuracy degrades smoothly, with PA-MPJPE changing from 40.2 to 45.0 mm from full to one-third frame rate. Peak-A remains near or above 1.0, indicating that expressive hand-motion peaks are not collapsed under these degradations. Peak-A values above 1 indicate peak hand speeds above the reference.

    D.3 Rotation Interpolation and Temporal Filtering Details

    CADENCE applies temporal processing to articulated SMPL-X rotations rather than to unconstrained 3D joint coordinates. Rotations are represented using the continuous 6D representation during learning, converted to valid rotation matrices before forward kinematics, and re-orthonormalized after temporal updates. The deployed temporal model does not require linear interpolation of reduced-rate 6D rotations back to the full frame rate; the per-joint temporal filters operate over the full input window with different effective bandwidths for different joint groups.

    For diagnostic variants that explicitly resample time, interpolation is applied on valid rotations rather than on arbitrary unnormalized 6D vectors. In practice, we convert 6D rotations to rotation matrices, interpolate rotations using a rotation-aware procedure, and then convert back to the representation used by the model. This avoids treating the 6D representation as an unconstrained Euclidean signal and prevents invalid rotations from entering the SMPL-X forward kinematics.

    Appendix E Runtime Accounting

    Table19 reports throughput for the main inference configurations and the dominant runtime components. All measurements are obtained on one A100-80GB GPU using bf16 inference. Batch-1 throughput measures low-latency inference, while batch-32 throughput measures batched throughput.

    The base per-frame estimator processes the full-person crop and predicts whole-body SMPL-X parameters. Enabling the high-resolution hand pathway adds two hand-crop encoder passes, improving finger articulation but reducing throughput. The temporal refiner is inexpensive relative to image encoding, running at approximately 6,900 FPS for a 32-frame window.

    Interpretation.

    CADENCE is not bottlenecked by the temporal refiner. Runtime is dominated by visual encoding and, when enabled, the high-resolution hand pathway. This is expected: the hand pathway deliberately trades throughput for improved finger articulation by reusing the same high-capacity encoder on hand crops. Applications that require maximum throughput can run the per-frame estimator with the temporal refiner and skip the hand pathway.

    Appendix F Additional Qualitative Results

    This section describes layer-by-layer decoder refinement, a comparison with whole-body baselines, temporal examples, and failure cases. The corresponding figures are collected in AppendixG.

    F.1 Whole-Body Qualitative Results

    Figure4 shows additional CADENCE reconstructions on diverse 3DPW sequences, visualized as a layer-by-layer refinement progression. The structured decoder starts from a coarse initial estimate and progressively updates the mesh and joint locations across its six layers using iterative spatial feedback. The examples include walking, running, stair climbing, and seated poses with partial occlusion. They illustrate how the decoder refines global body structure and projected joint alignment over successive layers.

    F.2 Multi-Baseline Qualitative Comparison on Expressive Scenes

    Figure5 compares CADENCE qualitatively with recent whole-body or whole-human recovery methods on expressive UBody scenes. We compare against SMPLer-X [5], Multi-HMR [3], and SAM 3D Body [44]. To make the visual comparison controlled, all methods are run in single-person mode using the same detected person box where possible. Each panel shows the full-person overlay and a zoom strip containing the face and both hands cropped from the same image regions.

    The methods use different representations and processing assumptions in expressive regions such as hands and face. SAM 3D Body uses a different mesh representation from SMPL-X. We therefore show the panels only as qualitative context and avoid topology-specific or hand-accuracy claims. CADENCE’s high-resolution branch is finger-only and retains a whole-body SMPL-X output.

    F.3 Temporal Consistency Examples

    Figure6 compares per-frame predictions, a generic temporal smoother, and the deployed CADENCE temporal refiner on a sign-language clip with rapid finger articulation. Per-frame predictions exhibit large frame-to-frame acceleration. To isolate what is being smoothed rather than only how much, we tune the generic Savitzky–Golay smoother so that its residual wrist jitter matches the CADENCE refiner’s (2.5 vs. 2.6 mm/frame2). At this matched stability level, the generic smoother attenuates the hand-motion peaks, whereas CADENCE preserves them more closely: on this clip, CADENCE retains 99% of the per-frame peak finger speed compared with 46% for the matched generic smoother.

    F.4 Consecutive-Frame Visualizations Across Diverse Activities

    Figure7 shows CADENCE reconstructions on clips spanning different activity types, including dynamic athletic motion, classroom interaction, and expressive sign-language sequences. For each clip, consecutive frames are shown from left to right with the recovered SMPL-X overlay. These examples show how the recovered body and hand configurations evolve across neighbouring frames in diverse scenes.

    Videos.

    Video results, including continuous two-handed sign-language sequences, are on the project page, https://keniel123.github.io/cadence.

    F.5 Failure Cases

    Table20 summarizes the main failure modes, their likely causes, and possible future directions. These examples are consistent with the limitations in Sec.4.9. The most common failure modes arise from monocular ambiguity, severe occlusion, unusual camera viewpoints, motion blur, inaccurate person boxes, and difficult hand-object or hand-hand interactions.

    Appendix G Qualitative Figures

一句话：按帧独立估计再加时域平滑，代价是手语与手势里承载意义的快速指部动作被压平。

要点：

  • 问题机理：SMPL-X 全身估计器能从单图恢复身体、手与脸，但**逐帧应用**到视频上会产生抖动
  • 平滑的代价常被忽略：**足以稳住躯干的时域滤波，也会把快速的手指动作压平**——而这些动作在手语与手势里承载意义（仅看身体的基准测不出这一点）
  • CADENCE 因此做一个时域连贯、但**保留表现性手部运动**的全身 SMPL-X 系统

为什么值得看：动作捕捉进引擎前的最后一道工序就是去抖，而这一步最容易毁掉手部表演。把「躯干稳定」与「手指细节」分开处理，是让单目动捕真正能用于角色动画的关键——尤其是手语、指挥、精细手势这类内容。

中文摘要：SMPL-X 全身估计器能够从单张图像恢复身体、手部与面部网格，但逐帧应用到视频上会产生抖动的动作。常见的补救是时域平滑，而作者指出这背后有一个未被衡量的代价：足以稳住躯干的时域滤波，同时也把承载语义的快速手指动作压平——在手语与手势中这一点尤其致命，而只看身体的基准完全测不出这种损失。CADENCE 因此提出一个时域连贯的全身 SMPL-X 系统，在抑制抖动的同时保留表现性的手部运动。对单目动捕接进角色管线的团队，这解决的是「去抖之后表演就没了」这个长期痛点。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

CADENCE: Temporally Coherent Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery
that Preserves Expressive Hand Motion

Abstract

Whole-body SMPL-X estimators recover body, hand, and face meshes from single images, but applied frame by frame to video they produce jittery motion. Smoothing the output removes the jitter at a cost that body-only benchmarks do not measure: a temporal filter strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger strokes that carry meaning in sign language and gesture. We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video designed around this trade-off. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder, with a high-resolution hand pathway that reuses the same encoder on hand crops, produces each frame’s estimate. An offline temporal refiner then filters the SMPL-X rotation sequence: attention along the kinematic tree selects, for every joint and every frame, a mixture of learned zero-phase filters, so the torso is smoothed while fast finger strokes pass through. On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm; generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector. The per-frame estimator also obtains the lowest full-body mesh error (25.7 mm) and hand joint error (8.3 mm) among the compared methods on EHF.

1 Introduction

Sign-language understanding, avatar animation, and human motion analysis need 3D motion of the body, hands, and face together [29, 45]. SMPL-X [29] represents all three, and image-based estimators now recover detailed SMPL-X meshes from single frames [5, 22, 37, 3]. Applied independently to video, these estimators produce motion that shakes: small per-frame errors become high-frequency jitter in the limbs and fingers and flicker in global orientation. In sign language the hands carry the meaning, so unstable finger articulation is the most damaging form of this failure.

Temporal mesh recovery is well studied for body-only SMPL [17, 7, 41, 35, 39], but these models do not represent the hand, jaw, and expression parameters of SMPL-X. The usual alternative for whole-body video is to run a per-frame SMPL-X estimator and smooth its output. Generic smoothers treat the pose vector as one homogeneous signal, and this is where they fail on expressive motion. Shape is constant within a clip and the torso moves slowly, while a signer’s hand holds a handshape, moves sharply, and holds again. A single temporal bandwidth that removes body jitter also attenuates these hand strokes; a bandwidth wide enough to keep the strokes leaves body jitter in place. Body-only benchmarks such as 3DPW measure only the first half of this trade-off.

Two further properties make whole-body video harder than body-only video. Fingers occupy a small part of a full-body crop, so their articulation is hard to recover from whole-body features, and strong whole-body pipelines rely on hand crops or hand-specific encoders [25, 47]. The temporal stage also has to operate on rotations in a kinematic tree, where an error at the wrist moves every finger below it.

We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder [31] and a structured SMPL-X decoder produces each frame’s estimate, and a high-resolution hand pathway re-encodes hand crops with the same encoder weights to refine finger pose. An offline temporal refiner then processes the SMPL-X rotation sequence. Transformer attention over time and along the kinematic tree predicts, for every joint and every frame, mixing weights over a small bank of learned zero-phase filters, from near-identity to strongly low-pass. The selection starts low-pass for body joints and near-identity for hand, forearm, and jaw joints, so that body and hands are smoothed at different rates, and it can change within a clip as a hand moves between held handshapes and fast strokes.

On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 and lowers PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm relative to the per-frame input; five generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, where the trade-off between stability and hand motion is visible, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers and keeps a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, while a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector keeps 0.35. A single-rate version of the refiner, with one bandwidth shared by all joints, reaches comparable jitter (1.50 against 1.29) but keeps a peak amplitude of only 0.50.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A part-structured temporal refiner for SMPL-X rotation sequences that uses kinematic-tree attention to choose a learned zero-phase filter for every joint and frame (Sec.3.4), evaluated against five generic smoothers and a single-rate variant on 3DPW and on sign-language sequences (Sec.4.2).

  • •

    A high-resolution hand pathway that refines finger pose from hand crops with the shared encoder and no separate hand encoder (Sec.3.2), reducing EHF hand P-MVE from 22.6 to 12.2 mm (Sec.4.7).

  • •

    An evaluation of the full system on expressive whole-body (EHF, AGORA, UBody), body-centric video (3DPW, EMDB), and hand-object (ARCTIC) benchmarks (Secs.4.4, 4.5 and 4.6).

    • 2 Related Work

    Single-image and whole-body human mesh recovery.

    Human mesh recovery was first developed mainly for body-only SMPL [24], with progress driven by iterative regression, optimization-in-the-loop training, part-guided attention, and camera-aware conditioning [15, 19, 18, 21, 27]. Transformer-based models further improved monocular recovery through stronger global features and token-based reasoning [12, 9, 32]. For expressive recovery, SMPL-X [29] extends the body model with articulated hands, face, jaw, expression, and shape. Early whole-body systems such as ExPose, Hand4Whole, and PyMAF-X [8, 25, 47] used separate crops or specialised branches for body, hands, and face, improving local detail but increasing pipeline complexity. Recent unified methods, including SMPLer-X [5], OSX [22], AiOS [37], Multi-HMR [3], PromptHMR [40], PEAR [42], and SAM 3D Body [44], process the person more holistically and achieve strong single-image results.

    SAM 3D Body is the closest per-frame design to CADENCE’s estimator: a shared image encoder, a transformer decoder, keypoint query tokens, and a hand-specific refinement at inference. It differs in its DINOv3 backbone and in predicting a Momentum Human Rig mesh, a different body model and topology from SMPL-X, and its released pipeline wraps the network with a separate person detector and field-of-view estimator. All of these single-image methods leave temporal coherence to post-processing when applied to video, which is the problem CADENCE’s temporal refiner addresses.

    Hand detail and multi-scale visual features.

    Fine hand articulation is difficult to recover from a full-body crop because fingers occupy only a small image region. Multi-scale representations help combine semantic context with local precision [23, 36], and pose-estimation work such as ViTPose [43] shows earlier transformer features retain useful localization detail. Many whole-body methods use high-resolution hand crops and hand-specific encoders [25, 47], improving hand detail but separating the hand estimate from global body context and adding system complexity. CADENCE instead reuses its shared visual encoder on hand crops to predict finger pose, retaining the body, camera, shape, and face predictions from the whole-body estimate.

    Video-based and temporal mesh recovery.

    Temporal mesh recovery has advanced mainly for body-only SMPL, using temporal convolutions [16], adversarial motion priors  [17], past–future fusion [7], per-joint temporal modelling [41], and world- or camera-aware trajectories [35, 39]. Post-hoc methods such as SmoothNet [46] and MotionBERT [50] can also smooth existing predictions, while HTD-Refine [2] improves motion through test-time optimization. These approaches are mainly designed and evaluated for body pose, whereas expressive SMPL-X video recovery must account for hands, face, and body together.

    DanceHMR [33] is the closest whole-body video method to CADENCE: it recovers temporally coherent body and hand SMPL-X motion by injecting hand evidence as a residual into a body-centric token before a single shared temporal transformer, using frozen per-frame body and hand feature extractors and a close-up-aware training strategy that synthesizes truncated crops to handle vlog- and livestream-style upper-body footage. CADENCE targets the same failure mode, a shared temporal bandwidth that over-smooths fast hand motion, but addresses it differently: it refines pose directly in SMPL-X rotation space, offline, with kinematic-tree attention that selects a learned zero-phase filter for every joint and frame, a multi-rate design in the spirit of multi-rate video models such as SlowFast [11]. We also evaluate this trade-off directly, with hand-speed peak metrics on sign-language sequences (Sec.4.2).

    3 CADENCE

    Overview.

    Given monocular video frames I₁,…,I_T and per-frame person boxes, CADENCE estimates a sequence of SMPL-X [29] parameters. SMPL-X maps body pose, hand pose, facial expression, shape, and camera parameters to a mesh V∈ℝ^10475×3. At each frame, we predict a 341-dimensional parameter vector

    pₜ=[\underbraceθᵇᵒᵈʸₜ₁₂₆,\underbraceθˡʰₜ₉₀,\underbraceθʳʰₜ₉₀,\underbraceθʲᵃʷₜ₆,ψₜ (10),\underbraceθᵒʳₜ₆,βₜ (10),cₜ (3)],

    		(1)

    where rotations use the continuous 6D representation [49]. The body pose excludes the root orientation, which is predicted separately as θᵒʳₜ.

    CADENCE has three parts. First, a per-frame whole-body estimator predicts an initial SMPL-X estimate from each image. Second, a high-resolution hand pathway reuses the same visual encoder on hand crops and predicts finger pose. Third, an offline temporal refiner processes the per-frame pose sequence. The hand branch changes only finger-pose parameters; wrist, body-pose, global orientation, shape, expression, face, and camera parameters are retained from the per-frame estimate.

    3.1 Per-Frame Whole-Body Estimator

    CADENCE uses C-RADIOv4-SO400M [31] as a shared visual encoder. The encoder is frozen during the main training stages and is adapted with LoRA [13] in the final phase. We extract early, middle, and late visual features. Early features preserve local detail, middle features capture limb structure, and late features provide semantic context for global pose, shape, and camera estimation. Each feature map is projected to decoder width D=512.

    The decoder uses structured tokens. Query tokens represent the quantities to be predicted: camera, shape, global orientation, body joints, hands, jaw, and facial expression. Keypoint tokens represent where the articulated body lies in the image. The tokens are updated jointly by a 6-layer transformer decoder with self-attention, cross-attention to late visual features, and feed-forward blocks. After each layer, lightweight heads predict SMPL-X updates. Pose parameters are updated residually for coarse-to-fine refinement, while shape, expression, and camera are predicted directly.

    To make refinement spatially aware, CADENCE feeds its own predictions back into the decoder. The current SMPL-X estimate is converted to 3D joints by forward kinematics, projected to the image, and used to guide keypoint-token attention and local feature sampling in later layers. The decoder therefore progressively updates where it attends as the mesh estimate changes.

    3.2 High-Resolution Hand Pathway

    Hands occupy only a small part of a full-body crop, so finger articulation is difficult to recover from whole-body features alone. Crop-based pipelines improve hand detail using dedicated hand encoders, but this increases complexity and can separate the hand prediction from the global body context. CADENCE instead keeps a shared-encoder design.

    Given the current whole-body prediction, we crop the left and right hand regions around the predicted wrists from the original image and encode them with the same frozen C-RADIOv4 weights, adapted by a hand-specific LoRA. A whole-body 2D keypoint detector, ViTPose [43], provides the hand keypoints kₕ in each crop. Crop features Fʰⁱₕ are bilinearly sampled at these keypoints, and a learned hand query qₕ cross-attends to the sampled features to predict the finger pose of that hand:

    θ̂ʰₜ=H(qₕ,Fʰⁱₕ(kₕ)), h∈{lh,rh}.

    		(2)

    The prediction replaces only the 15 finger rotations of each hand in pₜ; wrist, body-pose, global-orientation, shape, expression, jaw, and camera parameters are kept from the whole-body estimate, so body metrics are unchanged whether the pathway runs or not. Both hands share encoder and branch weights, and horizontal-flip augmentation covers both orientations.

    Whole-body datasets provide little reliable supervision for finger articulation, so the pathway is trained as a hand-pose estimator on hand crops. Real 3D MANO annotations come from FreiHand [51], HanCo [52], and ReInterHand [26]. On COCO and UBody hand crops, where no reliable 3D ground truth exists, we distill finger pose from HaMeR [30], add a 2D reprojection loss on COCO, and down-weight UBody pseudo ground truth. Keypoints are jittered during training so that the pathway tolerates detector noise at inference.

    3.3 Kinematic-Aware Multi-Rate Temporal Refiner

    3.4 Kinematic-Aware Multi-Rate Temporal Refiner

    A single smoothing filter cannot serve the whole body. A bandwidth that removes body jitter also blurs fast finger motion; a bandwidth that preserves finger motion leaves body jitter untouched. Sign language makes this worse: a signer holds a handshape, moves it sharply, then holds again, so even the right bandwidth for one joint changes over time. The refiner therefore chooses a temporal bandwidth for every joint and every frame, conditioned on the motion of the whole kinematic chain.

    Input.

    The refiner takes the SMPL-X rotation sequence for a clip of T frames and reads out J=53 per-frame rotations: global orientation, the 21 body joints, the jaw, and both hands. Each rotation r_j,t∈ℝ⁶ is embedded together with its frame-to-frame velocity r_j,t-r_j,t-1 and acceleration r_j,t+1-2r_j,t+r_j,t-1, a learned joint identity, and a temporal position embedding, giving a token h_j,t∈ℝᵈ. The refiner uses pose only; it receives no image features.

    Kinematic-tree attention.

    Tokens are first updated by self-attention over time, one joint at a time, and then by self-attention over joints within a frame, masked to the SMPL-X kinematic tree:

    \begingatheredh_:,t←Attn(h_:,t,h_:,t,h_:,t;M), Mⱼₖ=\begincases0&dₜᵣₑₑ(j,k)≤2, -∞&otherwise,\endcases\endgathered

    		(3)

    where dₜᵣₑₑ is the number of edges between joints j and k in the tree. A wrist token thus sees its elbow and its finger joints in one pass, so the bandwidth chosen for a finger can depend on whether the arm is moving.

    Content-adaptive multi-rate filtering.

    A bank of F=4 learned kernels w_f∈ℝ^K (K=9) is applied to every joint’s rotation track. Each kernel is symmetric, which makes it zero-phase, and is softmax-normalised, which makes it a non-negative low-pass filter:

    r̃^(f)_j,t=∑ₖ₌₋₄⁴w_f,k r_j,t+k.

    		(4)

    The kernels are initialised to the identity and to Gaussians with σ=1,2,4 frames. For every joint and frame, a selector predicts mixing weights over the bank from the token and a clip-level motion context c (an MLP of the mean token):

    α_j,t=softmax(W(h_j,t+c)+bⱼ), r̂_j,t=∑_fα_j,t,f r̃^(f)_j,t,

    		(5)

    followed by Gram-Schmidt re-orthonormalisation. This per-joint, per-frame choice of bandwidth is what we mean by multi-rate. The per-joint bias bⱼ is initialised to select the σ=2 kernel for body and orientation joints and the identity kernel for the jaw, forearms, and hands, and W is zero-initialised, so the untrained refiner is a fixed part-rate filter that keeps fast hand motion. Because every kernel is a symmetric convex filter, any mixture of them is too: the output never lags the input and never amplifies it. When a hand holds a handshape, the selector can move to a smoother kernel; during a stroke it can stay near the identity. The single-rate variant in Sec.4.2 shares one kernel across all joints.

    The refiner operates offline on 32-frame windows with a hop of 16 frames, blended with a Hann window; shape, expression, and camera pass through unchanged.

    3.5 Training Objectives

    The per-frame estimator is supervised at each decoder layer with a combination of rotation, 3D joint, 2D keypoint, vertex, camera, shape, and expression losses:

    L_pf=λᵣₒₜLᵣₒₜ+λ_j3dL_j3d+λ_j2dL_j2d+λᵥLᵥ(6)
    +λ_camL_cam+λ_βL_β+λ_ψL_ψ.

    The hand pathway is trained with finger rotation, hand joint, and hand vertex losses, plus the 2D reprojection term on COCO crops described above:

    L_hand=λₕᵣₒₜLₕᵣₒₜ+λₕⱼLₕⱼ+λₕᵥLₕᵥ.

    		(7)

    The temporal refiner is trained on clips with the per-frame estimator frozen. It uses reconstruction and dynamics losses on forward-kinematic joints, together with a do-no-harm term that penalizes an increase in reconstruction error relative to the frozen per-frame estimate:

    Lₜₑₘₚ=L_pf+λ_dynL_dyn+λ_dnhL_dnh.

    		(8)

    Training proceeds in stages: first the per-frame decoder and prediction heads, then the hand pathway, then the temporal refiner on clips, and finally a short LoRA adaptation of the shared visual encoder. AppendixA gives the training schedule, window length, and data mixture.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    The per-frame estimator is trained on AGORA [28], BEDLAM [4], UBody [22], Motion-X [48], and 3DPW [38], with 2D keypoint supervision from COCO-WholeBody [14] and MPII [1]. We add 500K frames of public 2D images from COCO-WholeBody, MPII, and InstaVariety [16] with pseudo-SMPL-X labels from the public SMPLer-X-L [5] checkpoint, rejecting frames whose SMPLer-X 2D reprojection error exceeds 20 pixels; no test images are used. The hand pathway uses the hand data in Sec.3.2, and the temporal refiner trains on clips from the video sources. SectionA.6 lists per-source counts.

    Metrics.

    MPJPE and MPVPE (also written PVE or MVE) are mean Euclidean joint and vertex errors in millimetres; the PA- and P- prefixes denote errors after a similarity Procrustes alignment. For EHF [29], hand and face mesh errors are computed after wrist and neck alignment, following SMPLer-X [5]. 3DPW uses the standard 14-joint protocol and EMDB the 24-joint protocol; neither measures hands, absolute depth, or global placement. Acceleration error (Accel) is the mean difference between predicted and ground-truth joint accelerations, computed by central second differences over valid consecutive frames, in mm/s2. On sign-language sequences, Jitter is the mean norm of the predicted joints’ second difference, mean_t,j\lVertp_t+2,j-2p_t+1,j+p_t,j\rVert₂, in millimetres per frame step over valid three-frame runs, with body joints relative to the pelvis and hand joints relative to the wrist. It measures the smoothness of the prediction alone, without ground truth. Peak-R is the fraction of reference hand-velocity peaks that the prediction recovers, and Peak-A is the ratio of predicted to reference peak hand-velocity amplitude: 1 means matching peak size, values below 1 indicate attenuated strokes, and values above 1 overshoot. The sign-language reference motion is pseudo ground truth and contains jitter of its own, so we use these metrics to compare smoothers with each other rather than as absolute accuracy.

    Implementation.

    The C-RADIOv4-SO400M encoder [31] has about 472M parameters and is frozen except for LoRA adapters added in the final training stage. The per-frame estimator has 51.8M trainable parameters, the hand pathway 21.0M, and the temporal refiner 1.88M. Person crops are 384×288. One model is used for all benchmarks, without per-benchmark fine-tuning. We chose C-RADIOv4 because it is distilled from several foundation models, including DINOv3 and SAM, which lets the whole-body decoder and the hand pathway share one backbone; we have not compared it against a human-specific backbone.

    4.2 Temporal Coherence

    This section asks whether the refiner stabilizes whole-body motion without erasing fast hand motion. All smoothers below take the same stored per-frame CADENCE predictions as input, so the rows differ only in temporal processing. Single-rate is the CADENCE refiner with one temporal bandwidth shared by all joints. SmoothNet-WB is SmoothNet [46] retrained on the full 341-dimensional SMPL-X vector, including the hand channels.

    On 3DPW (Tab.1), the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2, the lowest in the table, and improves pose accuracy more than any other row: PA-MPJPE falls from 41.9 to 40.2 mm and MPJPE from 61.7 to 58.1 mm. The zero-phase classical filters reach 6.6 to 7.6 mm/s2 with small accuracy changes. The causal One-Euro filter reaches 6.2 mm/s2, but its phase lag raises PA-MPJPE to 50.5 mm. SmoothNet-WB reduces acceleration error to 7.7 mm/s2 while slightly increasing pose error.

    3DPW measures body joints only, so it cannot show what smoothing does to the hands. Table2 does. Every smoother reduces hand jitter relative to the per-frame input (8.02), and the refiner reaches the lowest value (1.29). The smoothers differ in what they remove with the jitter. SmoothNet-WB and the Gaussian filter keep only 0.35 and 0.49 of the peak hand speed; the refiner keeps 0.98 and recovers 0.90 of the peaks, against 0.93 for the unsmoothed input. The single-rate refiner reaches jitter similar to the Gaussian filter (1.50) and keeps a similar peak amplitude (0.50), so the difference between the two refiner rows comes from the per-joint bandwidth. The One-Euro filter has the lowest pose errors on this benchmark but keeps less peak amplitude (0.66) at higher jitter (1.89). On a single sign-language clip where a Savitzky–Golay filter is tuned to match the refiner’s residual wrist jitter, the refiner keeps 99% of the per-frame peak finger speed and the matched filter 46% (Fig.6). Among the compared smoothers, the refiner therefore gives the lowest hand jitter while keeping nearly all hand-speed peak amplitude.

    Diagnostics on matched clip subsets (AppendixD) confirm the per-joint bandwidth as the source of peak preservation: fixed filters with one shared bandwidth and with per-joint bandwidths reach the same jitter, but only the latter keeps the hand-speed peaks. The same section reports robustness to dropped frames and lower frame rates.

    4.3 Body Accuracy and Smoothness on 3DPW and EMDB

    Table3 places CADENCE among published methods on the body-only protocols of 3DPW and EMDB. Accel values for other methods are taken from their papers, and dashes mark values that were not reported.

    CADENCE’s acceleration error (5.4 mm/s2) is lower than that of TCMR, MPS-Net, WHAM, and TRAM (6.7 to 7.4) and slightly higher than that of GVHMR and GENMO (5.0 and 5.2), which are body-only and do not predict hands or face. CADENCE has the lowest 3DPW PVE (62.6 mm). Its joint errors are higher than those of the strongest body-focused methods: on 3DPW, SAM 3D Body and NLF-L+fit reach 33.2 and 33.6 mm PA-MPJPE against CADENCE’s 40.2 mm, and DanceHMR reaches 53.6 mm MPJPE against 58.1 mm. On EMDB, CADENCE has the lowest PA-MPJPE (37.2 mm) but higher MPJPE and PVE than SAM 3D Body and DanceHMR, which points to absolute depth and placement, not articulation, as the weaker part of the estimate. These protocols score body joints only and do not measure the hand and face output.

    4.4 Expressive Whole-Body Accuracy on EHF

    Table4 reports EHF, the standard expressive whole-body SMPL-X benchmark. CADENCE has the lowest full-body P-MVE (25.7 mm), body P-MPJPE (20.6 mm), and hand P-MPJPE (8.3 mm) among the listed methods. Its hand mesh error (12.2 mm) is higher than that of PyMAF-X (10.2 mm), which uses dedicated hand crops and a separate hand branch, and Multi-HMR (10.8 mm); SMPLer-X-L has the lowest face P-MVE. Lower joint error with higher mesh error suggests that the pathway recovers finger articulation better than finger surface shape.

    4.5 Whole-Body Generalization on AGORA and UBody

    Table5 evaluates whole-body mesh error on AGORA validation and UBody. CADENCE has the lowest full-body PA-PVE and PVE on both datasets and the lowest UBody hand PA-PVE (5.9 mm). DanceHMR has the lowest UBody hand PVE (22.2 against 28.2 mm); since that metric is not Procrustes-aligned, it also scores wrist placement, which the CADENCE hand pathway does not change.

    4.6 Hand-Object Video on ARCTIC

    EHF, AGORA, and UBody use fitted or pseudo ground truth for hands. ARCTIC [10] provides accurate 3D hand ground truth on video of two-handed object manipulation, a setting absent from CADENCE’s training data. We evaluate the unchanged model on 8 held-out sequences (296 frames), using crops built from ground-truth joint boxes because ARCTIC’s own crops are too tight for a whole-body model. CADENCE reaches body and hand PA-MPJPE of 49.80 and 32.02 mm, well above its error on EHF, AGORA, and UBody. Close-range manipulation and object occlusion are outside the training distribution, and this result is consistent with the occlusion sensitivity measured on AGORA (Sec.4.8).

    4.7 Hand Pathway Ablation

    Table6 traces the hand pathway’s development on EHF. Body P-MPJPE is identical in every row, because each variant writes only finger rotations. A first version that re-encodes hand crops at high resolution and predicts a zero-initialized residual on the finger pose reduces hand P-MVE from 22.6 to 16.6 mm; adding FreiHand and HanCo changes EHF error by only 0.1 mm, since EHF hands are already covered by the pseudo-labelled training data. The final pathway of Sec.3.2 samples crop features at ViTPose hand keypoints, predicts the finger pose directly, and adds ReInterHand and HaMeR distillation; it reduces hand P-MVE to 12.2 mm and hand P-MPJPE from 14.5 to 8.3 mm. Because the last row changes several factors at once, it does not isolate any single one; AppendixC compares feature source and parameterization under a matched budget, and Fig.3 shows examples before and after the pathway.

    4.8 Runtime and Occlusion

    On one A100-80GB GPU in bf16, the per-frame estimator runs at 27.9 FPS at batch size 1 and 307.6 FPS at batch size 32. With the hand pathway, which encodes two extra crops per frame, the full system runs at 13.1 and 71.5 FPS. The temporal refiner processes a 32-frame window at about 6,900 FPS, so its cost is negligible, and peak memory stays below 4 GiB (Tab.19). Applications that do not need finger detail can disable the hand pathway and keep the per-frame rate.

    To measure sensitivity to occlusion, we split 500 AGORA validation samples by their annotated occlusion percentage, which on AGORA comes mostly from other people in the scene. Body PA-MPJPE rises from 32.87 mm at low occlusion (<20%, 224 samples) to 42.11 mm at medium (20–50%, 136 samples) and 57.64 mm at high occlusion (≥50%, 140 samples); the Pearson correlation between occlusion percentage and error is 0.539.

    4.9 Limitations

    CADENCE processes one tracked person per box and does not detect people or resolve identity in multi-person scenes. The temporal refiner runs offline on fixed-length windows, so it is not causal and cannot be used for streaming without modification. Global orientation and limb depth remain ambiguous under the weak-perspective camera, foreshortening, and self-occlusion, which is consistent with the gap between CADENCE’s MPJPE and PA-MPJPE on 3DPW and EMDB. Hands are the least stable region under motion blur, hand-object contact, and hand-hand occlusion, as the ARCTIC result shows, and the hand pathway depends on an external 2D keypoint detector. The sign-language dynamics metrics rely on pseudo ground truth. SectionF.5 summarizes failure modes.

    5 Conclusion

    CADENCE recovers whole-body SMPL-X motion from monocular video with a per-frame estimator, a shared-encoder hand pathway, and an offline temporal refiner that smooths each joint at its own learned rate. On 3DPW, the refiner lowers acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while improving PA-MPJPE, and on sign-language sequences it reaches the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping 0.98 of the hand-speed peak amplitude, where generic and single-rate smoothing keep 0.35 to 0.50. Body-only video benchmarks do not measure this second property, and our results suggest that whole-body video methods should be evaluated on hand dynamics as well as on body acceleration. A causal version of the refiner for streaming input, and evaluation on hand dynamics with accurate rather than pseudo ground truth, are the most direct next steps.

    Acknowledgements.

    The authors acknowledge the use of the IRIDIS X High Performance Computing Facility and the Southampton-Wolfson AI Research Machine (SWARM) GPU cluster, funded by the Wolfson Foundation, at the University of Southampton.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation and Reproducibility Details

    This section lists which components are frozen and trained, the supervision used at each training stage, and the evaluation protocols.

    A.1 Model Inventory and Parameter Accounting

    Table7 summarizes the main components of CADENCE. The C-RADIOv4 encoder is shared by the per-frame estimator and the high-resolution hand pathway. The backbone weights remain frozen; in the final adaptation stage, only lightweight LoRA adapter weights are trained. The temporal refiner is trained after the per-frame estimator and hand pathway are fixed.

    Parameter accounting.

    Table8 reports the parameter count for each component. The frozen C-RADIOv4-SO400M encoder contains 472.35M parameters and is not updated during the main training stages. The per-frame SMPL-X estimator contains 51.8M trainable parameters, including the structured decoder, prediction heads, spatial feedback modules, and lightweight adaptation parameters where enabled. The high-resolution hand pathway adds 21.0M trainable parameters. The temporal refiner is lightweight, adding only 1.88M parameters. Thus, the per-frame and hand modules contain 72.8M trainable parameters, and full CADENCE including the temporal refiner contains 74.7M trainable parameters.

    Per-frame estimator.

    The per-frame estimator takes a person crop, resized to 384×288, and predicts an initial SMPL-X parameter vector. We use C-RADIOv4-SO400M as the shared visual encoder and extract multi-scale visual features. Early features preserve local spatial detail, middle features capture limb structure, and late features provide semantic context. Each feature map is projected to the decoder width before cross-attention.

    The decoder uses structured query tokens rather than a single global regression token. Separate tokens represent camera, shape, global orientation, body joints, left hand, right hand, jaw, and expression. Keypoint tokens represent the projected articulated body in image space. After each decoder layer, lightweight heads predict intermediate SMPL-X updates. The current SMPL-X estimate is converted to joints by forward kinematics, projected to the image, and used to update keypoint-token attention and local feature sampling in later decoder layers. This creates an iterative spatial-feedback loop in which the model refines both the parameter estimate and the image locations it uses for evidence.

    A.2 SMPL-X Parameterization

    CADENCE predicts a 341-dimensional SMPL-X parameter vector for each frame:

    pₜ=[θᵇᵒᵈʸₜ,θˡʰₜ,θʳʰₜ,θʲᵃʷₜ,ψₜ,θᵒʳₜ,βₜ,cₜ],

    where body pose contains 21 body joints in 6D rotation form (21×6=126), the left and right hands contain 15 joints each (15×6=90 per hand), the jaw is represented by one 6D rotation, expression has 10 dimensions, global orientation is one 6D rotation, body shape has 10 dimensions, and the weak-perspective camera has 3 dimensions. Rotations use the continuous 6D representation during learning and are projected to valid rotation matrices before SMPL-X forward kinematics.

    A.3 High-Resolution Hand Pathway

    Section3.2 describes the pathway. FreiHand and HanCo contain right hands only; horizontal-flip augmentation exposes the shared branch to both orientations, so no separate left-hand branch or explicit mirroring step is needed. Figure3 shows examples before and after the pathway.

    A.4 Temporal Refiner Details

    The temporal refiner is trained after the per-frame and hand components are fixed. It operates on stored per-frame CADENCE predictions rather than raw images. Each SMPL-X joint rotation is treated as a token over time. Tokens are first updated with temporal self-attention and then with attention restricted to the SMPL-X kinematic tree, allowing information to pass between each joint, its parent, and its children.

    Each joint chooses its bandwidth per frame from a bank of four learned zero-phase kernels, initialised as the identity and Gaussians with σ=1,2,4 frames. The selector’s per-joint prior starts body and global-orientation joints on the σ=2 kernel and the jaw, forearms, and hands on the identity kernel, and its learned weights are zero-initialised, so training starts from a fixed part-rate filter. Every kernel is symmetric and non-negative with unit sum, so the output cannot lag or amplify the input. The filtered rotations are re-orthonormalised before SMPL-X forward kinematics. The refiner has 1.88M parameters, uses pose only, and runs on 32-frame windows with a hop of 16 frames and Hann-weighted overlap.

    A.5 Losses and Training Schedule

    The per-frame estimator is supervised at each decoder layer using rotation, joint, vertex, 2D keypoint, camera, shape, and expression losses:

    L_pf=λᵣₒₜLᵣₒₜ+λ_j3dL_j3d+λ_j2dL_j2d+λᵥLᵥ
    +λ_camL_cam+λ_βL_β+λ_ψL_ψ.

    The hand pathway adds losses on finger rotations, hand joints, and hand vertices:

    L_hand=λₕᵣₒₜLₕᵣₒₜ+λₕⱼLₕⱼ+λₕᵥLₕᵥ.

    The temporal refiner is trained with reconstruction, velocity, acceleration, and do-no-harm objectives:

    Lₜₑₘₚ=L_pf+λ_dynL_dyn+λ_dnhL_dnh.

    The do-no-harm term is a hinge loss that penalizes temporal predictions when they increase reconstruction error relative to the frozen per-frame estimate.

    Training stages.

    CADENCE is trained in stages so that each module has a clear role. Table11 summarizes the training sequence.

    Optimization and augmentation.

    Training uses AdamW with mixed-precision acceleration. The decoder and prediction heads use a higher learning rate than the LoRA parameters during the final adaptation stage. We apply standard image augmentations including random scale, translation, horizontal flip, color jitter, and synthetic occlusion where appropriate. For video clips, we sample fixed-length windows and apply temporal subsampling during training to improve robustness to different motion speeds.

    A.6 Training Datasets

    CADENCE is trained from a mixture of whole-body SMPL-X data, in-the-wild video data, 2D keypoint supervision, and real hand-3D data. Whole-body datasets provide the main SMPL-X supervision. COCO-WholeBody and MPII provide additional 2D keypoint supervision. FreiHand and HanCo provide real hand-3D supervision for the canonical hand training mode. The temporal refiner is trained on clips from available video sources using stored per-frame CADENCE predictions.

    Sampling.

    During per-frame training, batches are sampled from a mixture of whole-body 3D datasets and 2D keypoint datasets. Loss masks ensure that each sample only contributes to losses for which annotations are available. During hand-pathway training, whole-body samples and canonical hand-only samples are mixed so that the hand branch learns both body-context hand refinement and detailed real hand articulation. During temporal training, the image encoder and per-frame decoder are frozen and the temporal refiner is trained from stored predictions, ensuring that controlled studies change only the temporal processing stage.

    A.7 Evaluation Protocols

    EHF is evaluated with Procrustes-aligned full-body mesh error and regional hand/face metrics. AGORA and UBody use whole-body mesh metrics with full-body and regional breakdowns. 3DPW uses the standard 14-joint body protocol, and EMDB uses the 24-joint body protocol. Acceleration error is computed from the difference of predicted and ground-truth central second differences over valid consecutive frames at the declared FPS.

    CADENCE predicts whole-body SMPL-X, but 3DPW and EMDB evaluate only the body quantities specified by their protocols. These benchmarks therefore do not measure hand accuracy, absolute depth, or global placement.

    Appendix B Extended Benchmark Results

    This section extends Tab.3 with additional 3DPW methods and compares SAM 3D Body on the expressive benchmarks.

    B.1 3DPW Extended Results

    3DPW is a body-centric benchmark. Although CADENCE predicts full SMPL-X parameters, evaluation follows the body protocol used by prior work. Table14 groups methods by representation to make the comparison clearer: whole-body SMPL-X methods, body-focused per-frame or fitting methods, and body-only temporal methods. Acceleration errors are listed in Tab.3.

    SAM 3D Body on EHF, AGORA, and UBody.

    Table3 compares SAM 3D Body [44] with CADENCE on 3DPW and EMDB; here we extend the comparison to EHF, AGORA, and UBody. SAM 3D Body predicts a Momentum Human Rig mesh, a different topology from SMPL-X with no public vertex regressor to SMPL-X, so we compare body joints instead: SAM 3D Body’s own shipped correspondence from its 70-keypoint output to the 13-joint LSP layout, paired with the same 13 SMPL-X joints via the standard SMPL-X joint regressor (7 upper-body joints only on UBody, whose close-up framing leaves hips, knees, and ankles out of frame in many clips). On this joint protocol, SAM 3D Body reaches 38.06/59.94/53.77 mm body PA-MPJPE on EHF/AGORA/UBody, next to CADENCE’s own published number on each dataset’s own protocol of 20.58/42.4/29.25 mm (EHF: 14-joint PA-MPJPE; AGORA/UBody: vertex PA-PVE). These are different metrics on different joint sets, shown for context, not as a matched comparison.

    Appendix C Hand Pathway Diagnostics

    All variants in this section use the same per-frame whole-body estimator, shared encoder, and EHF protocol, and change only the hand pathway. Because the pathway writes only finger rotations, body metrics are identical across variants.

    Table15 compares design choices under an identical single-stage training budget, with the final pathway from Tab.6 as reference. The feature source has the largest effect: sampling late-layer crop features gives 12.89 mm hand P-MVE and 8.72 mm hand P-MPJPE, against 14.93 and 10.07 mm with early-layer features only. The parameterization matters less: removing the zero-initialized residual or predicting the full hand pose directly changes either error by less than 0.5 mm.

    C.1 Per-Finger Diagnostics on Sign Language

    Table16 reports per-finger wrist-aligned PA-MPJPE on an internal UBody sign-language test split with 18,130 samples, chosen because signing contains frequent and varied hand articulation. Errors are largest at the fingertips, especially of the thumb and index finger, where opposition, self-occlusion, and fast motion make articulation hardest. CADENCE has lower error than SMPLer-X-H [5] and Multi-HMR-L [3] on every finger, with hand PA-MPVPE of 6.58 mm against 7.63 and 7.93 mm, and the fraction of joints within 5 mm (F@5 mm) is 7 to 9 points higher.

    Appendix D Temporal Refiner Diagnostics

    This section complements Sec.4.2. All variants start from the same stored per-frame CADENCE predictions, evaluation clips, and metric implementation, and change only the temporal stage.

    D.1 Single-Rate, Multi-Rate, and Component Ablations

    Table17 uses matched 32-frame clip subsets of 3DPW and SignAvatars/How2Sign, with identical stored inputs within each subset. The first block compares fixed filters with one shared bandwidth (single-rate) and with per-joint bandwidths (multi-rate). The second block removes one component at a time from an earlier version of the refiner, which added a residual rotation correction gated by a learned HOLD/STROKE phase on hand and jaw joints; the released refiner (Sec.3.4) does not use these components. Clip pools and conditioning signals differ from Sec.4.2, so absolute values are not comparable with Tabs.1 and 2.

    The single-rate and multi-rate filters have identical body accuracy, acceleration error, and jitter, but the multi-rate filter keeps more of the hand motion: Peak-R rises from 0.63 to 0.76 and Peak-A from 0.55 to 0.63. At equal smoothness, the per-joint bandwidth is therefore what preserves hand-speed peaks.

    In the earlier refiner, the component rows change body accuracy and acceleration error by at most 0.06 mm and 0.03 mm/s2. Removing the phase gate, the do-no-harm term, or the residual’s conditioning leaves all metrics within 0.01, which is why the released refiner drops the residual and the gate and keeps the filter selection. Removing kinematic-tree attention raises Peak-A from 0.61 to 0.74 at higher jitter (0.69 against 0.64).

    D.2 Low-Frame-Rate and Missing-Frame Robustness

    Temporal filters can be sensitive to frame rate and missing observations. We therefore evaluate CADENCE temporal refinement under simple test-time degradations: temporal downsampling and random frame dropping. In each case, the same per-frame model is used and only the temporal input sequence is degraded. For downsampling, we evaluate on the retained frames. For missing frames, dropped frames are masked during temporal refinement and metrics are computed on frames with available ground truth.

    The results show graceful degradation rather than collapse. Random frame dropping is handled robustly: PA-MPJPE rises from 40.2 to 40.8 mm when a quarter of frames are removed. Temporal downsampling is more demanding because the inter-frame interval grows, which both widens the motion gap the refiner must bridge and increases the measured finite-difference acceleration. Even so, accuracy degrades smoothly, with PA-MPJPE changing from 40.2 to 45.0 mm from full to one-third frame rate. Peak-A remains near or above 1.0, indicating that expressive hand-motion peaks are not collapsed under these degradations. Peak-A values above 1 indicate peak hand speeds above the reference.

    D.3 Rotation Interpolation and Temporal Filtering Details

    CADENCE applies temporal processing to articulated SMPL-X rotations rather than to unconstrained 3D joint coordinates. Rotations are represented using the continuous 6D representation during learning, converted to valid rotation matrices before forward kinematics, and re-orthonormalized after temporal updates. The deployed temporal model does not require linear interpolation of reduced-rate 6D rotations back to the full frame rate; the per-joint temporal filters operate over the full input window with different effective bandwidths for different joint groups.

    For diagnostic variants that explicitly resample time, interpolation is applied on valid rotations rather than on arbitrary unnormalized 6D vectors. In practice, we convert 6D rotations to rotation matrices, interpolate rotations using a rotation-aware procedure, and then convert back to the representation used by the model. This avoids treating the 6D representation as an unconstrained Euclidean signal and prevents invalid rotations from entering the SMPL-X forward kinematics.

    Appendix E Runtime Accounting

    Table19 reports throughput for the main inference configurations and the dominant runtime components. All measurements are obtained on one A100-80GB GPU using bf16 inference. Batch-1 throughput measures low-latency inference, while batch-32 throughput measures batched throughput.

    The base per-frame estimator processes the full-person crop and predicts whole-body SMPL-X parameters. Enabling the high-resolution hand pathway adds two hand-crop encoder passes, improving finger articulation but reducing throughput. The temporal refiner is inexpensive relative to image encoding, running at approximately 6,900 FPS for a 32-frame window.

    Interpretation.

    CADENCE is not bottlenecked by the temporal refiner. Runtime is dominated by visual encoding and, when enabled, the high-resolution hand pathway. This is expected: the hand pathway deliberately trades throughput for improved finger articulation by reusing the same high-capacity encoder on hand crops. Applications that require maximum throughput can run the per-frame estimator with the temporal refiner and skip the hand pathway.

    Appendix F Additional Qualitative Results

    This section describes layer-by-layer decoder refinement, a comparison with whole-body baselines, temporal examples, and failure cases. The corresponding figures are collected in AppendixG.

    F.1 Whole-Body Qualitative Results

    Figure4 shows additional CADENCE reconstructions on diverse 3DPW sequences, visualized as a layer-by-layer refinement progression. The structured decoder starts from a coarse initial estimate and progressively updates the mesh and joint locations across its six layers using iterative spatial feedback. The examples include walking, running, stair climbing, and seated poses with partial occlusion. They illustrate how the decoder refines global body structure and projected joint alignment over successive layers.

    F.2 Multi-Baseline Qualitative Comparison on Expressive Scenes

    Figure5 compares CADENCE qualitatively with recent whole-body or whole-human recovery methods on expressive UBody scenes. We compare against SMPLer-X [5], Multi-HMR [3], and SAM 3D Body [44]. To make the visual comparison controlled, all methods are run in single-person mode using the same detected person box where possible. Each panel shows the full-person overlay and a zoom strip containing the face and both hands cropped from the same image regions.

    The methods use different representations and processing assumptions in expressive regions such as hands and face. SAM 3D Body uses a different mesh representation from SMPL-X. We therefore show the panels only as qualitative context and avoid topology-specific or hand-accuracy claims. CADENCE’s high-resolution branch is finger-only and retains a whole-body SMPL-X output.

    F.3 Temporal Consistency Examples

    Figure6 compares per-frame predictions, a generic temporal smoother, and the deployed CADENCE temporal refiner on a sign-language clip with rapid finger articulation. Per-frame predictions exhibit large frame-to-frame acceleration. To isolate what is being smoothed rather than only how much, we tune the generic Savitzky–Golay smoother so that its residual wrist jitter matches the CADENCE refiner’s (2.5 vs. 2.6 mm/frame2). At this matched stability level, the generic smoother attenuates the hand-motion peaks, whereas CADENCE preserves them more closely: on this clip, CADENCE retains 99% of the per-frame peak finger speed compared with 46% for the matched generic smoother.

    F.4 Consecutive-Frame Visualizations Across Diverse Activities

    Figure7 shows CADENCE reconstructions on clips spanning different activity types, including dynamic athletic motion, classroom interaction, and expressive sign-language sequences. For each clip, consecutive frames are shown from left to right with the recovered SMPL-X overlay. These examples show how the recovered body and hand configurations evolve across neighbouring frames in diverse scenes.

    Videos.

    Video results, including continuous two-handed sign-language sequences, are on the project page, https://keniel123.github.io/cadence.

    F.5 Failure Cases

    Table20 summarizes the main failure modes, their likely causes, and possible future directions. These examples are consistent with the limitations in Sec.4.9. The most common failure modes arise from monocular ambiguity, severe occlusion, unusual camera viewpoints, motion blur, inaccurate person boxes, and difficult hand-object or hand-hand interactions.

    Appendix G Qualitative Figures

item.title: 面部管线要 FACS 可控的参数化头模，但高质量扫描太贵：FACET 说数据加不动，就改架构 ｜ FACET: A Data-Efficient Regional Parametric Head Model
item.description:
一句话：生产级面部管线要的是「表现力强、FACS 可控、能在一小池固定身份上训出来」。

要点：

  • 需求侧很具体：生产环境的面部管线需要参数化头模**表现力强、可由 FACS 控制，并且能建立在一小批固定身份之上**
  • 硬约束：更多训练身份当然更好，但**高质量配准的头模扫描采集非常昂贵**；当数据无法扩展时，剩下的杠杆就是**架构**
  • FACET 因此通过架构设计，把一个固定的身份池用足——并做**分区（regional）**建模，而不是整体一张网格

为什么值得看：数字人与角色面部的质量瓶颈常常是「扫描数据不够」。在数据不能扩的情况下用架构补，这条给出的正是这种受限条件下的解法——对没有扫描棚、只有少量高质量头模的团队尤其现实。

中文摘要：生产环境的面部管线需要参数化头模具备三个特性：足够的表现力、可由面部动作编码系统（FACS）控制，以及能够在一小批固定身份上构建。更多训练身份当然总有帮助，但高质量的配准头模扫描采集成本很高；当扩大数据规模不是一个选项时，剩下的杠杆就是架构。FACET 因此通过架构设计，把一个固定的身份池尽可能用足，并采用分区（regional）建模的方式来提升表现力与可控性。对缺少扫描棚、只能依赖少量高质量头模的团队，这条提供的正是受限条件下的现实解法。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-23

本期推送：2026-11-24

FACET: A Data-Efficient Regional Parametric Head Model

© cc

Abstract.

Production face pipelines need parametric head models that are expressive, FACS-controllable, and buildable on a small, fixed pool of identities. More training identities would always help, but high-quality registered head scans are expensive to capture; when scaling the data is not an option, the remaining lever is architecture. We present FACET, a parametric head model that makes the most of a fixed identity pool through architectural locality rather than more scans, and makes three contributions, each isolated against a matched global-PCA ablation on our own topology, training set, and normalization. (1) A regional identity decomposition into 16 anatomical regions bypasses the N-1 rank ceiling of a global PCA, driving held-out neutral-fit error from a 1.95 mm floor down to 0.23 mm on the same training identities. (2) A learned FACS action-unit expression model with per-identity neural personalization not only stays FACS-controllable but beats a properly-regularized global expression PCA at every component count—refuting the argument that FACS is too overcomplete to fit. (3) A dedicated neck/shoulder region reduces pose leakage into the pose-invariant upper face during unposing. Together, these show that architectural locality is the effective lever for a production head model under a fixed identity budget.

Keywords:

parametric head model, 3D morphable model, regional PCA, FACS action units, blendshape personalization, facial animation, unposing ††cc-license: by-nc-nd

1. Introduction

Parametric head models underpin production facial pipelines: a compact, riggable, DCC-compatible representation an artist can fit, edit, and animate. The dominant recipe, exemplified by FLAME [(Li et al., 2017)], learns global PCA identity and expression bases from a large scan corpus, and increasing fidelity has largely meant acquiring more scans—LSFM [(Booth et al., 2018)] reaches nearly ten thousand identities. For a production studio, though, high-quality registered head scans are expensive to capture, so the identity pool is a fixed set of a few hundred subjects rather than the thousands used by large-scale models. The question is therefore how to extract the most from a small pool.

When the identity pool is fixed, a global identity PCA on N subjects spans at most N-1 modes and no scan quality lifts that ceiling. The remaining lever is architecture: how much a model extracts from the identities it has. We substantiate this across the three axes of a complete head model with FACET. First, FACET decomposes identity into 16 anatomical regions, each with its own PCA basis blended by Laplacian handles; because each region is supported by the same subjects but spans a smaller patch, it exposes more usable identity dimensions than a basis capped at N-1 and improves held-out generalization—data efficiency, not merely compact editing. Second, it drives expression with learned FACS action-unit blendshapes personalized per identity by a small neural network, staying FACS-controllable while reusing an existing FACS-annotated capture deck. Third, it adds a dedicated neck/shoulder region that confines articulation during unposing, reducing pose leakage into the pose-invariant upper face.

2. Related Work

Identity and regional shape models.

Linear 3D morphable models capture identity variation with a single global PCA basis, and the dominant strategy for increasing fidelity has been to acquire more scans: FLAME [(Li et al., 2017)] learns its shape space from thousands of head scans, and LSFM [(Booth et al., 2018)] scales this to nearly ten thousand identities. These works motivate regionality through animation control, editing, or representational power. FACET instead frames regional PCA over 16 anatomical regions as a data-efficiency mechanism that bypasses the N-1 rank ceiling, and measures the resulting improvement in held-out generalization on a small identity pool.

FLAME [(Li et al., 2017)] explicitly rejects a FACS parameterization as overcomplete and adopts an orthonormal global expression PCA, an argument that shaped much subsequent work. FACS-driven bases nonetheless remain the lingua franca of production: ICT-FaceKit [(Li et al., 2020)] pairs hand-crafted action-unit blendshapes with a global identity PCA, and FaceScape [(Yang et al., 2020)] derives per-subject FACS blendshapes from a bilinear model fit to twenty captured expressions per subject. 3. Method

FACET is a production parametric head model on a single quad-dominant topology of 8,447 vertices, comprising three components: a regional identity model, a FACS action-unit expression model with per-identity neural personalization, and a head/neck/shoulder articulation with unposing.

A global identity PCA trained on N registered neutral scans spans at most N-1 modes. On a fixed identity pool, this rank ceiling—not scan resolution—bounds representable identity detail. FACET instead partitions the head into 16 anatomical regions and fits separate position- and Laplacian-coordinate PCA bases per region. Because each region draws its modes from the same N identities but spans a lower-dimensional patch of the surface, each region contributes up to 2(N-1) data-supported coefficients. For the 347-identity training pool used here, the regional ceiling is therefore 16·2·(347-1)=11,072 coefficients, rather than N-1=346 for one global PCA—data efficiency, not merely compact editing.

Unlike a global model, which forms vertices by adding shape offsets to a template, FACET reassembles the regions with a sparse linear solve. Each region’s PCA predicts target position and Laplacian coordinates; the head vertices p are recovered as the weighted least-squares fit

(1)

\beginsplitp^⋆(β)&=*arg minₚ \lVertW_L (Lp-δ)\rVert²+λ²\lVertW_P (p-ξ)\rVert², δ(β^L)&=μ_L+∑ᵣ₌₁¹⁶D^Lᵣ β^Lᵣ, ξ(β^P)=μ_P+∑ᵣ₌₁¹⁶D^Pᵣ β^Pᵣ,\endsplit

where L is the cotangent Laplacian; D^Lᵣ,β^Lᵣ and D^Pᵣ,β^Pᵣ are the Laplacian- and position-coordinate PCA bases and coefficients for region r; and λ is the main soft-position weight, fixed at 0.58 for all reported results. Per-vertex weights W_L and W_P overlap across boundaries. Because the overlapping weights are built into the system rather than applied after the fact, the assembled head is seamless and remains a single editable mesh [(Botsch and Sorkine, 2008)]. The hash encoders and MLPs use the fully-fused Instant-NGP [(Müller et al., 2022)] implementation, keeping personalization practical at interactive fitting rates. Formally, the expression offset at a vertex x is

(2)

\beginsplitE(w,β)=&∑ₐ₌₁^Awₐ ℕ_θ (φ(x), (γ+1)⊙Bₐ+τ, β) &+∑ₖ₌₁⁴gₖ(w) Cₖ(x;β),\endsplit

where wₐ activates FACS action unit a, Bₐ is its learnable blendshape, φ(x) the concatenated position/Laplacian hash-grid code, (γ,τ) the FiLM parameters regressed from φ(x), ℕ_θ the main MLP conditioned on the fitted shape coefficients β, and gₖ(w) the combo encoder driving a geometry-conditioned basis Cₖ. The combo term handles AU-combination correctives: a small encoder maps AU weights to K=4 coefficients, while the geometry-conditioned decoder (independent of the AU weights) emits a per-identity combo basis; the two meet only in a final linear combination. Shared protocol.

All variants use the FACET topology, an identical eye-placement normalization, and the same training pool of 347 consented identities; every weight in any compared model is estimated from this pool only. We evaluate on disjoint held-out test sets: 59 distinct neutral scans for identity (E1), and the same 59 identities across 19 expressions each for expression (E2). We report per-vertex vertex-to-vertex (V2V) error in mm on the held-out sets. For each claim we compare against a matched global-PCA ablation—not the released FLAME model—that shares this setup and differs only in the architectural variable under test.

E1: regional decomposition is data-efficient.

Figure 4 plots held-out neutral-fit V2V error against the total identity coefficient count. Both AU variants beat global PCA at everyK, including K=1000 where PCA has the most capacity: mean fit error settles at 1.67 mm (A) versus 1.56 mm (B) and 1.47 mm (C), with C

E3: neck/shoulder region reduces pose leakage.

The pose-invariant upper face (forehead and eye orbits) should not move when a model unposes neck and shoulder articulation. A global-PCA head model has no localized neck/shoulder split, so fitting it to posed neutral scans leaks pose into the upper-face identity geometry. Whole-head displacement is comparable (1.54 vs 1.58 mm mean), so the gap is specifically pose leaking into the upper face (Fig. 5).

Ethics and likeness.

All captures were collected from participants under informed-consent agreements.

When the identity pool is fixed, architectural locality is the lever: regional decomposition escapes the global rank ceiling, personalized FACS AUs beat global expression PCA while staying controllable, and a neck/shoulder region blocks pose leakage into the upper face.

Limitations.

Our evaluation uses small held-out pools (59 identities; 59×19 expressions), reflecting the fixed identity pool that motivates the work.

Conclusion.

FACET shows that when more scans are out of reach, a production head model on a fixed identity pool is well served by architectural locality—regional identity, personalized FACS expression, and localized articulation—with each choice validated by a matched ablation that isolates it.

item.content:encoded:
一句话：生产级面部管线要的是「表现力强、FACS 可控、能在一小池固定身份上训出来」。

要点：

  • 需求侧很具体：生产环境的面部管线需要参数化头模**表现力强、可由 FACS 控制，并且能建立在一小批固定身份之上**
  • 硬约束：更多训练身份当然更好，但**高质量配准的头模扫描采集非常昂贵**；当数据无法扩展时，剩下的杠杆就是**架构**
  • FACET 因此通过架构设计，把一个固定的身份池用足——并做**分区（regional）**建模，而不是整体一张网格

为什么值得看：数字人与角色面部的质量瓶颈常常是「扫描数据不够」。在数据不能扩的情况下用架构补，这条给出的正是这种受限条件下的解法——对没有扫描棚、只有少量高质量头模的团队尤其现实。

中文摘要：生产环境的面部管线需要参数化头模具备三个特性：足够的表现力、可由面部动作编码系统（FACS）控制，以及能够在一小批固定身份上构建。更多训练身份当然总有帮助，但高质量的配准头模扫描采集成本很高；当扩大数据规模不是一个选项时，剩下的杠杆就是架构。FACET 因此通过架构设计，把一个固定的身份池尽可能用足，并采用分区（regional）建模的方式来提升表现力与可控性。对缺少扫描棚、只能依赖少量高质量头模的团队，这条提供的正是受限条件下的现实解法。

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

(3) A dedicated neck/shoulder region reduces pose leakage into the pose-invariant upper face during unposing.
